docs.title: finitevolX
docs.text: Finite volume operators for JAX on Arakawa C-grids.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: finitevolX provides a suite of finite-volume operators for computational fluid dynamics on staggered Arakawa C-grids, implemented in JAX for high-performance, differentiable numerical simulations.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Staggered Grid Support: Full Arakawa C-grid implementation with T, U, V, and X grid points
  • JAX Integration: Built on JAX for automatic differentiation and GPU/TPU acceleration
  • Modular Operators: Clean separation of advection, diffusion, interpolation, reconstruction, vorticity, and elliptic solvers
  • WENO Schemes: High-order WENO reconstruction methods (3rd and 5th order)
  • Boundary Conditions: Flexible boundary condition handling with ghost cells
  • Type Safety: Full type hints with jaxtyping for array shapes

docs.title: From PyPI
docs.text: pip install finitevolx

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/jejjohnson/finitevolX
cd finitevolX
pip install -e .

docs.title: With uv (recommended for development and examples)
docs.text: uv sync --all-extras

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
import jax.numpy as jnp
from finitevolx import Advection2D, CartesianGrid2D

# Create a 2D Arakawa C-grid
grid = CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(64, 64, 1.0, 1.0)

# Initialize advection operator
advection = Advection2D(grid=grid)

# Create velocity and scalar fields (including one ghost-cell ring)
u = jnp.zeros((66, 66))
v = jnp.zeros((66, 66))
h = jnp.ones((66, 66))

# Compute the advective tendency -div(h * u_vec)
dh_dt = advection(h, u, v)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
See the scripts/ directory for complete double-gyre examples that all use the current class-based API and save sampled fields to Zarr instead of opening live plots:

  • scripts/swm_linear.py - Linear shallow-water model
  • scripts/shallow_water.py - Nonlinear shallow-water model
  • scripts/qg_1p5_layer.py - 1.5-layer quasi-geostrophic model

The Examples page shows the saved before/after figures and the artifacts written by each script.

docs.title: ⚠ BREAKING CHANGES
docs.text:
• coriolis: Coriolis2D / Coriolis3D outputs change for spatially varying f (by O(dy^2 * grad f) in the interior); uniform-f results are unchanged up to round-off. With a mask, velocities on dry faces are ignored (Coriolis3D included). The Coriolis2D.interp attribute is removed.
  • diagnostics: vertical_velocity returns [Nz, Ny, Nx] (was [Nz+1, Ny, Nx]) with w[k] the top face of T[k]; old w[k+1] on the physical levels is now w[k]. The z-ghost slabs of u and v are no longer integrated. Passing a raw float mask is deprecated in favour of Mask3D.
  • boundary: wall_boundaries(field, "u") / ("v") now zero the east / north wall face (index -2) and write -field[-3] to the outside slot -1 instead of zeroing index -1.
  • advection: WENO and TVD outputs change slightly (at most 4e-7 relative on the golden fields, more on fields far from O(1) amplitude, which were previously computed with an amplitude-dependent scheme).
  • advection: masked Advection1D/2D/3D and SphericalAdvection2D/3D tendencies change at coastal cells: no flux crosses a dry face, and naive / upwind1/2/3 / weno7 / weno9 no longer read land values (they fall back to narrower stencils near the coast). Unmasked outputs are unchanged.
  • diffusion: Diffusion2D/3D, diffusion_2d, their fluxes and SphericalDiffusion2D/3D return different values for a spatially varying kappa: each face now uses the mean of its two cells instead of the western / southern cell. With wall="open" both wall faces average the edge and ghost kappa (before: the west / south wall face used the ghost kappa and the east / north one the edge kappa). Scalar and constant kappa are unchanged.
  • diffusion: masked BiharmonicDiffusion2D/3D and SphericalBiharmonicDiffusion2D/3D return different values at wet cells within two cells of land: the coast is now no-flux for h and lap(h) and land values no longer enter the tendency. Unmasked results are unchanged.
  • multigrid: n_coarse is removed from build_multigrid_solver and MultigridSolver (the bottom solve is exact). The defaults change to n_pre = n_post = 3 and omega = 0.8 (were 6, 6, 0.95), MultigridLevel stores a stencil instead of cx / cy / wall, and make_multigrid_preconditioner raises for n_pre != n_post.
  • multigrid: build_multigrid_solver now defaults to bc="dirichlet". Callers solving a T-point pressure / free-surface problem with zero normal flux (e.g. the helm_solve of barotropic_filter) must pass bc="neumann" to keep the previous operator.
  • solvers: pressure_from_divergence(method="cg") now solves the Neumann problem by default, and with bc="dst" puts p = 0 on the cell faces (the old cell-centre Dirichlet result is gone). pressure_from_divergence no longer accepts method="capacitance", known_values or known_mask. method="capacitance" and known values require bc="dst"; method="cg" with bc="fft" (and bc="dct" for the streamfunction) raises.
  • solvers: method="spectral" results change for every streamfunction_from_vorticity / pv_inversion / pressure_from_divergence call: the wrappers take the full [Ny, Nx] array and return zeros on the ghost ring (and on the psi wall nodes); do not slice the interior by hand. Known values (known_values= and non-zero Dirichlet1D faces) now sit on the coast ring (the dry wall nodes) instead of the inner wet ring, every wet cell is solved for, and SolveDomain.all_known / effective_mask change accordingly. bc.mask with method="spectral", and non-zero Dirichlet faces or spectral known values on pressure_from_divergence, now raise; so do non-zero Dirichlet faces on a Mask2D whose outer coast is not on the four walls.

docs.title: Breaking changes — grid and mask submodule restructure (#207, #208)
docs.text:
The internal _src/grid/ and _src/mask/ packages were reorganised to support a layered abstraction over coordinate systems and grid dimensions. Public-API renames are listed below; users who imported through the top-level finitevolx namespace need to update class names but no import-path changes.

Grid module (refactor: restructure into base / cartesian / spherical / cylindrical layout)

  • ArakawaCGrid1D / 2D / 3D (the old concrete classes) → renamed to CartesianGrid1D / 2D / 3D.
  • SphericalArakawaCGrid2D / 3D → renamed to SphericalGrid2D / 3D. These are now siblings of CartesianGrid* under a common CurvilinearGrid* base, not subclasses.
  • The names ArakawaCGrid1D / 2D / 3D are reused as a new abstract topology layer (just Nx, Ny, Nz).
  • New abstract layer CurvilinearGrid1D / 2D / 3D adds the uniform metric (Lx, Ly, Lz, dx, dy, dz).
  • New CylindricalGrid stub (TODO).
  • Path moves: _src/grid/cgrid_mask.py → _src/mask/cgrid_mask.py, _src/grid/constants.py → _src/utils/constants.py.

Mask module (refactor: split into base / cartesian / spherical / cylindrical)

  • ArakawaCGridMask → renamed to Mask2D.
  • New Mask1D and Mask3D concrete classes. Mask3D includes a full vertical face mask (w) — see below.
  • StencilCapability → split into StencilCapability1D / 2D / 3D.
  • _src/mask/cgrid_mask.py → split into _src/mask/{base,cartesian}.py with TODO stubs at _src/mask/{spherical,cylindrical}.py.
  • New _src/mask/utils.py with public n-D-aware mask construction primitives: pool_bool, h_from_pooled, dilate_mask, count_contiguous, make_sponge.

Mask2D field renames (frees up w for the 3-D vertical face mask):

Old name New name w xy_corner (lenient) psi xy_corner_strict (strict) not_w, not_psi not_xy_corner, not_xy_corner_strict w_valid xy_corner_valid w_vertical_bound xy_corner_y_wall w_horizontal_bound xy_corner_x_wall w_cornerout_bound xy_corner_convex psi_irrbound_xids xy_corner_strict_irrbound_cols psi_irrbound_yids xy_corner_strict_irrbound_rows

The last pair also fixes a long-standing naming bug: the old _xids field stored column indices and _yids stored row indices.

Removed:

  • Mask2D.distbound1 / distbound2 / distbound3plus properties — these were exact aliases for ind_coast / ind_near_coast / ind_ocean.
  • visualize_masks() function — plotting code does not belong in the library. Equivalent inline code is available in docs/notebooks/demo_masks.py.

docs.title: Advection Operators
docs.text: This page covers the theory behind the advection operators in finitevolX: the flux-form finite-volume discretisation, what the inputs mean (cell averages), the formal order of the scheme, the available reconstruction schemes (upwind, TVD, WENO) with their measured accuracy, the mask, wall and spherical semantics, and a decision guide built from those measurements.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Advection moves scalar and vector fields along the flow. In the flux form (also called the conservative or divergence form), the transport of a scalar \(q\) by a velocity \(\mathbf{u}\) is written

\[ rac{\partial q}{\partial t} + abla \cdot (\mathbf{u}\,q) = 0 \]

Using \( abla \cdot (\mathbf{u}\,q) = \mathbf{u} \cdot abla q + q\, abla \cdot \mathbf{u}\), the advective form and flux form differ by a term proportional to \( abla \cdot \mathbf{u}\). Flux form is preferred because it:

  1. Conserves mass exactly in the discrete setting (telescoping property).
  2. Handles non-divergent flow correctly without an extra correction term.
  3. Is the natural form for finite-volume methods.

On the Arakawa C-grid, the scalar \(q\) lives at T-points and the velocities \(u\), \(v\) live at U/V-points (face centres). The tendency is computed at T-points; which T-points are written depends on the wall mode (see Walls, write region and periodic halos).

docs.title: Inputs Are Cell Averages
docs.text:
The operators are finite-volume schemes: h (the tracer argument) holds the cell average

\[ \bar{q}_{j,i} = \frac{1}{\Delta x\,\Delta y}\int_{y_{j-1/2}}^{y_{j+1/2}}\int_{x_{i-1/2}}^{x_{i+1/2}} q(x, y)\,dx\,dy , \]

not the value at the cell centre, and the tendency they return is the tendency of that cell average. Every reconstruction below turns the cell averages \(\bar{q}_{i-2}, \dots, \bar{q}_{i+2}\) into an estimate of the point value \(q(x_{i+1/2})\) on the face. The two readings agree to \(O(\Delta x^2)\) (\(\bar{q}_i = q(x_i) + \tfrac{\Delta x^2}{24} q''(x_i) + \dots\)), so the distinction only matters for schemes above second order. Initialise with cell averages and compare with cell averages to see the nominal order.

The largest polynomial degree \(d\) for which the face value of \(x^d\) is reproduced exactly (both flow signs; scripts/benchmark_advection.py --part exactness):

Method naive upwind1 upwind2 upwind3 weno3 weno5 / wenoz5 weno7 weno9 TVD limiters fed cell averages 1 0 1 2 1 2 3 4 1 fed point values 1 0 1 1 1 1 1 1 1

The WENO schemes are exact to the degree of their candidate stencils (\(k-1\) for \(k\) candidates), not to the degree of the optimal linear combination: on a polynomial the nonlinear weights differ from the linear ones. They still converge at the nominal rate on smooth data, where the weights tend to the linear weights (see the order tables below).

Feeding point values instead of averages costs nothing in 1-D with a constant velocity (the scheme is linear and translation-invariant, so the two readings have the same truncation order: the conservative finite-difference equivalence), but with a spatially varying velocity every scheme above second order drops to second order, because the face value is then multiplied by a different velocity on each face. Measured 1-D L∞ / L1 orders of the tendency of \(e^{\sin 2\pi x}\) (periodic, \(N = 128 \to 256\); --part convergence):

Method \(u = 1\), averages \(u = 1\), point values \(u(x) = 1 + \tfrac12\sin 2\pi x\), averages \(u(x)\), point values upwind3 3.0 / 3.0 3.0 / 3.0 3.0 / 3.0 2.2 / 2.1 weno5 5.0 / 5.0 5.0 / 5.0 5.0 / 5.0 2.0 / 2.0 wenoz5 5.0 / 5.0 5.0 / 5.0 5.0 / 5.0 2.0 / 2.0 weno7 5.1 / 6.1 5.1 / 6.1 5.1 / 6.1 2.0 / 2.0 weno9 8.6 / 8.8 9.0 / 8.9 8.4 / 8.8 2.0 / 2.0

docs.title: 2-D Case
docs.text:
The discrete tendency at interior T-point \((j, i)\) is

\[ \left.\frac{\partial \bar{q}}{\partial t}\right|_{j,i} = -\frac{f_{j,i+\frac{1}{2}}^x - f_{j,i-\frac{1}{2}}^x}{\Delta x} -\frac{f_{j+\frac{1}{2},i}^y - f_{j-\frac{1}{2},i}^y}{\Delta y} \]

where the face-normal fluxes are

\[ f_{j,i+\frac{1}{2}}^x = u_{j,i+\frac{1}{2}} \cdot \hat{q}_{j,i+\frac{1}{2}}, \qquad f_{j+\frac{1}{2},i}^y = v_{j+\frac{1}{2},i} \cdot \hat{q}_{j+\frac{1}{2},i} \]

and \(\hat{q}\) is the reconstructed face value obtained from the cell averages of row \(j\) (column \(i\)) by one of the 1-D schemes described below.

docs.title: Formal Order
docs.text:
The 2-D (and 3-D) operators are unsplit: both directions' fluxes are computed from the same state, and the time integrator (e.g. rk3_ssp_step) advances their sum, so there is no splitting error and the temporal order is the integrator's. In space, each face value is a 1-D reconstruction along the face normal, and each face flux is the face-midpoint velocity times that value (midpoint quadrature along the face):

  • applied to the 2-D cell averages of one row, a 1-D reconstruction of order \(k\) returns the face average \(\frac{1}{\Delta y}\int q(x_{i+1/2}, y)\,dy\) to \(O(\Delta x^k)\), so with a constant velocity the scheme keeps the reconstruction's order \(k\) in the strict finite-volume sense;
  • with a spatially varying velocity, the midpoint velocity times the face-averaged \(q\) differs from the face average of \(u q\) by \(O(\Delta y^2)\), so the strict finite-volume order is 2 for every scheme above second order. (Order \(k\) would need several Gauss points per face, or a genuinely 2-D reconstruction; finitevolX does neither.)

Measured L∞ orders of the 2-D cell-average tendency against the exact one (\(N = 64 \to 128\), --part order2d): constant \((u, v)\): upwind3 3.0, weno5 5.0, weno9 8.8; divergence-free \(u(y)\), \(v(x)\): 2.1, 2.0, 2.0. In practice the high-order schemes still have far smaller errors on smooth flows (the second-order term has a small constant): see the accuracy benchmark.

docs.title: Face Values and Upwinding
docs.text:
Every reconstruction is upwinded on the sign of the face velocity: with \(u_{i+1/2} \ge 0\) it uses a left-biased stencil (upwind cell \(i\)), otherwise the mirrored right-biased one (upwind cell \(i+1\)), h_face = jnp.where(u >= 0, left_biased, right_biased), and the flux is h_face * u. The Reconstruction1D/2D/3D methods (upwind1_x, weno5_y, tvd_x(h, u, limiter=...), …) return that flux as a full [Ny, Nx] array with a zero ghost ring.

upwind_flux(q, u, dim, rec_funcs, mask_hierarchy) is the coastal tier blender, not a two-state flux: it evaluates every reconstruction in rec_funcs ({stencil_size: fn(q, u) -> flux}) and, at each face, keeps the one whose stencil size the mask hierarchy assigns to the upwind cell:

import jax.numpy as jnp
from finitevolx import CartesianGrid2D, Mask2D, Reconstruction2D, upwind_flux

grid = CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(8, 8, 1.0, 1.0)
recon = Reconstruction2D(grid=grid)
mask = Mask2D.from_dimensions(grid.Ny, grid.Nx)
hier = mask.get_adaptive_masks(direction="x", stencil_sizes=(2, 4, 6))
rec_funcs = {2: recon.upwind1_x, 4: recon.weno3_x, 6: recon.weno5_x}
q = jnp.ones((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))
u = jnp.ones((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))
fe = upwind_flux(q, u, dim=1, rec_funcs=rec_funcs, mask_hierarchy=hier)
# fe: [Ny, Nx] east-face flux, ghost ring zero

The advection operators build these dictionaries themselves; call it directly only to compose a custom tier ladder.

docs.title: Reconstruction Schemes
docs.text:
The key design choice is how to estimate the face value \(\hat{q}\) from the cell averages. The operators' default is method="upwind1".

Method Nominal order Measured order L∞ / L1 Cells read per face Mask tier (fallback) Non-oscillatory naive (centred) 2 2.0 / 2.0 2 — (dry face zeroed) No (dispersive) upwind1 1 1.0 / 1.0 1 2 Yes (monotone) upwind2 2 2.0 / 2.0 2 4 (→ upwind1) No upwind3 3 3.0 / 3.0 3 4 (→ upwind1) No (small undershoots) weno3 3 1.0 / 2.0 3 4 (→ upwind1) Essentially (ENO) weno5 5 5.0 / 5.0 5 6 (→ weno3 → upwind1) Essentially (ENO) wenoz5 5 5.0 / 5.0 5 6 (→ wenoz3 → upwind1) Essentially (ENO) weno7 7 5.1 / 6.1 7 8 (→ weno5 → …) Essentially (ENO) weno9 9 8.6 / 8.8 9 10 (→ weno7 → …) Essentially (ENO) minmod, van_leer, superbee, mc 2 1.0 / 2.0 3 4 (→ upwind1) Yes (TVD)

"Measured order" is the 1-D rate of the tendency of \(e^{\sin 2\pi x}\) from cell averages (\(N = 128 \to 256\)), a smooth field with extrema. At smooth extrema the TVD limiters clip to first order (hence L∞ 1, L1 2), and the Jiang–Shu weights of WENO3 and WENO7 degrade (WENO3-JS is first order in L∞ there, WENO7-JS fifth); WENO-Z does not. Advection3D and SphericalAdvection3D accept every method except upwind2 / upwind3.

docs.title: Total Variation Diminishing (TVD)
docs.text:
TVD schemes add a flux limiter \(\phi(r)\) to a first-order upwind base. For \(u_{i+1/2} \ge 0\) the code (Reconstruction*.tvd_x) evaluates

\[ \hat{q}_{i+\frac{1}{2}} = \bar{q}_i + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\phi(r)\,(\bar{q}_{i+1} - \bar{q}_i), \qquad r = \frac{\bar{q}_i - \bar{q}_{i-1}}{\bar{q}_{i+1} - \bar{q}_i} \]

(upwind slope over downwind slope), and the mirror image for \(u < 0\): \(\hat{q}_{i+1/2} = \bar{q}_{i+1} + \tfrac12\phi(r)(\bar{q}_i - \bar{q}_{i+1})\) with \(r = (\bar{q}_{i+1} - \bar{q}_{i+2}) / (\bar{q}_i - \bar{q}_{i+1})\). The four limiters are symmetric, \(\phi(r)/r = \phi(1/r)\), so this equals the other common form \(\bar{q}_i + \tfrac12\phi(1/r)(\bar{q}_i - \bar{q}_{i-1})\). The denominator of \(r\) is guarded relative to the slopes, \(r = \Delta_{\text{up}} / (\Delta_{\text{down}} + \operatorname{sign}(\Delta_{\text{down}})\,(10^{-6}\lvert\Delta_{\text{up}}\rvert + \sqrt{\text{tiny}}))\): it scales exactly with the field, keeps the sign of a tiny downwind slope, and a flat stencil gives \(r = 0\) with a finite gradient.

The limiter keeps \(\phi\) in the TVD region, so with an SSP time integrator under its CFL limit the total variation \(\sum_i \lvert\bar{q}_{i+1} - \bar{q}_i\rvert\) cannot increase: no new extrema, no undershoots.

Limiter \(\phi(r)\) Character Minmod \(\max(0,\min(1,r))\) Most diffusive; never overshoots van Leer \((r + \lvert r\rvert)/(1 + \lvert r\rvert)\) Smooth limiter Superbee \(\max(0, \max(\min(2r, 1), \min(r, 2)))\) Sharpest TVD; squares smooth peaks MC \(\max(0, \min((1+r)/2, 2, 2r))\) Between van Leer and superbee

docs.title: Weighted Essentially Non-Oscillatory (WENO)
docs.text: WENO schemes achieve high-order accuracy in smooth regions while avoiding spurious oscillations near discontinuities. The key idea is to compute several candidate reconstructions from different sub-stencils and blend them with nonlinear weights that de-emphasise sub-stencils containing large gradients.

docs.title: WENO3 (3rd order)
docs.text:
Two 2-point candidate stencils blended with nonlinear weights \(\omega_0, \omega_1\):

\[ q_0 = \tfrac{3}{2}\bar{q}_i - \tfrac{1}{2}\bar{q}_{i-1}, \qquad q_1 = \tfrac{1}{2}\bar{q}_i + \tfrac{1}{2}\bar{q}_{i+1} \] \[ \hat{q}_{i+\frac{1}{2}} = \omega_0\,q_0 + \omega_1\,q_1 \]

Weights are derived from the smoothness indicators \(\beta_k\) (variance measures of the sub-stencil). Near discontinuities \(\omega_k \to 0\) for stencils crossing the discontinuity, automatically reducing to 1st-order.

docs.title: WENO5 (5th order)
docs.text:
Three 3-point candidate stencils with optimal weights \((d_0, d_1, d_2)\):

\[ \hat{q}_{i+\frac{1}{2}} = \omega_0\,q_0 + \omega_1\,q_1 + \omega_2\,q_2 \]

Achieves 5th-order accuracy in smooth regions.

docs.title: WENOz5 (improved WENO5)
docs.text: Borges et al. (2008) modification of WENO5 that uses a higher-order global smoothness indicator \(\tau_5 = |\beta_0 - \beta_2|\) to scale the weights, achieving less dissipation near smooth extrema while remaining ENO near discontinuities.

docs.title: Relative epsilons: the scheme does not depend on the amplitude
docs.text:
Every WENO weight is \(g_k / (b_k + \varepsilon)^2\) (JS) or \(g_k (1 + \tau / (b_k + \varepsilon))\) (Z) on the normalised indicators \(b_k = \beta_k / \sum_j \beta_j\), with a dimensionless \(\varepsilon = 10^{-6}\): the textbook weights with a floor relative to the stencil's own smoothness, \(\varepsilon \sum_j \beta_j\), instead of an absolute constant. Rescaling the field therefore rescales the reconstruction exactly (checked to rounding, \(\sim 10^{-15}\), from amplitude \(10^{-9}\) to \(10^{3}\) by tests/test_scale_covariance.py; before #243 an absolute \(10^{-8}\) moved WENO tendencies by up to 3 % at amplitude \(10^3\), and the TVD guard made van Leer first order at \(10^{-9}\)).

Two details keep the gradient exact and finite. The weights depend only on ratios of indicators (they are homogeneous of degree 0), so the normalising sum is held out of the gradient (stop_gradient): by Euler's theorem that changes nothing, and the normalised quantities are O(1) at any amplitude, float32 included. A flat stencil (\(\sum_j\beta_j = 0\), an ocean at rest or a plateau) gives the linear weights and a finite gradient. Cost against the absolute form (CPU, \(256^2\), jitted): forward unchanged within noise; gradient about +25 % for weno5, unchanged for weno9, and +50 % for the TVD limiters (still the cheapest gradients).

docs.title: Measured Accuracy and Cost
docs.text:
Solid-body rotation of a Gaussian, \(q_0 = e^{-r^2 / 2\sigma^2}\) with \(\sigma = 0.05\) centred at \((\tfrac12, \tfrac34)\), rotated once about \((\tfrac12, \tfrac12)\) on \([0, 1]^2\) by \((u, v) = 2\pi(\tfrac12 - y, x - \tfrac12)\); \(N = 64\), cell-average initial condition, Advection2D (closed walls, no mask), rk3_ssp_step at CFL 0.25 (805 steps), float64. rel-L2 is \(\lVert\bar q(1) - \bar q_0\rVert_2 / \lVert\bar q_0\rVert_2\); min / max are over the interior after one revolution (initially 0 and 0.968). ms is the fastest of 50 jitted forward tendencies on a \(256^2\) grid (one Advection2D.__call__), measured on a shared 2-vCPU Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz VM (JAX 0.10.1, CPU): indicative only. Regenerate with uv run python scripts/benchmark_advection.py --part benchmark.

Method rel-L2 min max ms (\(256^2\)) naive 0.49 −0.16 0.822 0.09 upwind1 0.80 0 0.145 0.10 upwind2 0.57 −0.11 0.617 0.17 upwind3 0.13 −7.7e-3 0.815 0.21 weno3 0.38 0 0.473 0.65 weno5 3.3e-2 −1.5e-11 0.929 0.83 wenoz5 1.5e-2 −1.8e-8 0.949 0.82 weno7 5.4e-3 0 0.959 1.35 weno9 6.4e-4 −7.1e-9 0.967 1.71 minmod 0.44 0 0.429 0.27 van_leer 0.27 0 0.600 0.38 superbee 0.15 0 0.817 0.50 mc 0.21 0 0.681 0.53

What it says:

  • WENO3-JS is a poor choice on its own: 0.38, worse than every TVD limiter except minmod and three times worse than the linear upwind3, at four times the cost of upwind3. It earns its place as the coastal fallback of weno5.
  • wenoz5 halves the weno5 error at the same cost; weno7 / weno9 cut the wenoz5 error by another ~3× / ~25× for ~1.6× / ~2× the cost.
  • The TVD limiters are the only schemes guaranteed free of undershoots; among them superbee and MC are the most accurate on this smooth bump.
  • The WENO undershoots are tiny (\(\le 2\times10^{-8}\) of the peak) but not guaranteed zero; naive and upwind2 are dispersive (undershoots of 16 % and 11 % of the peak).

docs.title: Masks: Land-Safe Advection
docs.text:
Every method of Advection1D/2D/3D and SphericalAdvection2D/3D is land-safe when the operator is constructed with a mask. The mask is a constructor field (Advection2D(grid=grid, mask=mask)), not a __call__ argument: __init__ pre-builds the adaptive stencil hierarchy (2, 4, 6, 8, 10) in both horizontal directions once, and every call reuses it.

  • Dry inputs are zeroed with jnp.where before any stencil reads them (h on dry T-cells, u on dry U-faces, v on dry V-faces), so NaN or a fill value on land reaches neither the output nor the gradient.
  • Narrower stencils near the coast. Each T-point's StencilCapability2D gives the widest centred stencil that stays wet in each direction (tiers 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 = 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 cells). Every upwind-biased method goes through upwind_flux and, at each face, uses the highest tier of its own ladder that the upwind cell supports (the "Mask tier" column above), so no chosen stencil reads a land cell. naive reads only the two cells beside the face and needs no ladder.
  • No flux through a dry face. The face fluxes on every face with mask.u / mask.v false are zeroed before the divergence, as in Diffusion2D, so no mass crosses the coastline: in a closed basin \(\sum A\,\partial_t\bar q = 0\) to rounding.
  • Dry output is exactly zero (jnp.where(mask.h, out, 0)), and an all-ocean mask reproduces mask=None bit for bit.
  • wall="open" together with a mask raises NotImplementedError.
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
from finitevolx import Advection2D, CartesianGrid2D, Mask2D

grid = CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(16, 16, 1.0, 1.0)
wet = np.ones((grid.Ny, grid.Nx), dtype=bool)
wet[:2, :] = wet[-2:, :] = wet[:, :2] = wet[:, -2:] = False  # land walls
wet[7:11, 7:11] = False  # an island
mask = Mask2D.from_mask(wet)
adv = Advection2D(grid=grid, mask=mask)  # hierarchy built once, here

h = jnp.where(mask.h, 1.0, jnp.nan)  # NaN on land is fine
u = jnp.ones((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))  # [Ny, Nx] U-points
v = 0.5 * jnp.ones((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))  # [Ny, Nx] V-points
for method in ("naive", "upwind3", "weno5", "weno9", "van_leer"):
    dh = adv(h, u, v, method=method)  # [Ny, Nx]
    assert bool(jnp.isfinite(dh).all())
    assert abs(float(dh.sum())) < 1e-10  # no mass crosses the coastline

docs.title: Walls, Write Region and Periodic Halos
docs.text:
All advection operators take wall="closed" (default) or wall="open".

Operator wall="closed" writes wall="open" writes Advection1D [2:-2] [1:-1] Advection2D, SphericalAdvection2D [2:-2, 2:-2] [1:-1, 1:-1] Advection3D, SphericalAdvection3D [1:-1, 2:-2, 2:-2] [1:-1, 1:-1, 1:-1]
  • Closed treats the domain walls as no-flux and never reads the ghost flux cells: the outermost row / column of physical cells gets no tendency from advection alone, so the caller must account for it.
  • Open overwrites the wall faces with the first-order upwind flux of the caller-filled ghost ring (ghost = value for a Dirichlet inflow, a copy for outflow, a wrap for periodic), keeps the requested scheme on the interior faces, and writes the full interior; the flux stays single-valued, so mass is conserved exactly.
  • In 3-D the z axis is a batch axis: the horizontal reconstruction and divergence are applied to every level by array slicing (no vmap), and the ghost slabs k = 0, Nz-1 stay zero.

Periodic halo. For the tendency of the physical cells to equal the periodic scheme's (full-order stencils across the seam, not the boundary fallbacks), build the grid with \(H - 1\) extra cells on each periodic side, fill the outer \(H\) cells of every field by wrapping, and keep the physical cells [H:-H]. Measured minimum \(H\), the same for the Cartesian and the spherical operators:

Method \(H\) (wall="open") \(H\) (wall="closed") upwind1 1 2 naive, upwind2, upwind3, weno3, TVD limiters 2 2 weno5, wenoz5 3 3 weno7 4 4 weno9 5 5

With wall="open" a one-cell ghost ring still conserves mass exactly (the seam face is first-order upwind, the same on both sides); a halo strictly between 1 and \(H\) does not (the two seam faces then use different boundary fallbacks).

docs.title: Spherical Advection
docs.text:
SphericalAdvection2D/3D reuse the Cartesian reconstructions (they read no metric) and change only the divergence:

\[ \frac{\partial \bar{q}}{\partial t} = -\frac{1}{R\cos\varphi} \left[\frac{\partial (q u)}{\partial \lambda} + \frac{\partial (q v \cos\varphi)}{\partial \varphi}\right] \]

with \(\cos\varphi\) at the T-rows for the cell area and at the V-rows for the meridional faces. The divergence telescopes against spherical_area_weights (\(R^2\cos\varphi_T\,\Delta\lambda\,\Delta\varphi\)): \(\sum A\,\partial_t\bar q\) is the net flux through the faces bounding the written cells. With wall="closed" that region is [2:-2, 2:-2], so on a zonally periodic grid the seam-adjacent columns get no tendency; use wall="open" with a wrapped halo (table above) for a conservative periodic seam. Mask semantics are the Cartesian ones.

docs.title: Transports and Other Fluxes
docs.text:
Transports instead of velocities. The face value depends on the velocity only through its sign, so the operators are linear in u, v. Passing positively weighted transports, e.g. U = h_u * u, V = h_v * v with a layer thickness interpolated to the faces, therefore returns \(-\nabla\cdot(q\,\mathbf{U})\), the tendency of the thickness-weighted tracer \(h q\) (thickness-weighted advection). There is no dedicated API for it: compute the face thickness yourself (e.g. Interpolation2D.T_to_U / T_to_V), and divide by the updated thickness if you need \(q\).

rusanov_flux (local Lax–Friedrichs, \(F = \tfrac12 a (q_L + q_R) - \tfrac12\lvert a\rvert_\varepsilon (q_R - q_L)\)) returns a reduced-shape array: given q of length \(N\) along axis and the face velocity a on the \(N - 1\) faces between adjacent cells, it returns the flux on those \(N - 1\) faces, unlike the other fluxes, which are full ghost-padded C-grid fields. Take its divergence with jnp.diff along the same axis:

import jax.numpy as jnp
from finitevolx import (
    Advection2D,
    CartesianGrid2D,
    Interpolation2D,
    interior,
    rusanov_flux,
)

grid = CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(16, 16, 1.0, 1.0)
y, x = jnp.meshgrid(jnp.arange(grid.Ny), jnp.arange(grid.Nx), indexing="ij")
q = jnp.sin(0.4 * x) + jnp.cos(0.3 * y)  # [Ny, Nx] T-points
u = jnp.cos(0.2 * y)  # [Ny, Nx] U-points
v = jnp.sin(0.25 * x)  # [Ny, Nx] V-points

# Face k between T-cells k and k+1 is the U-point (V-point) of index k.
fx = rusanov_flux(q, u[:, :-1], axis=-1, eps=0.0)  # [Ny, Nx-1]
fy = rusanov_flux(q, v[:-1, :], axis=-2, eps=0.0)  # [Ny-1, Nx]
dq = interior(
    -(
        jnp.diff(fx, axis=-1)[1:-1, :] / grid.dx
        + jnp.diff(fy, axis=-2)[:, 1:-1] / grid.dy
    ),
    q,
)  # [Ny, Nx]; reads the wall faces, like wall="open"
# With eps=0 the Rusanov flux of the cell values is first-order upwind:
adv = Advection2D(grid=grid)
assert jnp.allclose(dq, adv(q, u, v, method="upwind1", wall="open"))

# Transports: the operator is linear in the velocity.
h = 2.0 + 0.1 * jnp.cos(0.3 * x)  # [Ny, Nx] layer thickness at T-points
interp = Interpolation2D(grid=grid)
U = interp.T_to_U(h) * u  # [Ny, Nx] face transport
V = interp.T_to_V(h) * v  # [Ny, Nx] face transport
dhq = adv(q, U, V, method="weno5")  # -div(q U): tendency of h q

docs.title: Quick Usage
docs.text:
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
from finitevolx import CartesianGrid2D, Advection2D, Mask2D

grid = CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(64, 64, 1e6, 1e6)

# Construct once; the operator is method-agnostic.
adv = Advection2D(grid=grid)

# T-point tracer (cell averages) and U/V-point velocities
q = jnp.ones((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))   # T-point tracer
u = jnp.zeros((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))  # U-point velocity
v = jnp.zeros((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))  # V-point velocity

# Default upwind1 (no mask)
dq_dt = adv(q, u, v)

# Choose a method per-call
dq_dt_tvd = adv(q, u, v, method="van_leer")
dq_dt_weno = adv(q, u, v, method="weno5")

# With a land mask: the mask is a constructor field, so build a second
# operator instance with `mask=`.  The adaptive stencil hierarchy is
# pre-built once in `__init__` and reused on every call (docs/masks.md).
ocean_mask = np.ones((grid.Ny, grid.Nx), dtype=bool)
ocean_mask[20:30, 20:30] = False  # an island
mask = Mask2D.from_mask(ocean_mask)
adv_masked = Advection2D(grid=grid, mask=mask)
dq_dt_masked = adv_masked(q, u, v, method="weno5")
# shape [Ny, Nx], non-zero only in [2:-2, 2:-2] and on wet cells

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text:
Built from the measured accuracy table (solid-body Gaussian, \(N = 64\), one revolution; rel-L2 in brackets).

Must the tracer never undershoot (positive-definite, bounded)?
├── Yes → a TVD limiter (no undershoot with SSP-RK under its CFL limit)
│         ├── most accurate on smooth bumps    → superbee (0.15) or mc (0.21)
│         ├── smooth limiter, no peak squaring → van_leer (0.27)
│         └── most dissipative                 → minmod (0.44)
└── No ↓

Is accuracy on smooth fields the priority?
├── Yes → WENO (undershoots <= 2e-8 of the peak here, not guaranteed zero)
│         ├── default choice               → wenoz5 (1.5e-2; weno5 3.3e-2, same cost)
│         ├── more accuracy, ~1.6-2x cost  → weno7 (5.4e-3) / weno9 (6.4e-4)
│         └── not weno3 on its own         → (0.38: worse than upwind3 and
│                                             superbee / mc / van_leer)
└── No → cheap and fairly accurate:  upwind3 (0.13; undershoots ~1 %)
         monotone, most dissipative: upwind1 (0.80)
         avoid naive / upwind2 for tracers (dispersive: 16 % / 11 % undershoots)

Does the domain have land / islands?
├── Yes → construct the operator with mask=Mask2D.from_mask(wet):
│         every method is land-safe (coastal fallback, no flux through land)
└── No  → omit the mask

Periodic in x or y?  → wall="open" with the halo H of the table above.

docs.title: Building with agents
docs.text: finitevolX exists so that a staggered-grid model is assembled from parts that already know their stagger, their ghost cells and their masks. Coding agents tend to re-implement what they cannot see — a shifted slice divided by dx, a ghost-row copy, a DST Poisson solver, an RK3 loop — and each one is a place for an off-by-half-a-cell error, a leaking coastline or a non-conservative flux. finitevolX ships three things that let agents find the real thing instead.

docs.title: The capability index
docs.text: The capability index lists every public name in finitevolx, grouped by the module that defines it, with a one-line summary; then the public API of spectraldiffx and gaussx, which finitevolX builds on (its spectral solvers and transforms are re-exported from spectraldiffx). It is regenerated from the code and checked in the test suite, so it never drifts.

docs.title: The Claude Code plugin
docs.text:
The repository is a Claude Code plugin marketplace. In any project:

/plugin marketplace add jejjohnson/finitevolX
/plugin install finitevolx@finitevolx

The plugin adds:

  • finite-volume-models-with-finitevolx (skill) — loads whenever a task discretises a PDE on a staggered grid, writes a stencil or a ghost-cell fill, advects a tracer, inverts vorticity or PV, or time-steps a model: what lives where, the rules (the caller owns the ghost ring, use the operator that names the stagger, masks are passed to operators, closed walls by default, constants are parameters), a worked example, and a "don't write it — use finitevolX" table.
  • finitevolx-reuse-reviewer (subagent) — a read-only check of a diff for finite-volume code finitevolX already provides, and for misuse (unfilled ghosts, wrong stagger, NaN on land).

docs.title: llms.txt
docs.text: For other agents and tools, the docs site serves llms.txt: a curated map of finitevolX and its key pages.

docs.title: Rules for your project's AGENTS.md
docs.text:
Paste this into the agent instructions of a project that builds on finitevolX:

## Finite-volume numerics: build on finitevolX

This project discretises its equations on Arakawa C-grids with finitevolX
(stencils, operators, masks, boundary conditions, advection, elliptic
solvers, time steppers). Before writing a stencil, a ghost-cell fill, an
advection scheme, a Poisson / Helmholtz solver or a time-stepping loop,
search the capability index
(https://jejjohnson.github.io/finitevolX/capabilities/) or
`finitevolx.__all__`, and compose what exists:

- Arrays are `[Ny, Nx]` with one ghost ring; `T[j, i]` is a cell centre,
  `U[j, i]` its east face, `V[j, i]` its north face, `X[j, i]` its NE
  corner. Use the operator that names the mapping
  (`Difference2D.diff_x_T_to_U`, `Interpolation2D.U_to_T`) instead of
  writing the slice.
- Operators write only the interior. Fill every field's ghost ring
  (`enforce_periodic`, a `BoundaryConditionSet`) before the next operator
  reads it, including inside the time stepper's right-hand side.
- Build a `Mask2D.from_mask(wet)` once and pass it as `mask=` to the
  operators; don't multiply by a mask afterwards or keep `NaN` on land.
- Advect with `Advection2D(...)(q, u, v, method="weno5")`; invert with
  `streamfunction_from_vorticity` / `pv_inversion`; step with
  `rk3_ssp_step` or a finitevolX diffrax solver.
- Pass physical constants explicitly; never hard-code them in a model
  meant to run nondimensionally.

docs.title: Working on finitevolX itself
docs.text: Contributors (and their agents) follow AGENTS.md in the repository: the module map, the boundaries with spectraldiffx and gaussx, "reuse before you write", the C-grid, operator, mask, boundary-condition, solver and unit contracts and the tests that enforce them, and recipe skills for adding stencil operators, advection schemes, boundary conditions, forcing terms, elliptic solvers, time integrators and notebooks.

docs.title: Boundary Conditions
docs.text: This page covers the theory behind the boundary condition (BC) system in finitevolX, explains the ghost-cell approach used on the Arakawa C-grid, and provides guidance for composing and applying BCs.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
All spatial operators in finitevolX write only to interior cells [1:-1, 1:-1] and read the one-cell ghost ring to compute stencils at the boundary. The physical boundary condition is therefore encoded in the ghost cells: the BC layer sets ghost values such that the interior stencil evaluates to the correct physical quantity at the domain wall.

This design cleanly separates the operator code (which never checks for boundaries) from the boundary logic (which only writes to ghost cells). It also allows arbitrary BCs to be applied by simply overwriting ghost cells before the next operator call.

docs.title: The Ghost-Cell Method
docs.text:
For a field with interior values \(\phi_1, \phi_2, \ldots\) and ghost cell \(\phi_0\), the physical boundary is modelled as lying exactly between the first interior cell and the ghost cell. This gives the standard ghost-cell relationships:

Dirichlet (\(\phi_{\text{wall}} = g\)):

\[ \phi_{\text{wall}} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\phi_1 + \phi_0) = g \implies \phi_0 = 2g - \phi_1 \]

Neumann (\(\partial\phi/\partial n\big|_{\text{wall}} = g\), outward normal):

\[ \frac{\phi_0 - \phi_1}{\Delta n} = g \implies \phi_0 = \phi_1 + g\,\Delta n \]

where \(\phi_0\) is the ghost cell and \(\phi_1\) the adjacent interior cell. The ghost cell lies outward of the interior on every face, so the same formula holds on all four faces: \(g\) is the true gradient along the outward normal (e.g. \(g = -\partial\phi/\partial y\) on the south wall).

Periodic (\(\phi_0 = \phi_{N-1}\), \(\phi_N = \phi_1\)):

The ghost cell simply copies the opposite interior edge.

docs.title: Dirichlet1D
docs.text:
Fixes the value of the field at the domain wall. The ghost cell is set to the reflection that makes the average equal to the target value:

\[ \phi_{\text{ghost}} = 2\,v_{\text{target}} - \phi_{\text{interior}} \]

Physical use cases: - No-slip walls for the tangential velocity: \(v = 0\) on a west / east wall. - No normal flow through a wall: \(u = 0\) on a west / east wall, with point="U" (see below). - Fixed surface elevation: \(\eta = 0\) on rigid lid. - Streamfunction: \(\psi = 0\) on closed coastline (used by DST Poisson solver).

docs.title: Staggered fields: point=
docs.text:
The formula above places the wall half a cell outside the first interior node, which is right for every cell-centred direction: T on all four faces, V on the west / east faces, U on the south / north faces. With same-index staggering the other pairs have a node on the wall: U[:, 0] and U[:, Nx-2] are the west and east wall faces, V[0, :] and V[Ny-2, :] the south and north ones, and an X field has a node on all four walls (U[:, Nx-1], V[Ny-1, :] are outside the domain).

Every atom except Periodic1D takes a static point="T" | "U" | "V" | "X" (default "T"). For a node on the wall the condition is imposed on that node: Dirichlet1D writes value to it, Neumann1D / Robin1D use the one-sided gradient between it and the first interior node, Slip1D writes a * interior, and the outside slot on the east / north side gets the odd mirror \(2\phi_{\text{wall}} - \phi_{\text{adjacent}}\). Periodic1D needs no point: wrapping by one period is right for every stagger (U[:, 0] is the same face as U[:, Nx-2]).

Normal velocity needs point=

Dirichlet1D("east", 0.0) on a U-field sets the ghost column U[:, Nx-1] = -U[:, Nx-2] and leaves the east wall face U[:, Nx-2] untouched, so mass flows through a "closed" wall. Use Dirichlet1D("east", 0.0, point="U"), or BoundaryConditionSet.closed(point="U") for the whole basin.

import finitevolx as fvx

bc_u = fvx.BoundaryConditionSet.closed(point="U")  # u = 0 on W/E faces, no-slip on S/N
bc_v = fvx.BoundaryConditionSet.closed(point="V")  # v = 0 on S/N faces, no-slip on W/E
u, v = bc_u(u, dx, dy), bc_v(v, dx, dy)
# Difference2D(grid).divergence(u, v) now integrates to zero over the basin.

docs.title: Neumann1D
docs.text:
Fixes the outward-normal gradient \(\partial\phi/\partial n = g\):

\[ \phi_{\text{ghost}} = \phi_{\text{interior}} + g\,\Delta n \]

Physical use cases: - Free-slip walls: \(\partial u_{\parallel}/\partial n = 0\). - No-flux tracer BC: \(\partial T/\partial n = 0\) on insulating walls. - Pressure BC: \(\partial p/\partial n = 0\) on solid walls.

docs.title: Periodic1D
docs.text:
Wraps the field: the ghost cell on one face copies the last interior cell on the opposite face.

Physical use cases: - Doubly-periodic channels and basins. - Zonal re-entrant channels (periodic in x, closed in y).

enforce_periodic helper

For fully periodic domains the helper enforce_periodic(field, ...) is available as a thin wrapper that applies Periodic1D on all four faces simultaneously. Prefer BoundaryConditionSet for per-face control.

docs.title: Reflective1D
docs.text:
Reflects the field about the boundary:

\[ \phi_{\text{ghost}} = \phi_{\text{interior}} \quad (\text{even reflection}) \]

This is Neumann with \(g = 0\). Used for free-slip walls where the normal velocity is zero and the tangential velocity has zero normal gradient.

docs.title: Slip1D
docs.text:
General slip boundary condition controlled by a scalar coefficient = a:

\[ \phi_{\text{ghost}} = (2a - 1)\,\phi_{\text{interior}} \]

where:

  • a = 1.0 (default) gives free-slip (even reflection),
  • a = 0.0 gives no-slip (odd reflection, equivalent to Dirichlet with \(g=0\)),
  • 0 < a < 1 gives partial-slip, interpolating smoothly between free-slip and no-slip.

This BC is typically used for velocity components at solid walls, with the choice of coefficient controlling how strongly the tangential velocity is damped at the boundary.

docs.title: Outflow1D
docs.text:
Zero-gradient outflow condition (equivalent to Neumann with \(g=0\)):

\[ \phi_{\text{ghost}} = \phi_{\text{interior}} \]

Used at open boundaries where the flow leaves the domain and the outward gradient is assumed zero.

docs.title: Extrapolation1D
docs.text:
Linear extrapolation from the two innermost interior cells:

\[ \phi_{\text{ghost}} = 2\,\phi_1 - \phi_2 \]

More accurate than zero-gradient for smoothly varying fields at open boundaries. Avoids spurious reflections from the domain edge.

docs.title: Robin1D
docs.text:
Mixed (Robin / third-kind) condition: a linear combination of value and gradient:

\[ a\,\phi_{\text{wall}} + b\,\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial n}\bigg|_{\text{wall}} = g \]

With \(\phi_{\text{wall}} = (\phi_{\text{ghost}} + \phi_{\text{interior}})/2\) and \(\partial\phi/\partial n = (\phi_{\text{ghost}} - \phi_{\text{interior}})/\Delta n\) (outward normal, same on every face), the ghost value is

\[ \phi_{\text{ghost}} = \frac{g - (a/2 - s)\,\phi_{\text{interior}}}{a/2 + s}, \qquad s = \frac{b}{\Delta n} \]

Used for sponge-layer or radiation boundary conditions in more advanced setups.

docs.title: Sponge1D
docs.text:
Relaxation towards a target profile \(\phi^*\) within a sponge layer of specified half-width:

\[ \phi_{\text{ghost}} = \phi_{\text{interior}} + \lambda(\phi^* - \phi_{\text{interior}}) \]

Used at open boundaries to absorb outgoing waves and prevent reflections.

docs.title: BoundaryConditionSet
docs.text:
Applies one BC atom on each of the four faces of a 2-D field. Faces are processed in south → north → west → east order, so west/east BCs overwrite corner ghost cells filled by south/north BCs:

from finitevolx import BoundaryConditionSet, Dirichlet1D, Periodic1D

# Closed basin: Dirichlet ψ=0 on all walls
bc_set = BoundaryConditionSet(
    south=Dirichlet1D(face="south", value=0.0),
    north=Dirichlet1D(face="north", value=0.0),
    west=Dirichlet1D(face="west",  value=0.0),
    east=Dirichlet1D(face="east",  value=0.0),
)

psi = bc_set(psi, dx=grid.dx, dy=grid.dy)

The same set can describe the boundary of an elliptic solve: pass it as bc= to streamfunction_from_vorticity, pressure_from_divergence or pv_inversion. All-Dirichlet1D faces select the DST, all zero Neumann1D faces the DCT and all Periodic1D faces the FFT; a set's mask is used by the mask-based methods (method="spectral" raises on a bc.mask); and non-zero Dirichlet1D values are imposed on each face's wall nodes:

bc_set = BoundaryConditionSet(
    mask=mask,
    south=Dirichlet1D(face="south", value=0.0),
    north=Dirichlet1D(face="north", value=0.1),
    west=Dirichlet1D(face="west",  value=0.0),
    east=Dirichlet1D(face="east",  value=0.0),
)
psi = fvx.streamfunction_from_vorticity(zeta, dx, dy, bc=bc_set, method="cg")

When time-stepping, a Dirichlet1D value sits on the wall face, half a cell outside the first wet T cell. ψ lives at X points, and the X nodes 0 and N-2 lie on the walls, so a solve pins those wall nodes (the coast ring of the ψ mask) to the face value: the same wall. For the T-point pressure_from_divergence the face is half a cell from any cell centre, so non-zero Dirichlet1D faces raise there. See Known Boundary Values for arbitrary per-cell values and interior observations.

docs.title: FieldBCSet
docs.text:
Maps a BC set to a named field in a state dictionary or pytree. Useful for model state vectors with multiple fields, each needing different BCs:

from finitevolx import BoundaryConditionSet, Dirichlet1D, FieldBCSet, Neumann1D

# Free-slip velocity BCs: zero normal flow on the wall faces (point="U"),
# zero tangential gradient on the south / north walls
bc_u = BoundaryConditionSet(
    south=Neumann1D(face="south", value=0.0),
    north=Neumann1D(face="north", value=0.0),
    west=Dirichlet1D(face="west", value=0.0, point="U"),
    east=Dirichlet1D(face="east", value=0.0, point="U"),
)
bcs = FieldBCSet(bc_map={"u": bc_u, "h": BoundaryConditionSet.open()})

Each atom carries its own point, so FieldBCSet needs no stagger information of its own.

docs.title: pad_interior
docs.text:
Pads a field array from an interior-only view to the full [Ny, Nx] ghost-ring layout. Useful when you have a field defined only on interior points and need to apply ghost-cell BCs:

from finitevolx import pad_interior

q_interior = jnp.ones((Ny - 2, Nx - 2))   # interior only
q_full     = pad_interior(q_interior, mode="constant", constant_values=0.0)

Supported modes match jnp.pad: "constant", "edge", "reflect", "wrap".

docs.title: enforce_periodic
docs.text:
Convenience wrapper: applies periodic BCs in x, y, or both directions:

from finitevolx import enforce_periodic

q = enforce_periodic(q, x=True, y=True)   # both directions

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text:
What physical condition applies?
│
├── Fixed value at wall (ψ=0, T=T_wall, tangential velocity)
│   └── Dirichlet1D(face=..., value=...)
│
├── No normal flow through a wall (u on W/E, v on S/N)
│   └── Dirichlet1D(face=..., value=0, point="U" / "V")
│
├── Zero normal gradient (free-slip, insulating)
│   └── Reflective1D  or  Neumann1D(face=..., value=0)
│
├── Specified normal gradient (heat flux, wind stress)
│   └── Neumann1D(face=..., value=g)
│
├── No-slip (u=0, v=0 at wall)
│   └── Slip1D  or  Dirichlet1D(value=0)
│
├── Periodic domain
│   └── Periodic1D  or  enforce_periodic(field)
│
├── Open boundary, outflow
│   ├── Zero gradient   → Outflow1D  or  Reflective1D
│   └── Linear extrap   → Extrapolation1D
│
└── Open boundary with wave absorption
    └── Sponge1D  or  Robin1D

docs.title: Upstream: spectraldiffx
docs.text: Spectral transforms (DCT / DST / FFT), the rectangular spectral Poisson / Helmholtz solvers and their eigenvalues, and the spectral capacitance solver. finitevolX re-exports most of the solver API (listed above); the rest — spectral derivatives, spherical-harmonic and Chebyshev machinery — is used from here, never re-implemented.

docs.title: Arakawa C-Grid Discretization
docs.text: This document describes the numerical discretization scheme used throughout finitevolX, explaining the same-size array convention, ghost-cell layout, variable co-location, and the slicing patterns that implement each stencil.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: finitevolX uses an Arakawa C-grid, a staggered finite-volume mesh where different physical variables live at different grid locations. The key departure from many textbook implementations is that every array has the same total shape [Ny, Nx], including one ring of ghost cells on each side. There are no separate [Ny, Nx+1] or [Nx-1, Ny-1] arrays.

docs.title: Why same-shape storage?
docs.text:
The textbook way to discretise a staggered grid is to give each variable the exact array shape it needs. For an Nx × Ny grid of cell centres T, this typically means:

T : [Ny,     Nx    ]    cell centres        — Nx*Ny    values
U : [Ny,     Nx + 1]    east faces          — Nx+1 columns
V : [Ny + 1, Nx    ]    north faces         — Ny+1 rows
X : [Ny + 1, Nx + 1]    NE corners          — both sides extended

Each array is exactly the right size, and U[j, i] lives at the east face of T[j, i] for i ∈ [0, Nx-1], with U[j, Nx] being the rightmost boundary face. This is a perfectly defensible convention — and it's what many production ocean models use.

finitevolX makes a different choice: every staggered field has the same shape [Ny, Nx] as T, with a one-cell ghost ring on each side. The physical interior occupies [1:-1, 1:-1]; the outer ring carries boundary-condition data set by the caller. Under this convention, U[j, i] still lives at the east face of T[j, i], but now the index i = Nx-1 falls in the ghost ring instead of being an extra "boundary face" slot.

The advantages of same-shape storage compound across the rest of the library:

  1. Static shapes for JAX JIT. Every array has the same shape, derived from a single (Ny, Nx) pair on the Grid object. JIT-compiled kernels have one statically known shape for every field, no special cases for U/V/X.

  2. Free broadcasting in field arithmetic. Expressions like h * u**2 + v**2 - p just work — no reshaping, no padding, no jnp.pad shims. This is especially useful for diagnostics (kinetic energy, Bernoulli potential, vorticity) that mix all four point types.

  3. Leading batch axes for free. The 2-D Cartesian operators, diagnostics and boundary conditions take [*batch, Ny, Nx]: a time series, an ensemble, a stack of layers, without vmap. Their stencils slice the trailing two axes (h[..., 1:-1, 2:]) and interior pads back only the axes that lost a ghost ring, so the leading axes pass through untouched. Because every input has the same leading shape, there are no "this one is Nx+1-wide and the others are Nx" gotchas, under vmap either.

  4. One ghost-cell convention to learn. All four point types share the same [1:-1, 1:-1] interior slice. Boundary conditions are applied uniformly: write into the ghost ring, then call the operator. You never have to remember "U has an extra east column but V has an extra north row."

  5. Clean composition of stencils. A finite-difference operator reads arr[1:-1, 2:] and arr[1:-1, 1:-1], writes the result to out[1:-1, 1:-1], and leaves the ghost ring at zero. Every shifted slice has the same (Ny-2, Nx-2) shape because the ghost ring absorbs the edge — a single-step shift never reads outside the array bounds.

The cost is that you have to internalise one fixed convention: index 0 and index N-1 along each axis are ghost; real data lives at [1:-1]. Once that's in muscle memory, the rest of the library is remarkably uniform — the same slicing patterns appear in every operator in this document.

docs.title: Variable Co-location
docs.text:
Four distinct locations are used, identified by letter:

Symbol Name Physical location Same-index meaning T cell centre (j·dy, i·dx ) T[j, i] lives at (j, i ) U east face (j·dy, (i+½)·dx ) U[j, i] lives at (j, i+½ ) V north face ((j+½)·dy, i·dx ) V[j, i] lives at (j+½, i ) X NE corner ((j+½)·dy, (i+½)·dx ) X[j, i] lives at (j+½, i+½ )

The "same-index" rule means that array index [j, i] encodes the south-west corner of the stencil neighbourhood:

   X[j,i] ---V[j,i]--- X[j,i+1]
     |           |           |
   U[j,i]  T[j,i]  U[j,i+1]
     |           |           |
  X[j-1,i]--V[j-1,i]--X[j-1,i+1]

docs.title: Ghost Cells
docs.text: For a grid with Nx × Ny total cells, the physical interior occupies indices [1:-1, 1:-1] (shape (Ny-2) × (Nx-2)). The outer ring — rows 0 and Ny-1, columns 0 and Nx-1 — consists of ghost cells reserved for boundary conditions.

docs.title: T-point ghost cells
docs.text:
col:   0    1    2  ...  Nx-2  Nx-1
row 0: [g]  [g]  [g] ...  [g]  [g]   ← ghost (south)
row 1: [g]  [ ]  [ ] ...  [ ]  [g]   ← first interior row
  ...        interior               ...
row Ny-2:[g][ ]  [ ] ...  [ ]  [g]   ← last interior row
row Ny-1:[g] [g] [g] ...  [g]  [g]   ← ghost (north)
        ^                        ^
     ghost                    ghost
     (west)                   (east)

docs.title: U-point ghost cells
docs.text:
U[j, i] sits at east face (j, i+1/2).

Index Physical meaning Who sets it? U[j, 0] West boundary face (j, ½) BC layer (e.g. periodic copy) U[j, 1..Nx-2] Interior east faces Forward operators (diff_x_T_to_U, T_to_U) U[j, Nx-1] Outside domain Unused / left zero U[0, i], U[Ny-1, i] South/north ghost rows BC layer

U[j, Nx-2] is the east boundary face — it sits inside [1:-1, 1:-1] and is computed by forward operators using the east ghost T-cell T[j, Nx-1].

docs.title: V-point ghost cells
docs.text:
V[j, i] sits at north face (j+½, i).

Index Physical meaning Who sets it? V[0, i] South boundary face (½, i) BC layer V[1..Ny-2, i] Interior north faces Forward operators (diff_y_T_to_V, T_to_V) V[Ny-1, i] Outside domain Unused / left zero V[j, 0], V[j, Nx-1] West/east ghost cols BC layer

V[Ny-2, i] is the north boundary face — computed using north ghost T.

docs.title: X-point ghost cells
docs.text:
X[j, i] sits at NE corner (j+½, i+½).

Index Physical meaning Who sets it? X[0, i] South ghost X-row BC layer X[j, 0] West ghost X-col BC layer X[1..Ny-2, 1..Nx-2] Interior corners Forward operators (T_to_X, diff_y_U_to_X, etc.) X[Ny-1, i], X[j, Nx-1] Outside domain Unused / left zero

docs.title: Ghost asymmetry: forward vs backward
docs.text:
The same [1:-1, 1:-1] write range has different ghost-cell implications depending on direction:

Operator direction Last interior output uses... First interior output reads... T→U (forward x) east ghost T T[j, Nx-1] — T→V (forward y) north ghost T T[Ny-1, i] — V→X (forward x) east ghost V V[j, Nx-1] — U→X (forward y) north ghost U U[Ny-1, i] — U→T (backward x) — west ghost U U[j, 0] V→T (backward y) — south ghost V V[0, i] X→U (backward y) — south ghost X X[0, i] X→V (backward x) — west ghost X X[j, 0] U→V (cross) north ghost U U[Ny-1, i] — V→U (cross) east ghost V V[j, Nx-1] —

Operators write only to [1:-1, 1:-1]. Ghost cells remain at their initialised value (typically zero). Callers are responsible for filling ghosts via boundary-condition helpers (pad_interior, enforce_periodic, BoundaryConditionSet, etc.) before the next operator call.

docs.title: Vertical staggering in 3D
docs.text:
In 3D the horizontal staggering repeats at each z-level. Every [k, :, :] slab looks exactly like the 2D picture above:

T[k, j, i]  cell centre  at ( k,    j,    i    )
U[k, j, i]  east face    at ( k,    j,    i+½  )
V[k, j, i]  north face   at ( k,    j+½,  i    )
X[k, j, i]  NE corner    at ( k,    j+½,  i+½  )

All of these are [Nz, Ny, Nx], still same-shape, and the horizontal operators in Difference3D / Interpolation3D / Vorticity3D simply apply the corresponding 2D stencil at each fixed k. The vertical ghost convention mirrors the horizontal: k = 0 and k = Nz - 1 are top/bottom ghost shells, and the physical interior is k = 1 … Nz - 2 (see Multilayer vs. 3D for the distinction with multilayer/baroclinic models).

The vertical interfaces — the faces between T[k, j, i] and T[k+1, j, i], where vertical velocity w lives — follow the same same-index rule as the horizontal faces:

w[k, j, i]  at ( k+½,  j,  i )    ← top face of T[k, j, i]

w[k] is the top face of cell k (equivalently the bottom face of cell k+1). With the physical levels k = 1 … Nz-2:

w[Nz-1]   outside the domain (top face of the top ghost slab)
w[Nz-2]   surface (top face of the top physical level)
  ...
w[1]      interface between T[1] and T[2]
w[0]      floor (bottom face of T[1]; zero for a rigid bottom)

just as U[:, 0] / U[:, Nx-2] are the west / east wall faces and U[:, Nx-1] is outside the domain. Mask3D.w and vertical_velocity both use this convention, so h, u, v, w and every mask share the [Nz, Ny, Nx] shape and broadcast without reshaping:

mask = Mask3D.from_mask(wet)                          # mask.w.shape == (Nz, Ny, Nx)
w = vertical_velocity(u, v, dx, dy, dz, mask=mask)    # w.shape == (Nz, Ny, Nx)

vertical_velocity integrates the horizontal divergence of the physical levels upward from w[0] = 0 (w[k] = w[k-1] − div_h[k] · dz) and never reads the z-ghost slabs of u and v. (Until #210 it returned a separate [Nz+1, Ny, Nx] array with w[0] the floor and also integrated the ghost slabs.)

docs.title: Creating a Grid
docs.text:
from finitevolx import CartesianGrid2D

# 64 physical cells in each direction; 66×66 total array shape
grid = CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(nx_interior=64, ny_interior=64,
                                     Lx=1.0, Ly=1.0)
# grid.Nx == 66, grid.Ny == 66
# grid.dx == 1/64, grid.dy == 1/64

All field arrays are then allocated as jnp.zeros((grid.Ny, grid.Nx)).

docs.title: Difference Operators
docs.text: Every finite-difference stencil is a one-cell shift divided by the grid spacing. The direction of the shift (forward or backward) is determined by which point type the output lives at.

docs.title: Forward differences (T → face / corner)
docs.text:
Method Stencil formula Writes to diff_x_T_to_U dh/dx[j, i+½] = (h[j, i+1] - h[j, i]) / dx U-points diff_y_T_to_V dh/dy[j+½, i] = (h[j+1, i] - h[j, i]) / dy V-points diff_y_U_to_X du/dy[j+½, i+½] = (u[j+1, i] - u[j, i]) / dy X-points diff_x_V_to_X dv/dx[j+½, i+½] = (v[j, i+1] - v[j, i]) / dx X-points

Example slice for diff_x_T_to_U (writes to [1:-1, 1:-1]):

# dh_dx[j, i+1/2] = (h[j, i+1] - h[j, i]) / dx
out = out.at[1:-1, 1:-1].set((h[1:-1, 2:] - h[1:-1, 1:-1]) / dx)

The slice h[1:-1, 2:] gives h[j, i+1] for i ranging over interior columns; h[1:-1, 1:-1] gives h[j, i].

docs.title: Backward differences (face / corner → T)
docs.text:
Method Stencil formula Writes to diff_x_U_to_T du/dx[j, i] = (u[j, i] - u[j, i-1]) / dx T-points diff_y_V_to_T dv/dy[j, i] = (v[j, i] - v[j-1, i]) / dy T-points diff_y_X_to_U dq/dy[j, i+½] = (q[j, i] - q[j-1, i]) / dy U-points diff_x_X_to_V dq/dx[j+½, i] = (q[j, i] - q[j, i-1]) / dx V-points

Example slice for diff_x_U_to_T:

# du_dx[j, i] = (u[j, i+1/2] - u[j, i-1/2]) / dx
#             = (u[j, i]     - u[j, i-1]   ) / dx
out = out.at[1:-1, 1:-1].set((u[1:-1, 1:-1] - u[1:-1, :-2]) / dx)

docs.title: Divergence, Curl, and Laplacian
docs.text:
diff = Difference2D(grid=grid)

divergence = diff.divergence(u, v)   # du/dx + dv/dy at T-points
curl       = diff.curl(u, v)         # dv/dx - du/dy at X-points
laplacian  = diff.laplacian(h)       # d²h/dx² + d²h/dy² at T-points

Discrete-non-divergence property: A velocity derived from a corner-streamfunction ψ via u = -diff_y_X_to_U(ψ), v = diff_x_X_to_V(ψ) is exactly non-divergent at interior T-points.

docs.title: Interpolation Operators
docs.text: Each interpolation moves a field between co-location points by averaging the two nearest neighbours along the relevant axis.

docs.title: Averaging table
docs.text:
Method Formula Source → Target T_to_U h[j, i+½] = ½(h[j,i] + h[j,i+1]) T → U T_to_V h[j+½, i] = ½(h[j,i] + h[j+1,i]) T → V T_to_X h[j+½, i+½] = ¼(h[j,i]+h[j,i+1]+h[j+1,i]+h[j+1,i+1]) T → X U_to_T u[j, i] = ½(u[j,i+½] + u[j,i-½]) = ½(u[j,i]+u[j,i-1]) U → T V_to_T v[j, i] = ½(v[j+½,i] + v[j-½,i]) = ½(v[j,i]+v[j-1,i]) V → T X_to_T 4-point average over q[j,i], q[j-1,i], q[j,i-1], q[j-1,i-1] X → T U_to_X u[j+½,i+½] = ½(u[j,i] + u[j+1,i]) U → X V_to_X v[j+½,i+½] = ½(v[j,i] + v[j,i+1]) V → X X_to_U q[j,i+½] = ½(q[j,i] + q[j-1,i]) X → U X_to_V q[j+½,i] = ½(q[j,i] + q[j,i-1]) X → V U_to_V 4-point average over u[j,i], u[j+1,i], u[j,i-1], u[j+1,i-1] U → V V_to_U 4-point average over v[j,i], v[j-1,i], v[j,i+1], v[j-1,i+1] V → U

Example slice for T_to_U:

# h_on_u[j, i+1/2] = 0.5 * (h[j, i] + h[j, i+1])
out = out.at[1:-1, 1:-1].set(0.5 * (h[1:-1, 1:-1] + h[1:-1, 2:]))

The key: h[1:-1, 1:-1] is h[j, i] and h[1:-1, 2:] is h[j, i+1] for interior column indices i = 1 … Nx-2.

docs.title: Kinetic Energy and Bernoulli Potential
docs.text: These operators live in finitevolx._src.operators.diagnostics and follow the same conventions.

docs.title: Kinetic energy at T-points
docs.text:
ke[j, i] = ½ (u²_on_T[j, i] + v²_on_T[j, i])

where the face-squared fields are averaged to cell centres:

u²_on_T[j, i] = ½ (u[j, i+½]² + u[j, i-½]²)
              = ½ (u[j, i]²   + u[j, i-1]²)

v²_on_T[j, i] = ½ (v[j+½, i]² + v[j-½, i]²)
              = ½ (v[j, i]²   + v[j-1, i]²)

# ke[j, i] at T-points
u2 = u**2;  v2 = v**2
u2_on_T = 0.5 * (u2[1:-1, 1:-1] + u2[1:-1, :-2])   # U → T in x
v2_on_T = 0.5 * (v2[1:-1, 1:-1] + v2[:-2, 1:-1])   # V → T in y
out = out.at[1:-1, 1:-1].set(0.5 * (u2_on_T + v2_on_T))

docs.title: Bernoulli potential at T-points
docs.text:
p[j, i] = ke[j, i] + g · h[j, i]

Both ke and h are at T-points, so this is a simple elementwise sum restricted to the interior:

out = out.at[1:-1, 1:-1].set(ke[1:-1, 1:-1] + gravity * h[1:-1, 1:-1])

docs.title: Slicing Reference
docs.text:
The table below collects all the slice patterns used in stencil implementations. Ny, Nx denote the total array sizes.

Pattern Meaning (rows = j, cols = i) Shape arr[1:-1, 1:-1] interior at (j, i), both directions (Ny-2, Nx-2) arr[1:-1, 2:] interior rows, one step east (Ny-2, Nx-2) arr[1:-1, :-2] interior rows, one step west (Ny-2, Nx-2) arr[2:, 1:-1] interior cols, one step north (Ny-2, Nx-2) arr[:-2, 1:-1] interior cols, one step south (Ny-2, Nx-2) arr[2:, 2:] one step north-east (Ny-2, Nx-2) arr[:-2, :-2] one step south-west (Ny-2, Nx-2)

Notice that every shifted slice has the same shape as the unshifted interior slice. This is possible because arrays have one ghost-cell ring on each side, so a single-step shift never reads outside the array bounds.

docs.title: Ghost-Cell Interaction at Stencil Boundaries
docs.text:
The first and last interior points see one ghost neighbour. For example, diff_x_T_to_U at the first interior U-column (i=1, output out[j, 1]) uses h[j, 1] (interior T-point) and h[j, 2] (second interior T-point) — no ghosts involved.

However, diff_x_U_to_T at i=1 uses u[j, 1] and u[j, 0]. If u[j, 0] is a ghost (zero by default), the result at i=1 reflects that zero ghost rather than a physical extrapolation. This is intentional: the caller sets ghost values via the boundary-condition layer before calling operators.

A consequence: the composition diff_x_U_to_T(diff_x_T_to_U(h)) equals d²h/dx² only at columns i = 2 … Nx-3 (deep interior), because the intermediate dh_u field has a zero ghost at i = 0 that pollutes column i = 1.

docs.title: Concrete example
docs.text:
For h[j, i] = c·i·dx and no boundary conditions applied:

dh_u = diff_x_T_to_U(h)
# dh_u[j, 0] = 0      ← ghost U-face, NOT written by the operator
# dh_u[j, 1] = c      ← first interior U-face
# dh_u[j, 2..Nx-2] = c ← rest of interior

result = diff_x_U_to_T(dh_u)
# result[j, 1] = (c - 0) / dx = c/dx   ← non-zero, ghost pollutes i=1
# result[j, 2..Nx-3] = (c - c) / dx = 0 ← correct 2nd derivative

This is correct operator behaviour. The ghost U-face at i=0 is the west boundary face U[j, ½]; its value must be supplied by the BC layer (periodic, no-slip, etc.), not by the forward-difference stencil. Always apply boundary conditions to intermediate fields before chaining operators.

docs.title: Example: Advection Step
docs.text:
A typical shallow-water advection step uses all four co-location points:

from finitevolx import (
    CartesianGrid2D, Difference2D, Interpolation2D, Vorticity2D,
    enforce_periodic,
)
import jax.numpy as jnp

grid  = CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(64, 64, 1.0, 1.0)
diff  = Difference2D(grid=grid)
interp = Interpolation2D(grid=grid)
vort  = Vorticity2D(grid=grid)

# ---- assume u, v, h are shape (66, 66) with updated ghosts ----

# 1. Potential vorticity at X-points
f     = jnp.zeros((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))           # Coriolis (T-points)
q     = vort.potential_vorticity(u, v, h, f)   # X-points

# 2. PV flux (energy-conserving corner-product form)
qu, qv = vort.pv_flux_energy_conserving(q, u, v)   # U- and V-points

# 3. Kinetic energy and Bernoulli potential
from finitevolx._src.operators.diagnostics import bernoulli_potential
p = bernoulli_potential(h=h, u=u, v=v)         # T-points

# 4. Tendencies
du_dt = -diff.diff_x_T_to_U(p) + qv           # U-points
dv_dt = -diff.diff_y_T_to_V(p) - qu           # V-points
dh_dt = -diff.divergence(h_u, h_v)            # T-points (h*u fluxes)

Every intermediate array has the same shape (66, 66). The ghost ring carries boundary-condition data; the interior [1:-1, 1:-1] carries the physical solution.

docs.title: Finite-Difference Operators
docs.text: This page covers the theory behind the finite-difference operators in finitevolX, explains the staggered-grid indexing conventions, and provides practical guidance for choosing and composing operators.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Ocean and atmosphere models compute spatial derivatives of scalar and vector fields at each time step. On an Arakawa C-grid the variables live at different staggered locations, so the derivative of a quantity at one location must be evaluated at a different location — and the rule for where the output lives is determined by the direction and sign of the shift.

The core question is:

Given a field at location A, how do we compute its derivative and what location does the result live at?

finitevolX answers this through a consistent forward / backward convention that is the backbone of all higher-level operators (divergence, vorticity, Laplacian, diffusion, advection, etc.).

docs.title: Staggered Grid Locations
docs.text:
All arrays share the same shape [Ny, Nx] with a one-cell ghost ring on each side. The physical interior is [1:-1, 1:-1]. Four location types are defined:

Symbol Location Array indices Description T Cell centre T[j, i] at (j, i) Scalars: thickness, pressure, temperature U East face U[j, i] at (j, i+½) x-velocity, x-flux V North face V[j, i] at (j+½, i) y-velocity, y-flux X NE corner X[j, i] at (j+½, i+½) Vorticity, PV, corner quantities

Same-index convention

U[j, i] stores the value at the east face of cell (j, i), i.e. at position (j, i+½). Similarly V[j, i] is at the north face (j+½, i). This means the forward difference T → U uses h[i+1] − h[i], whereas the backward difference U → T uses u[i] − u[i−1].

docs.title: Forward differences
docs.text:
A forward difference moves the output one half-step in the positive direction relative to the input:

\[ T \xrightarrow{\partial/\partial x} U, \qquad T \xrightarrow{\partial/\partial y} V, \qquad U \xrightarrow{\partial/\partial y} X, \qquad V \xrightarrow{\partial/\partial x} X \] Operator Stencil Use case diff_x_T_to_U \((h_{i+1} - h_i)/\Delta x\) Pressure gradient force, diffusion flux diff_y_T_to_V \((h_{j+1} - h_j)/\Delta y\) Pressure gradient force, diffusion flux diff_y_U_to_X \((u_{j+1} - u_j)/\Delta y\) Part of vorticity \(\partial u / \partial y\) diff_x_V_to_X \((v_{i+1} - v_i)/\Delta x\) Part of vorticity \(\partial v / \partial x\)

docs.title: Backward differences
docs.text:
A backward difference moves the output one half-step in the negative direction:

\[ U \xrightarrow{\partial/\partial x} T, \qquad V \xrightarrow{\partial/\partial y} T, \qquad X \xrightarrow{\partial/\partial y} U, \qquad X \xrightarrow{\partial/\partial x} V \] Operator Stencil Use case diff_x_U_to_T \((u_i - u_{i-1})/\Delta x\) Divergence, tracer tendency from flux diff_y_V_to_T \((v_j - v_{j-1})/\Delta y\) Divergence, tracer tendency from flux diff_y_X_to_U \((q_j - q_{j-1})/\Delta y\) Coriolis & vorticity-flux term diff_x_X_to_V \((q_i - q_{i-1})/\Delta x\) Coriolis & vorticity-flux term

Forward → Backward pairs

Every forward operator has a corresponding backward operator that reverses the shift. Composing diff_x_T_to_U followed by diff_x_U_to_T gives a second-order centred difference at T-points (i.e. the Laplacian in x), which is the basis for the diffusion operator.

docs.title: Divergence
docs.text:
The discrete divergence of a 2-D velocity field \((u, v)\) at T-points:

\[ \delta_{j,i} = \frac{u_{j,i+\frac{1}{2}} - u_{j,i-\frac{1}{2}}}{\Delta x} + \frac{v_{j+\frac{1}{2},i} - v_{j-\frac{1}{2},i}}{\Delta y} \]

This is the composition of two backward differences: diff_x_U_to_T + diff_y_V_to_T. It is available as Difference2D.divergence(u, v) or the standalone divergence_2d(u, v, dx, dy).

docs.title: Curl (Relative Vorticity)
docs.text:
The discrete curl of \((u, v)\) at X-points (corners):

\[ \zeta_{j+\frac{1}{2}, i+\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{v_{j+\frac{1}{2}, i+1} - v_{j+\frac{1}{2}, i}}{\Delta x} - \frac{u_{j+1, i+\frac{1}{2}} - u_{j, i+\frac{1}{2}}}{\Delta y} \]

This is diff_x_V_to_X − diff_y_U_to_X, available as Difference2D.curl(u, v).

docs.title: Laplacian
docs.text:
The 5-point discrete Laplacian at T-points:

\[ \nabla^2 h_{j,i} = \frac{h_{j,i+1} - 2h_{j,i} + h_{j,i-1}}{\Delta x^2} + \frac{h_{j+1,i} - 2h_{j,i} + h_{j-1,i}}{\Delta y^2} \]

Available as Difference2D.laplacian(h). Used directly in the diffusion and multigrid solver operators.

docs.title: Perpendicular Gradient (Geostrophic Velocity)
docs.text:
The operator grad_perp maps a T-point streamfunction \(\psi\) to C-grid face velocities via the geostrophic relation \((u, v) = (-\partial\psi/\partial y,\, +\partial\psi/\partial x)\), using a compact 4-point stencil that reads T-point ghost cells directly:

\[ u_{j, i+\frac{1}{2}} = -\frac{\psi_{j+1,i} + \psi_{j+1,i+1} - \psi_{j-1,i} - \psi_{j-1,i+1}}{4\,\Delta y} \] \[ v_{j+\frac{1}{2}, i} = +\frac{\psi_{j,i+1} + \psi_{j+1,i+1} - \psi_{j,i-1} - \psi_{j+1,i-1}}{4\,\Delta x} \]

The resulting velocity field is discretely non-divergent: \(\delta(u, v) = 0\) at all interior T-points. This is the standard geostrophic velocity reconstruction used in QG models.

docs.title: Ghost-Cell Conventions
docs.text:
All operators write only to [1:-1, 1:-1] interior cells. The one-cell ghost ring is used as follows:

Difference direction Ghost consumed Slice Forward x (T → U) East T ghost T[:, Nx−1] h[1:-1, 2:] at last col Forward y (T → V) North T ghost T[Ny−1, :] h[2:, 1:-1] at last row Backward x (U → T) West U ghost U[:, 0] u[1:-1, :-2] at first col Backward y (V → T) South V ghost V[0, :] v[:-2, 1:-1] at first row

Caller responsibility

Ghost cells for backward operators (west U-face, south V-face) are not filled by any forward operator — the caller must set them via boundary conditions before composing operators. Leaving them at zero is equivalent to imposing a homogeneous Dirichlet condition on the flux, which is correct for closed-wall BCs but wrong for periodic or open boundaries.

docs.title: 3-D Extension
docs.text: Difference3D applies the same 2-D horizontal stencils independently to each z-level. Array shapes are [Nz, Ny, Nx] and only the interior [1:-1, 1:-1, 1:-1] is written.

docs.title: Quick Usage
docs.text:
import jax.numpy as jnp
from finitevolx import CartesianGrid2D, Difference2D

grid = CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(ny=64, nx=64, Ly=1e6, Lx=1e6)
diff = Difference2D(grid=grid)

h  = jnp.ones((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))  # T-point field

# Forward difference: h at T-points → pressure gradient at U-points
dh_dx = diff.diff_x_T_to_U(h)   # shape [Ny, Nx], values at U-points

# Backward difference: u at U-points → divergence contribution at T-points
u = jnp.zeros((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))
v = jnp.zeros((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))
div = diff.divergence(u, v)      # shape [Ny, Nx], values at T-points

# Curl: relative vorticity at X-points
zeta = diff.curl(u, v)           # shape [Ny, Nx], values at X-points

# Laplacian: ∇²h at T-points
lap_h = diff.laplacian(h)        # shape [Ny, Nx], values at T-points

# Geostrophic velocity from streamfunction
psi = jnp.zeros((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))
u_geo, v_geo = diff.grad_perp(psi)  # u at U-points, v at V-points

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text:
What derivative do you need?
│
├── ∂(·)/∂x from T-points → diff_x_T_to_U  (result at U-points)
├── ∂(·)/∂y from T-points → diff_y_T_to_V  (result at V-points)
├── ∂(·)/∂y from U-points → diff_y_U_to_X  (result at X-points)
├── ∂(·)/∂x from V-points → diff_x_V_to_X  (result at X-points)
│
├── ∂(·)/∂x from U-points → diff_x_U_to_T  (result at T-points)
├── ∂(·)/∂y from V-points → diff_y_V_to_T  (result at T-points)
├── ∂(·)/∂y from X-points → diff_y_X_to_U  (result at U-points)
├── ∂(·)/∂x from X-points → diff_x_X_to_V  (result at V-points)
│
├── ∇·(u, v) at T-points  → diff.divergence(u, v)
├── ζ = ∇×(u, v) at X-pts → diff.curl(u, v)
├── ∇²h at T-points       → diff.laplacian(h)
└── geostrophic u, v      → diff.grad_perp(psi)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Arakawa & Lamb (1977) — Staggered C-grid layout and half-index notation
  • Sadourny (1975) — Discretisation of the shallow-water equations on a C-grid
  • Veros ocean model — C-grid operator conventions

docs.title: Elliptic Solvers for Ocean Models
docs.text: This page covers the theory behind the elliptic solvers in finitevolX, explains when each method applies, and provides practical guidance for choosing a solver.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Many ocean and atmosphere modelling tasks require solving 2-D elliptic partial differential equations of the form

\[ ( abla^2 - \lambda)\,\psi = f \]

where \( abla^2 = \partial^2/\partial x^2 + \partial^2/\partial y^2\) is the discrete 5-point Laplacian, \(\lambda\) is a Helmholtz parameter, and \(f\) is a known right-hand side.

Common physical applications:

Problem Equation \(\lambda\) Streamfunction from vorticity \( abla^2 \psi = \zeta\) 0 (Poisson) Pressure correction \( abla^2 p = abla \cdot \mathbf{u}\) 0 (Poisson) QG PV inversion \(( abla^2 - 1/R_d^2)\,\psi = q\) \(1/R_d^2\) (Helmholtz) Implicit diffusion \(( abla^2 - 1/( u\,\Delta t))\,T = -T^n/( u\,\Delta t)\) \(1/( u\,\Delta t)\)

docs.title: Boundary Conditions
docs.text:
The choice of boundary condition determines which spectral transform is used:

BC type Physical meaning Transform finitevolX solver Dirichlet \(\psi = 0\) on the virtual nodes one step outside the input array DST-I solve_poisson_dst / solve_helmholtz_dst Neumann \(\partial\psi/\partial n = 0\) half a cell outside the first / last input node DCT-II solve_poisson_dct / solve_helmholtz_dct Periodic \(\psi\) wraps in both directions FFT solve_poisson_fft / solve_helmholtz_fft

The direct solvers treat every input node as an unknown, so where the wall ends up depends on what you pass them. The convenience wrappers (streamfunction_from_vorticity, pv_inversion, pressure_from_divergence) slice the unknowns of their C-grid staggering out of the [Ny, Nx] array, solve, and embed the result in zeros, so the wall is the C-grid wall. On a from_interior grid the T cells are [1:-1] and the walls are the faces at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\); X node \(i\) sits at \(x = i\,\Delta x\), so the walls are the X nodes 0 and N-2 (index N-1 is outside the domain):

Wrapper (staggering) bc Unknowns Transform Wall ψ (X) "dst" [1:-2, 1:-2] DST-I \(\psi = 0\) on the wall nodes 0, N-2 ψ (X) "dct" [0:-1, 0:-1] DCT-I \(\partial\psi/\partial n = 0\) about the wall nodes 0, N-2 ψ (X) "fft" [1:-1, 1:-1] FFT periodic, period N-2 p (T) "dct" [1:-1, 1:-1] DCT-II \(\partial p/\partial n = 0\) on the faces p (T) "dst" [1:-1, 1:-1] DST-II \(p = 0\) on the faces p (T) "fft" [1:-1, 1:-1] FFT periodic, period N-2

This is the same wall method="cg" imposes through masked_laplacian with the Mask2D of the same staggering (xy_corner_strict for ψ, h for p), so every combination converges at second order.

When to use which BC

  • Dirichlet (DST): Streamfunction inversion in a closed basin (\(\psi = 0\) on coastline). Most common for vorticity inversion.
  • Neumann (DCT): Pressure correction with solid walls (\(\partial p / \partial n = 0\)).
  • Periodic (FFT): Doubly-periodic domains (idealised studies, turbulence simulations).

docs.title: Inhomogeneous Dirichlet Boundary Conditions
docs.text:
The table above assumes the boundary values are zero. Prescribed, non-zero values \(\psi = g\) on \(\partial\Omega\) — SSH from a parent model, a tide gauge, reanalysis data — reduce to the homogeneous case by the lifting trick. Split \(\psi = \psi_{\text{lift}} + \psi_{\text{hom}}\) with \(\psi_{\text{lift}} = g\) on the boundary; by linearity

\[ (\nabla^2 - \lambda)\,\psi_{\text{hom}} = f - (\nabla^2 - \lambda)\,\psi_{\text{lift}}, \qquad \psi_{\text{hom}} = 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega . \]

Discretely, the known cells \(K\) are the coast ring \(C\) — the dry cells with a wet neighbour, where masked_laplacian puts its homogeneous wall (for ψ, the C-grid wall nodes) — plus any observed wet cells \(O\), and the effective unknowns are \(E = W \setminus O\), every other wet cell. Every stencil neighbour of an \(E\) cell is in \(E\) or \(K\), so the 5-point equations at \(E\) split into \(A_{EE}\,\psi_E + A_{EK}\,g_K = f_E\), i.e.

\[ A_{EE}\,\psi_E = f_E - A_{EK}\,g_K . \]

This is exact block elimination: the lift is simply "\(g\) on \(K\), zero elsewhere", the correction \(A_{EK} g_K\) is the unmasked stencil applied to that lift (the lift lives on dry coast cells), and the homogeneous solve runs on the effective mask. Accuracy is set by the stencil alone (second order).

Solver How it takes known values CG operator on the effective mask (\(-A_{EE}\) is SPD for \(\lambda \ge 0\)) CG + multigrid multigrid preconditioner built on the effective mask Spectral (DST) ψ rectangle only: \(E\) is the X basin [1:-2, 1:-2] and \(K\) its wall nodes (rows / columns 0 and N-2) Capacitance solver built on the wet mask (its unknowns are every wet cell, \(\psi = 0\) on the coast); no observed cells

In finitevolX, pass known_values= (and optionally known_mask=) to streamfunction_from_vorticity or pv_inversion, or a BoundaryConditionSet as bc= (the T-point pressure_from_divergence refuses known values: its Dirichlet wall is on the cell faces); see the usage guide. The Known Boundary Values tutorial derives all of this from scratch — notation, block structure, pseudocode, a NumPy implementation, a convergence study, and gradients with respect to the boundary data.

docs.title: Spectral Solver Theory
docs.text:
All three spectral solvers follow the same three-step algorithm:
