  1. Forward transform: project \(f\) onto the spectral basis.
  2. Spectral division: divide each coefficient by its eigenvalue.
  3. Inverse transform: recover \(\psi\) in physical space.

The eigenvalues of the discrete 5-point Laplacian depend on the transform:

Transform Eigenvalue \(\lambda_k\) Null mode DST-I (\(N\) interior pts) \(-4/\Delta x^2 \cdot \sin^2\!\bigl(\pi(k+1)/(2(N+1))\bigr)\) None (all \(< 0\)) DCT-II (\(N\) pts) \(-4/\Delta x^2 \cdot \sin^2\!\bigl(\pi k/(2N)\bigr)\) \(k=0\) (\(\lambda_0 = 0\)) FFT (\(N\) pts) \(-4/\Delta x^2 \cdot \sin^2\!\bigl(\pi k/N\bigr)\) \(k=0\) (\(\lambda_0 = 0\))

The 2-D eigenvalue grid is the outer sum of 1-D eigenvalues: \(\Lambda_{j,i} = \lambda_j^y + \lambda_i^x - \lambda\).

For the Poisson equation (\(\lambda = 0\)) with Neumann or periodic BCs, the \((0,0)\) eigenvalue is zero (null space = constant solution). The solvers handle this by enforcing a zero-mean gauge: the \((0,0)\) spectral coefficient is set to zero, selecting the unique zero-mean solution.

Complexity

All spectral solvers run in \(O(N_y N_x \log(N_y N_x))\) time — the cost of the forward and inverse transforms. There is no iterative convergence loop.

docs.title: Irregular Domains: Capacitance Matrix Method
docs.text: Real ocean basins are not rectangles. The capacitance matrix method (Buzbee, Golub & Nielson, 1970) extends fast spectral solvers to domains defined by a binary mask.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
Given a mask \(M\) (True = ocean, False = land) and the \(N_b\) coast points \(\{b_k\}\) (land cells adjacent to ocean, where \(\psi = 0\); every ocean cell is an unknown, as in masked_laplacian / CG):

  1. Precompute (offline, \(O(N_b)\) spectral solves):
  2. For each boundary point \(b_k\), solve the rectangular problem \(L_{\text{rect}}\,g_k = e_{b_k}\) to get Green's function \(g_k\).

  3. Build the capacitance matrix \(C_{k,l} = g_l(b_k)\) and invert it.

  4. Solve (online, two rectangular solves + an \(O(N_b^2)\) correction):

  5. Compute the rectangular solution: \(u = L_{\text{rect}}^{-1} f\).
  6. Enforce \(\psi(b_k) = 0\) by solving \(C \alpha = u[B]\) for correction coefficients (the precomputed factorisation of \(C\)).
  7. Return \(\psi = L_{\text{rect}}^{-1}(f - \sum_k \alpha_k e_{b_k})\), a second rectangular solve, so the Green's functions are never stored.

The online cost is two rectangular solves plus the \(O(N_b^2)\) back-substitution: measured on a 2-vCPU CPU it is 5–11× the spectral solve on a rectangle, as fast as CG + multigrid at 128² and 2–3.6× faster at 256² (see the Solver Comparison).

Setup cost and memory

The solver stores the \(N_b \times N_b\) capacitance matrix, and the setup costs \(N_b\) rectangular solves plus an \(O(N_b^3)\) factorisation. For a circular basin with an island at 256² (\(N_b = 795\)) that is 5.8 MiB and about 4 s (9 MiB and 5 s for the 1 020 coast nodes of the 256² rectangle); both grow with the length of the coastline, so for very long coastlines or a mask that changes, use CG + multigrid.

docs.title: Iterative Solver: Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient
docs.text:
For problems where the capacitance matrix is too large, or when you need flexibility (e.g., variable coefficients), finitevolX provides a preconditioned Conjugate Gradient (CG) solver via Lineax.

The CG method iteratively minimises the quadratic form associated with the linear system \(A\psi = f\), where \(A\) is a symmetric operator (the masked Laplacian).

docs.title: Preconditioners
docs.text:
Preconditioning transforms the system \(Ax = b\) into \(M^{-1}Ax = M^{-1}b\) where \(M^{-1} \approx A^{-1}\). A good preconditioner clusters the eigenvalues of \(M^{-1}A\) near 1, dramatically reducing the number of CG iterations.

finitevolX provides three preconditioners, each suited to different problem characteristics. The table below ranks them from simplest to most powerful:

Preconditioner Setup cost Per-iteration cost CG iterations, 128² / 256² (measured) Spectral (FFT / DST) None 1 transform pair 31–63 (FFT), 15–48 (DST): grows with \(N\) Nyström \(k\) matvecs \(O(kN)\) dot product not measured (low rank: little gain on these problems) Multigrid Offline hierarchy build (20–60 ms) 1 V-cycle (\(O(N)\)) 5–7, independent of \(N\)

The iteration counts are for a rectangle and a circular basin with an island, \(\lambda \in \{0, 4\}\), \(\max|r| \le 2\times10^{-8}\max|f|\); unpreconditioned CG takes 340–760. The full table is in the Solver Comparison.

docs.title: Spectral Preconditioner
docs.text:
Applies the rectangular spectral solver (DST/DCT/FFT) as an approximate inverse: \(M^{-1} r = L_{\text{rect}}^{-1} r\).

Pros:

  • Essentially free — one forward + one inverse transform per iteration
  • No setup cost
  • Exact inverse only when the operator is the transform's: it works on the whole array with its wall at the array edge, so even on the ψ basin of a rectangle (wall nodes 0 and N-2) CG still needs 15 (DST) to 63 (FFT) iterations

Cons:

  • Ignores the mask: the rectangular solve doesn't know about land cells, so the preconditioner becomes less effective as the domain deviates from a rectangle
  • Cannot handle variable coefficients \(c(x,y)\) — it always assumes \(c = 1\)
  • Effectiveness degrades for highly irregular coastlines

Best for: a quick, setup-free solve. It is the wrappers' default preconditioner; CG + multigrid needs 3–13× fewer iterations.

docs.title: Nyström Preconditioner
docs.text:
Builds a low-rank approximate inverse by probing the operator with \(k\) random vectors. The resulting preconditioner captures the dominant spectral directions of \(A^{-1}\).

Pros:

  • Operator-only access: works with any matvec callable, no need to know the operator's structure
  • Can partially capture variable-coefficient and mask effects
  • Rank \(k\) is tunable — trade setup cost for preconditioner quality

Cons:

  • Setup requires \(k\) operator applications (can be expensive for large \(k\))
  • Low-rank: misses fine-scale structure, especially for poorly conditioned problems
  • Per-iteration cost is \(O(kN)\) rather than \(O(N \log N)\) for spectral
  • Quality depends on the rank \(k\) relative to the effective rank of \(A^{-1}\)

Best for: Problems where the operator is available only as a callable (no analytic structure to exploit), or as a complement when spectral preconditioning is insufficient but multigrid is not needed.

docs.title: Multigrid Preconditioner
docs.text:
Applies a single multigrid V-cycle from a zero initial guess. Because multigrid captures both high- and low-frequency components of \(A^{-1}\) across the grid hierarchy, it provides a spectrally complete approximation.

Pros:

  • Handles variable coefficients \(c(x,y)\) natively — the hierarchy is built with the actual operator
  • Handles masked/irregular domains natively — masks are coarsened through the hierarchy
  • \(O(N)\) cost per iteration (geometric series over grid levels)
  • Grid-independent iteration counts: CG + multigrid takes 5–7 iterations at 128² and 256² (unpreconditioned CG: 340–760)
  • The V-cycle is symmetric (n_pre == n_post), as CG requires

Cons:

  • Requires an offline build step (build_multigrid_solver, NumPy / SciPy) that precomputes the level hierarchy; rebuild it when the mask, coefficient or \(\lambda\) changes
  • More complex implementation

Best for: masked domains (it is the fastest CG measured) and variable-coefficient problems. Any grid shape coarsens (no divisibility constraint).

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text:
Is c(x,y) spatially varying?
├── Yes → Multigrid preconditioner
│         (spectral and Nyström can't represent variable coefficients well)
└── No (constant coefficient) ↓

Can you build the multigrid hierarchy (the operator is the 5-point
masked Helmholtz operator)?
├── Yes → Multigrid preconditioner (5–7 iterations, fastest CG)
└── No ↓

Is the operator close to the rectangular constant-coefficient one?
├── Yes → Spectral preconditioner (no setup, 15–63 iterations)
└── Operator-only access → Nyström preconditioner (rank 30–100)

docs.title: Factory Function
docs.text:
make_preconditioner dispatches to any of the three preconditioners based on a string key, which is convenient when the preconditioner choice is configurable:

pc = fvx.make_preconditioner("spectral", dx=dx, dy=dy, lambda_=1.0)
pc = fvx.make_preconditioner("nystrom", matvec=A, shape=(64, 64), rank=50)
pc = fvx.make_preconditioner("multigrid", mg_solver=mg)

docs.title: Multi-Layer / Batched Solves
docs.text:
QG PV inversion often requires solving a separate Helmholtz equation for each vertical mode, each with its own \(\lambda_k = 1/R_{d,k}^2\):

\[ (\nabla^2 - \lambda_k)\,\psi_k = q_k, \quad k = 1, \ldots, n_l \]

finitevolX handles this efficiently via jax.vmap:

  • Array lambda_: Pass a 1-D array of shape (nl,) and a PV field of shape (..., nl, Ny, Nx). Each layer is solved with its own \(\lambda_k\).
  • Scalar lambda_: All layers/batch elements use the same parameter.
  • Batch dimensions: Leading dimensions beyond (nl, Ny, Nx) are automatically preserved and vmapped over.

All spectral solvers are tracer-safe — they use jnp.where guards instead of Python if branches, so they work correctly inside jax.vmap and jax.jit even when lambda_ is a JAX tracer.

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text:
Is the domain a full rectangle?
├── Yes → Use spectral solver (method="spectral")
│         ├── ψ = 0 on boundary → bc="dst"
│         ├── ∂ψ/∂n = 0 on boundary → bc="dct"
│         └── Periodic → bc="fft"
└── No (masked/irregular domain) ↓

Fixed mask and λ, many solves, setup affordable (N_b up to ~1000)?
├── Yes → Use capacitance method (method="capacitance")
│         Pre-build with build_capacitance_solver()
└── No (mask or λ changes, very long coastline) ↓

Default → Use CG (method="cg")
          with preconditioner=make_multigrid_preconditioner(mg)
          (the default spectral preconditioner needs no setup but
          3–13× more iterations)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Buzbee, Golub & Nielson (1970) — On direct methods for solving Poisson's equations (capacitance matrix method)
  • Arakawa & Lamb (1977) — Computational design of the basic dynamical processes of the UCLA general circulation model
  • Vallis (2017) — Atmospheric and Oceanic Fluid Dynamics, Ch. 5 (QG potential vorticity inversion)
  • Hestenes & Stiefel (1952) — Methods of conjugate gradients for solving linear systems

docs.title: Elliptic Solvers: Usage Guide
docs.text: This page covers practical usage of finitevolX's elliptic solver module, from quick-start examples to multi-layer PV inversion on masked domains. The snippets run in order: later ones reuse the names the Quick Start defines.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
The fastest way to solve an elliptic problem: use a convenience wrapper.

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
import finitevolx as fvx

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

# 1. A 64 x 64-cell basin, 100 km on a side.  Arrays are [Ny, Nx] = [66, 66]:
#    the interior plus one ghost ring.
grid = fvx.CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(64, 64, 1e5, 1e5)
dx, dy, Ny, Nx = grid.dx, grid.dy, grid.Ny, grid.Nx

# 2. Vorticity at the X points, where psi lives (X node i sits at x = i dx)
x = jnp.arange(Nx)[None, :] * dx
y = jnp.arange(Ny)[:, None] * dy
zeta = jnp.sin(jnp.pi * x / grid.Lx) * jnp.sin(jnp.pi * y / grid.Ly)  # [Ny, Nx]

# 3. Invert for the streamfunction, psi = 0 on the C-grid walls
psi = fvx.streamfunction_from_vorticity(zeta, dx, dy, bc="dst")  # [Ny, Nx]

Pass the full [Ny, Nx] array and get the full array back: the wrappers know which nodes are unknowns (see Staggering and walls), so do not slice the interior by hand.

The masked examples below use a circular basin with an island, and a physical Helmholtz parameter \(\lambda = 1/R_d^2 > 0\):

# Ocean at T points (True = wet); Mask2D derives the psi (X) and p (T) masks
jj, ii = np.mgrid[:Ny, :Nx]
ocean = np.zeros((Ny, Nx), dtype=bool)
ocean[1:-1, 1:-1] = True
ocean &= (ii - Nx / 2) ** 2 + (jj - Ny / 2) ** 2 < (0.45 * Nx) ** 2
ocean &= (ii - 0.62 * Nx) ** 2 + (jj - 0.55 * Ny) ** 2 > (0.1 * Nx) ** 2
mask = fvx.Mask2D.from_mask(ocean)  # psi uses mask.xy_corner_strict, p uses mask.h

Rd = 2e4             # deformation radius [m]
lambda_ = 1 / Rd**2  # (∇² − λ) is negative definite for λ ≥ 0

docs.title: Convenience Wrappers
docs.text: finitevolX provides three high-level wrappers that handle solver dispatch internally. All three accept the same method, mask, capacitance_solver, and preconditioner keyword arguments.

docs.title: Streamfunction from Vorticity
docs.text:
Solves \(\nabla^2 \psi - \lambda\psi = \zeta\) for ψ at X points.

Spectral (rectangular domain)CG (masked domain)Capacitance (masked domain, fast) 
# Dirichlet BCs (ψ = 0 on the C-grid wall nodes, X index 0 and N-2) — most common
psi = fvx.streamfunction_from_vorticity(zeta, dx, dy, bc="dst")

# With a Helmholtz parameter (QG inversion, λ = 1/Rd²)
psi = fvx.streamfunction_from_vorticity(
    zeta, dx, dy, bc="dst", lambda_=lambda_
)

# A Mask2D gives the psi mask xy_corner_strict: psi = 0 on the coast nodes
psi = fvx.streamfunction_from_vorticity(
    zeta, dx, dy, method="cg", mask=mask, lambda_=lambda_
)

# One-time precomputation, for this mask and this λ
solver = fvx.build_capacitance_solver(mask, dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_)

# Reuse for many solves
psi = fvx.streamfunction_from_vorticity(
    zeta, dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_, method="capacitance",
    capacitance_solver=solver,
)

A plain array mask= is taken as the mask of the field being solved for (ψ: X points); a Mask2D supplies the right one itself.

docs.title: Pressure from Divergence
docs.text:
Solves \(\nabla^2 p = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}\) (always Poisson, \(\lambda = 0\)) for p at T points.

div_u = zeta  # any T-point field; the Neumann solve drops its mean (gauge)

# Neumann BCs (∂p/∂n = 0 on the cell faces) — standard for pressure with solid walls
p = fvx.pressure_from_divergence(div_u, dx, dy, bc="dct")

# The same Neumann wall on a masked basin: zero flux through every coast face
p = fvx.pressure_from_divergence(div_u, dx, dy, method="cg", mask=mask)

bc is honoured by every method or rejected, never ignored. The CG wall is the spectral one of the same bc: with method="cg", bc="dct" (the default) is zero flux through every wet–dry face and returns the solution with zero mean on each connected wet region; bc="dst" holds p = 0 on the wet–dry faces, half a cell out (the DST-II wall). The default preconditioner is the spectral solve with the same bc. method="capacitance" raises for pressure (it would hold p = 0 at the dry cell centres, not on the faces), and so do known_values / known_mask; bc="fft" is for the rectangular spectral solve only.

docs.title: Staggering and walls
docs.text: The wrappers know the staggering of what they solve for (ψ at X points, p at T points), pass only its unknowns to the transform and return them embedded in zeros, so the wall is the C-grid wall for every bc and method; see the wall table.

docs.title: PV Inversion (Multi-Layer)
docs.text:
Solves \((\nabla^2 - \lambda_k)\,\psi_k = q_k\) for each vertical mode, with \(\lambda_k = 1/R_{d,k}^2 \ge 0\).

Single layerMulti-layer (per-mode λ)With vertical mode decomposition 
pv = zeta
psi = fvx.pv_inversion(pv, dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_, bc="dst")

# lambda_ array: one value per vertical mode, 1/Rd² per mode
lambdas = 1.0 / jnp.array([40e3, 20e3, 10e3]) ** 2

# pv shape: (nl, Ny, Nx) or (batch, nl, Ny, Nx)
pv = jnp.stack([zeta, 0.5 * zeta, 0.1 * zeta])
psi = fvx.pv_inversion(pv, dx, dy, lambda_=lambdas, bc="dst")

# Decompose layer PV into vertical modes
H_layers = jnp.array([500.0, 1500.0, 3000.0])  # thicknesses [m]
g_prime = jnp.array([9.81, 0.025, 0.0125])     # reduced gravities [m s⁻²]
A_vert = fvx.build_coupling_matrix(H_layers, g_prime)
radii, Cl2m, Cm2l = fvx.decompose_vertical_modes(A_vert, f0=1e-4)
lambdas_k = 1.0 / radii**2  # 1/Rd_k² ≥ 0 per mode

# Transform to mode space
pv_layers = jnp.stack([zeta, 0.5 * zeta, 0.1 * zeta])
pv_modes = fvx.layer_to_mode(pv_layers, Cl2m)

# Invert each mode with its own λ_k
psi_modes = fvx.pv_inversion(pv_modes, dx, dy, lambda_=lambdas_k, bc="dst")

# Transform back to layer space
psi_layers = fvx.mode_to_layer(psi_modes, Cm2l)

docs.title: Known Boundary Values (Inhomogeneous Dirichlet)
docs.text:
Tutorial

For the full derivation — notation, the block linear system, pseudocode, a from-scratch NumPy implementation, convergence and gradients — see the Known Boundary Values tutorial.

By default every solver assumes \(\psi = 0\) on the boundary. When the boundary values are known but non-zero — SSH from a parent model, a tide gauge, reanalysis at an open boundary — pass them as known_values. streamfunction_from_vorticity and pv_inversion accept it (pressure_from_divergence refuses it, see below):

# psi rising from 0 (south) to 1e3 (north): a throughflow of 1e3 m² s⁻¹
g = 1e3 * y / grid.Ly * jnp.ones((Ny, Nx))  # [Ny, Nx]; only the known cells are read
psi = fvx.streamfunction_from_vorticity(
    zeta, dx, dy, method="cg", mask=mask, known_values=g
)

Which cells are known. The coast ring — the dry cells adjacent to at least one wet cell, around the outer walls and any islands — plus any extra wet cells you mark with known_mask. The coast is exactly where method="cg" puts its ψ = 0 wall: for ψ with a Mask2D it is the C-grid wall nodes (X rows / columns 0 and N-2 of a rectangle). Every wet cell is solved for. The returned solution equals known_values exactly on the known cells (so ψ carries the prescribed values on the dry wall nodes); values of known_values elsewhere are ignored. Inspect the ring with fvx.coast_ring(mask). The T-point pressure_from_divergence raises on known values: its Dirichlet wall is on the cell faces, while the lifting pins values at cell centres (the ghost cells, half a cell outside).

Under the hood this is the lifting trick: put the known values in a field \(\psi_{\text{lift}}\) (zero elsewhere), solve the homogeneous problem

\[ (\nabla^2 - \lambda)\,\psi_{\text{hom}} = f - (\nabla^2 - \lambda)\,\psi_{\text{lift}} \]

on the remaining cells, and return \(\psi = \psi_{\text{lift}} + \psi_{\text{hom}}\).

CG (any mask)CapacitanceSpectral (rectangular basin) 
psi = fvx.streamfunction_from_vorticity(
    zeta, dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_, method="cg", mask=mask, known_values=g
)

# Build on the SAME mask: its unknowns are every wet cell with
# psi = 0 on the coast, exactly the cells left to solve.
solver = fvx.build_capacitance_solver(mask, dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_)
psi = fvx.streamfunction_from_vorticity(
    zeta, dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_, method="capacitance", mask=mask,
    capacitance_solver=solver, known_values=g,
)

# No mask: solves the psi basin of the rectangle -- wet X nodes
# [1:-2, 1:-2] -- with the known values on its wall nodes (rows/columns
# 0 and N-2).  Requires bc="dst".
psi = fvx.streamfunction_from_vorticity(
    zeta, dx, dy, bc="dst", lambda_=lambda_, known_values=g
)

The spectral path solves exactly the problem method="cg" solves with the rectangle's Mask2D (its xy_corner_strict is wet on [1:-2, 1:-2]), and with known_values = 0 it is the ordinary bc="dst" solve.

docs.title: Sparse observations: known_mask
docs.text:
Interior observations are pinned the same way as the boundary ring (method="cg" only):

obs = jnp.zeros((Ny, Nx), dtype=bool).at[20, 30].set(True).at[25, 45].set(True)
values = jnp.zeros((Ny, Nx)).at[20, 30].set(120.0).at[25, 45].set(-50.0)

psi = fvx.streamfunction_from_vorticity(
    zeta, dx, dy, method="cg", mask=mask,
    known_values=values, known_mask=obs,
)
# psi[20, 30] == 120.0 and psi[25, 45] == -50.0 exactly

docs.title: Multi-layer PV inversion
docs.text:
known_values broadcasts against pv: a (Ny, Nx) field is shared by all layers, an (nl, Ny, Nx) array gives each layer its own values. Each layer's correction uses its own \(\lambda_k\).

psi = fvx.pv_inversion(
    pv, dx, dy, lambda_=lambdas, method="cg", mask=mask,
    known_values=g,   # (Ny, Nx) or (nl, Ny, Nx)
)

docs.title: Boundary conditions as a BoundaryConditionSet
docs.text:
bc also accepts a BoundaryConditionSet. Its face types choose the transform (all Dirichlet1D → "dst", all zero Neumann1D → "dct", all Periodic1D → "fft"), its mask feeds the mask-based methods, and non-zero Dirichlet1D values become known values on each face's wall nodes (the coast cells on the row / column just outside the wet cells: X rows 0 / N-2 and columns 0 / N-2 of a rectangle). That needs a basin whose outer coast lies on the four walls (a rectangle; island coasts are allowed and stay at zero): on any other Mask2D non-zero face values raise, so pass known_values on fvx.coast_ring(mask) instead. A zero face value can be a Python number or a concrete array (jnp.array(0.0)); a traced value cannot be inspected and counts as non-zero.

rect_mask = fvx.Mask2D.from_mask(np.pad(np.ones((Ny - 2, Nx - 2), dtype=bool), 1))
bc = fvx.BoundaryConditionSet(
    mask=rect_mask,                              # a Mask2D, or omit for method="spectral"
    south=fvx.Dirichlet1D("south", value=0.0),
    north=fvx.Dirichlet1D("north", value=1e3),   # prescribed psi on the north wall
    west=fvx.Dirichlet1D("west", value=0.0),
    east=fvx.Dirichlet1D("east", value=0.0),
)
psi = fvx.streamfunction_from_vorticity(zeta, dx, dy, bc=bc, method="cg")

West/east win on a node shared by two faces, as when the set fills ghost cells. An explicit known_values overrides the face values, and an all-zero set (BoundaryConditionSet.closed()) is the ordinary homogeneous solve. method="spectral" raises on a bc.mask (it solves the rectangle), and pressure_from_divergence raises on non-zero Dirichlet1D faces: a T-point Dirichlet value belongs on the face, which the cell-centred lifting cannot reach.

docs.title: Using the lifting directly
docs.text:
For your own solver or a solve loop that reuses the setup, use SolveDomain and KnownValueLifting:

# Setup (once): derived masks, then a solver on the effective domain
domain = fvx.SolveDomain(mask, known_mask=obs)
lifter = fvx.KnownValueLifting(domain, dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_)
eff = domain.effective_mask.astype(float)
A = lambda x: fvx.masked_laplacian(x, eff, dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_)

# Per step (JIT-friendly): correct, solve, reconstruct
known_values = jnp.where(obs, values, g)
rhs_corrected, value_lift = lifter.preprocess(zeta, known_values)
psi_hom, info = fvx.solve_cg(A, rhs_corrected, rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-10)
psi = lifter.postprocess(psi_hom * eff, value_lift)

The solver's unknowns must be exactly domain.effective_mask (every wet cell not in known_mask), with zero on the coast: build a CG operator on domain.effective_mask.

For multigrid, use it as the CG preconditioner — the wrapper then does the lifting for you:

mg = fvx.build_multigrid_solver(
    np.asarray(domain.effective_mask, dtype=float), dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_
)
psi = fvx.streamfunction_from_vorticity(
    zeta, dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_, method="cg", mask=mask,
    known_values=known_values, known_mask=obs,
    preconditioner=fvx.make_multigrid_preconditioner(mg),
)

The multigrid operator (default bc="dirichlet") is masked_laplacian's stencil with dry neighbours zero, so it is the same operator CG solves; the known-value lifting is done by the wrapper, so a standalone multigrid solve needs the lifted right-hand side.

docs.title: Direct Spectral Solvers
docs.text: For maximum control, use the spectral solvers directly. They treat every input node as an unknown (see the wall table), so here you do pass the unknowns of your staggering yourself.

docs.title: Poisson Solvers
docs.text:
f_in = zeta[1:-2, 1:-2]  # psi's unknowns: the wet X nodes of the rectangle

# Dirichlet (DST-I): ψ = 0 one node outside the input on every side
psi_in = fvx.solve_poisson_dst(f_in, dx, dy)

# Neumann (DCT-II): ∂p/∂n = 0 half a cell outside the input (zero-mean gauge)
p_in = fvx.solve_poisson_dct(div_u[1:-1, 1:-1], dx, dy)

# Periodic (FFT): doubly-periodic domain (zero-mean gauge)
psi_per = fvx.solve_poisson_fft(f_in, dx, dy)

# What streamfunction_from_vorticity(zeta, dx, dy, bc="dst") returns
psi = jnp.zeros_like(zeta).at[1:-2, 1:-2].set(psi_in)

docs.title: Helmholtz Solvers
docs.text:
# (∇² − λ)ψ = f with λ = 1/Rd² > 0
psi_in = fvx.solve_helmholtz_dst(f_in, dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_)
psi_in = fvx.solve_helmholtz_dct(f_in, dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_)
psi_in = fvx.solve_helmholtz_fft(f_in, dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_)

All Helmholtz solvers handle lambda_=0 internally (via tracer-safe null-mode guards), so they work correctly inside jax.vmap:

# Batched solve with per-layer lambda
lambdas = 1.0 / jnp.array([40e3, 20e3, 10e3]) ** 2
rhs_batch = jnp.stack([f_in, 0.5 * f_in, 0.1 * f_in])

psi_batch = jax.vmap(
    lambda r, l: fvx.solve_helmholtz_dst(r, dx, dy, l)
)(rhs_batch, lambdas)

docs.title: Capacitance Matrix Solver
docs.text: The capacitance method extends spectral solvers to irregular domains defined by a mask.

docs.title: Building the Solver
docs.text:
The offline step factorises the capacitance matrix. It costs \(N_c\) rectangular solves plus a dense \(N_c \times N_c\) factorisation (\(N_c\) = number of coast cells) and stores the \(N_c \times N_c\) matrix, so it grows with the coastline: see the measured build times and memory in the Solver Comparison. The solver's unknowns are every wet cell, with \(\psi = 0\) on the coast (the dry cells next to water): the same problem method="cg" solves on that mask, so the two agree to CG's tolerance.

# Binary mask: True = ocean, False = land
ocean_mask = np.ones((Ny, Nx), dtype=bool)
ocean_mask[:5, :] = ocean_mask[-5:, :] = False  # land border
ocean_mask[:, :5] = ocean_mask[:, -5:] = False

# Build solver (offline)
solver = fvx.build_capacitance_solver(
    ocean_mask, dx, dy,
    lambda_=lambda_,  # Helmholtz parameter, λ ≥ 0
    base_bc="dst",    # rectangular base solver (the default)
)

base_bc picks the rectangular base ("dst", the default, "fft" or "dct"). It only matters beyond the array edge, so every base gives the same solution when the mask's wet cells stay off the array edge (a dry ghost ring); "fft" and "dct" raise when a wet cell touches the edge, where only "dst" reproduces masked_laplacian. A singular base ("fft" / "dct" at \(\lambda = 0\)) is handled exactly, but "dst" is non-singular for every \(\lambda \ge 0\). A plain array mask is used as it is: it is the ψ mask, not a T mask.

docs.title: Using with Mask2D
docs.text:
When you have a Mask2D, pass it directly — the solver uses its ψ (X-point) mask xy_corner_strict, so ψ = 0 falls on the C-grid wall nodes:

cgrid_mask = fvx.Mask2D.from_mask(ocean)
solver = fvx.build_capacitance_solver(cgrid_mask, dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_)

docs.title: Online Solve
docs.text:
psi = solver(zeta)  # JIT-compilable, vmap-compatible

The solver returns \(\psi = 0\) on every dry cell (the coast included) and solves the 5-point equation on every wet cell; the online cost is two rectangular solves plus an \(O(N_c^2)\) back-substitution.

docs.title: Conjugate Gradient Solver
docs.text: For domains where the capacitance matrix is too large, use the preconditioned CG solver.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
psi_mask = jnp.asarray(mask.xy_corner_strict, dtype=float)  # psi's wet nodes
rhs = zeta * psi_mask

# Define the operator: (∇² − λ) with psi = 0 on the dry neighbours
def A(x):
    return fvx.masked_laplacian(x, psi_mask, dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_)

# Solve with a spectral preconditioner
psi, info = fvx.solve_cg(
    A, rhs,
    preconditioner=fvx.make_spectral_preconditioner(dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_, bc="fft"),
    rtol=1e-8,
    atol=1e-8 * float(jnp.max(jnp.abs(rhs))),
)
psi = psi * psi_mask  # zero out land points

Scale atol to the right-hand side as above rather than passing atol=0.0: lineax's stopping rule divides each residual entry by atol + rtol |rhs_i|, which is 0 where the masked right-hand side is zero, and the resulting NaN stops CG after one iteration (solve_cg then reports converged=False).

docs.title: Convergence Info
docs.text:
solve_cg returns a CGInfo named tuple:

psi, info = fvx.solve_cg(A, rhs)
print(f"Converged: {info.converged}")
print(f"Iterations: {info.iterations}")
print(f"Residual norm: {info.residual_norm:.2e}")

solve_cg does not raise when CG fails (pass throw=True for that): hitting max_steps, an indefinite operator (lambda_ < 0) or a preconditioner of the wrong sign all return converged=False. converged is checked on the explicit residual of the un-preconditioned system, max|rhs - A(x)| <= atol + rtol max|rhs|, and residual_norm is the L2 norm of that residual. The solve is differentiable with respect to lambda_ and dx, also with a preconditioner built from them. Its output can be non-zero on land (the spectral preconditioners ignore the mask), so multiply by the mask as above; the wrappers do.

docs.title: Preconditioners
docs.text:
Spectral (cheapest)Nyström (operator-only)Multigrid (most powerful)Factory (dispatches by name)Custom 
M_inv = fvx.make_spectral_preconditioner(
    dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_, bc="fft"
)

Uses the rectangular spectral solver on the whole array as an approximate inverse. No setup and one transform pair per iteration, but it ignores the mask and puts its wall at the array edge, so it is not exact even on a rectangular basin: CG still takes 15–63 iterations at 128²–256² (see the Solver Comparison).

M_inv = fvx.make_nystrom_preconditioner(
    A, shape=(Ny, Nx), rank=100, key=jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
)
psi, info = fvx.solve_cg(A, rhs, preconditioner=M_inv, rtol=1e-8)

Builds a low-rank approximate inverse by probing the operator with random vectors. Only needs matvec access — useful when you have a black-box operator with no analytic structure to exploit.

Nyström is a niche preconditioner

For standard Helmholtz/Poisson problems on known grids, the spectral or multigrid preconditioners are significantly more effective. Nyström captures only rank directions of the inverse; the remaining directions receive a scalar fallback, so the iteration count may not improve much over unpreconditioned CG. Consider Nyström only when no other preconditioner is available (e.g., a non-standard operator known only through matvec).

mg = fvx.build_multigrid_solver(mask, dx, dy, lambda_=lambda_)  # coeff= for c(x, y)
M_inv = fvx.make_multigrid_preconditioner(mg)
psi, info = fvx.solve_cg(A, rhs, preconditioner=M_inv, rtol=1e-8)

A single multigrid V-cycle as an approximate inverse. Captures both high- and low-frequency error across the grid hierarchy, handles variable coefficients and masked domains natively, and its operator is exactly masked_laplacian on the same mask. CG needs 5–7 iterations at 128² and 256² on a rectangle and an island basin, independent of the grid size.

# Dispatches to spectral, nystrom, or multigrid
M_inv = fvx.make_preconditioner("spectral", dx=dx, dy=dy, lambda_=lambda_)
M_inv = fvx.make_preconditioner(
    "nystrom", matvec=A, shape=(Ny, Nx), key=jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
)
M_inv = fvx.make_preconditioner("multigrid", mg_solver=mg)

Convenient when the preconditioner choice is a configurable parameter.

def my_preconditioner(r):
    """Any callable (Ny, Nx) -> (Ny, Nx) that approximates A^{-1}."""
    return -r / (2 / dx**2 + 2 / dy**2 + lambda_)  # Jacobi: 1 / diag(A)

psi, info = fvx.solve_cg(A, rhs, preconditioner=my_preconditioner)

Which preconditioner should I use?

See the Preconditioner Decision Guide in the theory page and the measured Solver Comparison. TL;DR: on a masked domain, CG + multigrid takes the fewest iterations and is the fastest CG; the spectral preconditioners need no setup but 3–13× more iterations.

docs.title: JIT and vmap Compatibility
docs.text: All solvers are fully compatible with jax.jit and jax.vmap.

docs.title: JIT Compilation
docs.text:
@jax.jit
def invert_pv(pv_field, lambdas):
    return fvx.pv_inversion(pv_field, dx, dy, lambda_=lambdas, bc="dst")

psi = invert_pv(pv, lambdas)

docs.title: Batched Solves with vmap
docs.text:
# Solve the same equation for many RHS fields
@jax.jit
def batch_solve(rhs_batch):
    return jax.vmap(lambda r: fvx.solve_poisson_dst(r, dx, dy))(rhs_batch)

rhs_ensemble = jnp.stack([f_in, -f_in])
psi_batch = batch_solve(rhs_ensemble)  # (n_ensemble, Ny-3, Nx-3)

docs.title: Gradient Through Solves
docs.text:
Spectral solvers are differentiable — you can backpropagate through them:

def loss(rhs):
    psi = fvx.solve_poisson_dst(rhs, dx, dy)
    return jnp.sum(psi ** 2)

grad_rhs = jax.grad(loss)(f_in)

docs.title: Double-Gyre Example Scripts
docs.text: The repository ships three example scripts that use the finitevolx API for spatial operators and finitevolx.heun_step for time integration. Each script uses xarray for preprocessing and postprocessing, writes sampled fields to Zarr, and saves an animated GIF showing the field evolution over time.

docs.title: Running the examples
docs.text:
Install the repository with the example dependencies:

uv sync --all-extras

Then run any example directly:

uv run python scripts/swm_linear.py
uv run python scripts/shallow_water.py
uv run python scripts/qg_1p5_layer.py

Each script writes two artifacts by default:

  • a *.zarr directory with sampled model fields and diagnostics
  • a *.gif animated figure showing the field evolution over time

Use --output-dir to choose a different location for the artifacts.

docs.title: Linear shallow-water model
docs.text:
Script: scripts/swm_linear.py

  • Periodic beta-plane, double-gyre wind forcing
  • Linearised momentum and mass equations
  • xarray coordinates for the initial height anomaly, Coriolis field, and wind forcing
  • Zarr output fields: eta, u, v, speed, relative_vorticity, kinetic_energy, mass_anomaly

docs.title: Nonlinear shallow-water model
docs.text:
Script: scripts/shallow_water.py

  • Periodic beta-plane, double-gyre wind forcing
  • Nonlinear continuity equation with total depth H + eta
  • Compact Bernoulli and advective closure in the momentum equation
  • Zarr output fields: eta, u, v, speed, relative_vorticity, kinetic_energy, minimum_depth

docs.title: 1.5-layer QG model
docs.text:
Script: scripts/qg_1p5_layer.py

  • Closed-basin Atlantic-style double-gyre (no-normal-flow solid walls, ψ = 0)
  • Potential-vorticity advection with Advection2D
  • Streamfunction inversion through solve_helmholtz_dst (homogeneous Dirichlet BCs)
  • Basin-scale defaults tuned toward the MQGeometry double-gyre benchmark (Lx = Ly = 5120 km, f0 = 9.375e-5 s^-1, beta = 1.754e-11 m^-1 s^-1)
  • Saved figure shows relative vorticity rather than streamfunction so the eddy field matches the expected diagnostic
  • Zarr output fields: q, psi, u, v, speed, relative_vorticity, pv_enstrophy

docs.title: Stability checks
docs.text: The repository test suite installs the script dependencies through the test extra and runs smoke tests that execute all three scripts on small grids, reopen the generated Zarr stores, and check that the saved fields remain finite and within expected ranges. These automated checks complement the longer manual runs used to generate the figures shown above.

docs.title: Interpolation Operators
docs.text: This page covers the theory behind the interpolation (averaging) operators in finitevolX, explains why staggered-grid interpolation is necessary, and gives practical guidance for composing operators.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
On an Arakawa C-grid, scalars live at T-points (cell centres) while velocities live at U/V-points (face centres) and vorticity at X-points (corners). Many operations require a quantity at a location other than where it is naturally defined:

  • Computing kinetic energy requires u² and v² both at T-points, but they are stored at U- and V-points respectively.
  • The Coriolis term \((f\,v)\) at U-points requires v to be interpolated from V-points to U-points (a cross-face average).
  • The potential vorticity \(((\zeta + f)/h)\) requires h to be interpolated to X-points where \(\zeta\) is defined.

finitevolX provides a complete set of second-order linear (arithmetic) averaging operators that move quantities between all four location types.

docs.title: Staggered Grid Locations
docs.text:
All arrays share the same shape [Ny, Nx] with a one-cell ghost ring.

Symbol Position Stored value T (j, i) — cell centre Scalars: \(h\), \(T\), \(p\) U (j, i+½) — east face x-velocity \(u\) V (j+½, i) — north face y-velocity \(v\) X (j+½, i+½) — NE corner Vorticity \(\zeta\), PV \(q\)

docs.title: 1-D (2-point) averages
docs.text:
For 1-D arrays or for a single direction in 2-D:

\[ \text{T} \to \text{U}: \quad h_{i+\frac{1}{2}} = \tfrac{1}{2}(h_i + h_{i+1}) \] \[ \text{U} \to \text{T}: \quad u_i = \tfrac{1}{2}(u_{i+\frac{1}{2}} + u_{i-\frac{1}{2}}) \]

These are the building blocks for all 2-D averages.

docs.title: Face-to-face averages (bilinear 4-point)
docs.text:
Moving between the two face types (U ↔ V) requires a 4-point bilinear average because the target point is displaced in both directions:

\[ u_{j+\frac{1}{2},i} = \tfrac{1}{4} \bigl(u_{j,i+\frac{1}{2}} + u_{j+1,i+\frac{1}{2}} + u_{j,i-\frac{1}{2}} + u_{j+1,i-\frac{1}{2}}\bigr) \] \[ v_{j, i+\frac{1}{2}} = \tfrac{1}{4} \bigl(v_{j+\frac{1}{2},i} + v_{j-\frac{1}{2},i} + v_{j+\frac{1}{2},i+1} + v_{j-\frac{1}{2},i+1}\bigr) \]

These cross-face averages are used in the Coriolis operator (interpolating the cross-component velocity to the target face) and in the energy-conserving momentum advection scheme.

docs.title: T ↔ X (corner) averages (bilinear 4-point)
docs.text: \[ h_{j+\frac{1}{2}, i+\frac{1}{2}} = \tfrac{1}{4}   \bigl(h_{j,i} + h_{j,i+1} + h_{j+1,i} + h_{j+1,i+1}\bigr) \quad (\text{T} \to \text{X}) \] \[ q_{j,i} = \tfrac{1}{4}   \bigl(q_{j+\frac{1}{2},i+\frac{1}{2}} + q_{j-\frac{1}{2},i+\frac{1}{2}}       + q_{j+\frac{1}{2},i-\frac{1}{2}} + q_{j-\frac{1}{2},i-\frac{1}{2}}\bigr) \quad (\text{X} \to \text{T}) \]

docs.title: Complete Operator Map
docs.text:
The table below lists every averaging operator in Interpolation2D and its physical interpretation.

Method From → To Average Typical use T_to_U T → U ½(T_i + T_{i+1}) Height at east face (pressure gradient) T_to_V T → V ½(T_j + T_{j+1}) Height at north face (pressure gradient) T_to_X T → X ¼(T_{j,i} + T_{j,i+1} + T_{j+1,i} + T_{j+1,i+1}) h at corners for PV = (ζ+f)/h U_to_T U → T ½(U_i + U_{i-1}) u² at T-points for kinetic energy V_to_T V → T ½(V_j + V_{j-1}) v² at T-points for kinetic energy X_to_T X → T ¼(X_{j+½,i+½} + X_{j-½,i+½} + X_{j+½,i-½} + X_{j-½,i-½}) Vorticity from corner to centre U_to_X U → X ½(U_j + U_{j+1}) u at corners for vorticity-flux V_to_X V → X ½(V_i + V_{i+1}) v at corners for vorticity-flux X_to_U X → U ½(X_j + X_{j-1}) Vorticity at face for Coriolis X_to_V X → V ½(X_i + X_{i-1}) Vorticity at face for Coriolis U_to_V U → V ¼(4-point bilinear) Cross-velocity for Coriolis term V_to_U V → U ¼(4-point bilinear) Cross-velocity for Coriolis term

docs.title: Ghost-Cell Conventions
docs.text:
All operators write only to [1:-1, 1:-1]. The ghost ring provides the stencil data for the last interior cell:

Direction Ghost consumed Slice T → U (x-forward) East T ghost T[:, Nx−1] h[1:-1, 2:] T → V (y-forward) North T ghost T[Ny−1, :] h[2:, 1:-1] U → T (x-backward) West U ghost U[:, 0] u[1:-1, :-2] V → T (y-backward) South V ghost V[0, :] v[:-2, 1:-1]

Bilinear averages

T_to_X, U_to_V, V_to_U, and X_to_T each read ghost cells in both directions. Make sure the appropriate BCs are applied before calling these operators in a boundary region.

docs.title: 3-D Extension
docs.text: Interpolation3D applies the same 2-D horizontal stencils to each z-level independently. Array shapes are [Nz, Ny, Nx] and only the interior [1:-1, 1:-1, 1:-1] is written. Currently T_to_U, T_to_V, U_to_T, and V_to_T are provided.

docs.title: Quick Usage
docs.text:
import jax.numpy as jnp
from finitevolx import CartesianGrid2D, Interpolation2D

grid = CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(64, 64, 1e6, 1e6)
interp = Interpolation2D(grid=grid)

h = jnp.ones((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))   # T-point thickness
u = jnp.zeros((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))  # U-point velocity
v = jnp.zeros((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))  # V-point velocity
f = jnp.ones((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))   # T-point Coriolis parameter

# Height at east faces (for shallow-water pressure gradient)
h_u = interp.T_to_U(h)   # shape [Ny, Nx], values at U-points

# Height at NE corners (for potential vorticity)
h_q = interp.T_to_X(h)   # shape [Ny, Nx], values at X-points

# Cross-face velocity average (for Coriolis term)
v_on_u = interp.V_to_U(v)   # v interpolated to U-points
u_on_v = interp.U_to_V(u)   # u interpolated to V-points

# Coriolis parameter at velocity points
f_on_u = interp.T_to_U(f)   # f at U-points (x-average)
f_on_v = interp.T_to_V(f)   # f at V-points (y-average)

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text:
What quantity do you need and where?
│
├── Scalar from T-points to...
│   ├── U-points (east face)   → T_to_U
│   ├── V-points (north face)  → T_to_V
│   └── X-points (NE corner)   → T_to_X
│
├── Velocity from face to...
│   ├── U → T  (x-mean)        → U_to_T
│   ├── V → T  (y-mean)        → V_to_T
│   ├── U → X  (y-mean)        → U_to_X
│   ├── V → X  (x-mean)        → V_to_X
│   ├── X → T  (bilinear)      → X_to_T
│   ├── X → U  (y-mean)        → X_to_U
│   └── X → V  (x-mean)        → X_to_V
│
└── Cross-face velocity for Coriolis...
    ├── u at V-points           → U_to_V  (bilinear 4-pt)
    └── v at U-points           → V_to_U  (bilinear 4-pt)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Arakawa & Lamb (1977) — Staggered C-grid layout
  • Sadourny (1975) — Cross-face averaging in the shallow-water system
  • Veros ocean model — C-grid interpolation conventions

docs.title: Arakawa C-Grid Masks
docs.text:
finitevolX provides three mask classes — Mask1D, Mask2D, Mask3D — that describe land/ocean geometry on an Arakawa C-grid. Every class operator in the package takes an optional mask class attribute of the matching dimension, so masks travel with operators rather than getting threaded through every call. See the Operator API section below for the full pattern and the stagger → mask field mapping.

The rest of this page documents Mask2D — the 2-D class — but the same factories (from_mask, from_dimensions, from_center, from_u_face …) and the same staggered-derivation pipeline are available on Mask1D (no v-face, no corner) and Mask3D (adds a w vertical face and native 3-D classification / stencil capability).

docs.title: The Arakawa C-grid layout
docs.text:
Mask2D builds all staggered masks from a single cell-centre wet/dry field, following the Arakawa & Lamb (1977) grid layout:

y
^
:           :
w-----v-----w..
|           |
|           |
u     h     u
|           |
|           |
w-----v-----w..   > x
Point Location Variable h cell centre tracers, height, pressure u east face zonal velocity v north face meridional velocity xy_corner NE corner (lenient) vorticity xy_corner_strict NE corner (strict) streamfunction

All staggered points use the same-index, positive half-step convention: u[j, i] is the east face of h[j, i], v[j, i] is the north face, and xy_corner[j, i] is the NE corner — matching CartesianGrid2D. See the Arakawa C-grid discretization notes for the underlying convention and a comparison with negative half-step alternatives.

docs.title: Creating masks
docs.text:
All you need is a binary h-grid mask (True = ocean, False = land). The factory method derives everything else:

import numpy as np
from finitevolx import Mask2D

# Rectangular basin with land boundaries
n = 10
h_mask = np.ones((n, n), dtype=bool)
h_mask[0, :] = h_mask[-1, :] = False
h_mask[:, 0] = h_mask[:, -1] = False

# With an island
h_mask[4:7, 4:7] = False

masks = Mask2D.from_mask(h_mask)

For an all-ocean domain, use the shortcut:

masks = Mask2D.from_dimensions(ny=12, nx=12)

Or construct from any float field at a known grid position, where NaN marks dry cells:

# From a field at cell centres (T-points): SSH, temperature, pressure, …
masks = Mask2D.from_center(ssh_field)

# From a field at u-faces, v-faces, or xy-corners.  Pass `mode=` to
# choose the inversion strategy when the inverse mapping back to the
# h-grid is non-unique:
#   mode='permissive'  → h wet iff *any* surrounding face/corner wet
#   mode='conservative' → h wet iff *all* surrounding face/corner wet
masks = Mask2D.from_u_face(u_field, mode="permissive")
masks = Mask2D.from_v_face(v_field, mode="permissive")
masks = Mask2D.from_corner(vorticity_field, mode="conservative")

docs.title: Staggered variable locations
docs.text: Each variable type sits at a different position within a grid cell. The figures below show the actual staggered positions for several domain topologies:

docs.title: Land / coast classification
docs.text: The mask includes a 4-level classification (0 = land, 1 = coast, 2 = near-coast, 3 = open ocean):

docs.title: Vorticity boundary classification
docs.text:
At xy-corner points, cells are classified based on their relationship to adjacent velocity faces:

  • xy_corner_valid — interior: all 4 adjacent velocity faces are wet
  • xy_corner_y_wall — on a vertical (y-direction) boundary
  • xy_corner_x_wall — on a horizontal (x-direction) boundary
  • xy_corner_convex — at convex corners (both boundary types)

docs.title: Stencil capability and adaptive WENO
docs.text:
Each cell stores how many contiguous wet neighbours it has in each direction via StencilCapability2D. This drives adaptive stencil selection for WENO reconstruction near coastlines:

# Mutually-exclusive masks: largest usable stencil at each point
adaptive = masks.get_adaptive_masks(direction="x", source="h")
# adaptive[2]  → 1st-order upwind only
# adaptive[4]  → WENO3
# adaptive[6]  → WENO5
# adaptive[8]  → WENO7
# adaptive[10] → WENO9

docs.title: Jupyter notebook
docs.text: A complete interactive demo is available as a jupytext notebook: notebooks/demo_masks.py

docs.title: Operator API: how operators consume masks
docs.text:
Every class operator in finitevolx takes an optional mask class attribute of the matching dimension. The mask travels with the operator; once constructed, method calls don't need to pass the mask through per call.

import finitevolx as fvx

grid = fvx.CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(64, 64, 1e6, 1e6)
mask = fvx.Mask2D.from_mask(h_mask)

# Mask as a class attribute — set once, consumed on every call.
diff = fvx.Difference2D(grid=grid, mask=mask)
adv  = fvx.Advection2D(grid=grid, mask=mask)
diff_op = fvx.Diffusion2D(grid=grid, mask=mask)

# Unmasked operators are the default — just omit `mask=`.
diff_noop = fvx.Difference2D(grid=grid)   # mask=None

docs.title: The three-layer rule
docs.text:
finitevolx keeps masks out of the lowest two layers, so stencil and functional code stays coordinate-and-mask agnostic:

Layer Example Mask-aware? Layer 1 — raw stencils diff_x_fwd, avg_y_bwd, … in stencils.py No Layer 2 — functional helpers _curl_2d, divergence_2d, diffusion_2d, kinetic_energy, enstrophy, _geostrophic_velocity_sphere (private), arakawa_jacobian, … No Layer 3 — class operators Difference2D, Interpolation2D, Divergence2D, Vorticity2D, Coriolis2D, Advection2D, Diffusion2D, MomentumAdvection2D, Energetics2D, Strain2D, QGPotentialVorticity2D, ArakawaJacobian2D, and their 1D / 3D / Spherical* siblings Yes, via self.mask

The pointwise and stencil diagnostics below have Layer-3 class forms, so in a masked domain you don't need to mask them by hand:

Layer-2 helper Layer-3 class form kinetic_energy, bernoulli_potential, available_potential_energy Energetics2D(grid, mask) methods of the same name shear_strain, tensor_strain Strain2D.shear, Strain2D.tensor strain_magnitude_squared, okubo_weiss Strain2D.magnitude_squared(u, v), Strain2D.okubo_weiss(u, v) relative_vorticity_cgrid, sw_potential_vorticity Vorticity2D.relative_vorticity, Vorticity2D.potential_vorticity enstrophy, potential_enstrophy Vorticity2D.enstrophy(u, v), Vorticity2D.potential_enstrophy(u, v, h, f) qg_potential_vorticity, stretching_term, potential_vorticity_multilayer QGPotentialVorticity2D.__call__, .stretching, .multilayer arakawa_jacobian ArakawaJacobian2D(grid, mask) (full-shape output, zero ghost ring) _geostrophic_velocity_sphere (private) SphericalDifference2D.geostrophic_velocity(h, f, gravity) 
energetics = fvx.Energetics2D(grid=grid, mask=mask)
ke = energetics.kinetic_energy(u, v)       # dry T-cells exactly 0

strain = fvx.Strain2D(grid=grid, mask=mask)
ow = strain.okubo_weiss(u, v)              # T-points, dry T-cells exactly 0

Energetics2D, Strain2D, QGPotentialVorticity2D and ArakawaJacobian2D zero every field input on the dry interior cells of its stagger before any stencil reads it, and mask outputs with jnp.where, so interior land values stored as NaN (e.g. from Mask2D.from_center) neither leak into wet cells nor survive at dry ones. The ghost ring is BC-owned: it is passed through unchanged and must be finite.

SphericalDifference2D.geostrophic_velocity only guards the division (it sets the face-averaged f to 1 on dry faces); its 4-point stencils read h on neighbouring land cells for wet coastal faces, so land h must be finite there. The same holds for the other existing class operators, which mask outputs but do not sanitize inputs.

Diagnostics without a class form:

  • total_energy, total_enstrophy are domain reductions, not stencils. Pass them fields that are already masked (e.g. from the class forms above) so dry cells contribute zero.
  • vertical_velocity takes a per-call mask=Mask3D: it zeroes the divergence on dry T-points (mask.h) and its output on dry W-faces (mask.w); the output has the same [Nz, Ny, Nx] shape as mask.w.

If you do call a Layer-2 helper directly and want masked output, apply the mask at the call site: ke = jnp.where(mask.h, kinetic_energy(u, v), 0.0) (a plain * mask.h also works when the inputs are finite on land). For pointwise helpers whose inputs live on different staggers (e.g. okubo_weiss(sn, ss, omega) with sn at T-points and ss, omega at X-points), the class form also does the X → T averaging for you.

docs.title: Dimension → mask type mapping
docs.text:
Operators take the mask class matching their dimension:

Operator class Mask type Example *1D (Difference1D, Interpolation1D, Advection1D) Mask1D \| None Difference1D(grid=g, mask=Mask1D.from_mask(h)) *2D (every 2-D operator) Mask2D \| None Advection2D(grid=g, mask=Mask2D.from_mask(h)) *3D (every 3-D operator) Mask3D \| None Diffusion3D(grid=g, mask=Mask3D.from_mask(h))

Spherical 2-D / 3-D operators take the Cartesian Mask2D / Mask3D — the mask geometry is coordinate-agnostic at the post-compute-multiply layer. A dedicated SphericalMask2D / SphericalMask3D is a TODO for future work.

docs.title: Stagger → mask field mapping
docs.text:
The core convention is one operator output → one mask field, chosen by the operator's output stagger. Every operator follows the same mapping:

Output stagger Mask field Operators / methods T (cell centre) mask.h divergence, laplacian, U→T / V→T / X→T differences and interpolations, Advection*, Diffusion*, BiharmonicDiffusion*, Energetics2D.*, Strain2D.tensor / .magnitude_squared / .okubo_weiss, QGPotentialVorticity2D.*, ArakawaJacobian2D U (east face) mask.u T→U / X→U / V→U differences and interpolations, grad_perp u-component, Coriolis* du_cor, MomentumAdvection* du_adv, SphericalDifference2D.geostrophic_velocity u_g V (north face) mask.v T→V / X→V / U→V, grad_perp v-component, Coriolis* dv_cor, MomentumAdvection* dv_adv, SphericalDifference2D.geostrophic_velocity v_g X (NE corner) mask.xy_corner_strict curl, T→X / U→X / V→X, relative & potential vorticity, Vorticity2D.enstrophy / .potential_enstrophy, Strain2D.shear, pv_flux_* U/V-stagger outputs where applicable

The X-output mapping uses the strict 4-of-4 corner mask (xy_corner_strict) because a corner-output value is trusted only when all four surrounding T-cells are wet. The lenient xy_corner mask is not currently consumed by any operator — it's available for users building their own.

docs.title: Four patterns for mask application
docs.text:
Under the hood, operators apply masks in one of four patterns depending on what's safe. You don't need to know which is which for normal usage — the result is always "dry cells at the output stagger are exactly 0" — but the distinctions matter when customising or inheriting:

Pattern 1 — Post-compute multiply. Used by the majority of operators: Difference*, Interpolation*, Vorticity3D, Spherical*, Energetics2D, QGPotentialVorticity2D, ArakawaJacobian2D. Compute the output as if all-ocean, then multiply by the stagger-matched mask field at the end. Cheap and simple. The #206 diagnostic classes (Energetics2D, Strain2D, QGPotentialVorticity2D, ArakawaJacobian2D) use the NaN-safe variant: zero the inputs on dry cells first, then select with jnp.where(mask, out, 0) instead of multiplying.

Pattern 2 — Pass-down into sub-operators. Used by composed operators with no tricky division — Divergence2D, Vorticity2D, MomentumAdvection2D, Strain2D (its T-point combinations mask the X-point shear and vorticity before averaging them X → T, so a coastal T-cell averages in zeros from its dry corners). The outer class wires its mask into every internal sub-operator at __init__ time, so intermediate staggered fields are already zero at dry cells. The outer method trusts the pass-down and typically doesn't need an extra multiply.

  • Special case for Vorticity2D.potential_vorticity: the (zeta + f) / h division would produce NaN at every dry X-corner under pass-down (because h_on_q == 0). The method preserves the existing "NaN at wet zero-thickness" sentinel but replaces mask-induced NaNs with exact 0 via a final jnp.where(mask.xy_corner_strict, out, 0). Same fix applies to SphericalVorticity2D.potential_vorticity and Vorticity2D.potential_enstrophy (built on it). SphericalDifference2D.geostrophic_velocity faces the same division (a dry face can have f_on_face = 0): it sets the face-averaged f to 1 on every dry face right before dividing, so the value and its reverse-mode gradient stay finite, then masks with jnp.where. Vorticity2D.potential_vorticity likewise divides by 1 at dry corners, where pass-down masking makes h_on_q exactly 0.

Pattern 3 — Intermediate flux masking. Used by Diffusion2D and Diffusion3D only. Post-compute multiply is not sufficient for diffusion because the divergence at wet T-cells adjacent to land would be contaminated by polluted dry-side face fluxes. Instead the class wrappers apply the mask in three steps:

flux_x *= mask.u        # U-face stage
flux_y *= mask.v        # V-face stage
tendency *= mask.h      # final output

The shared kernel is _diffusion_2d_impl(h, kappa, dx, dy, mh, mu, mv) in finitevolx._src.diffusion.diffusion; Diffusion3D vmaps it per-z-slice with sliced masks (Pattern B in #209's terminology).

Pattern 4 — The masked harmonic operator applied twice. Used by BiharmonicDiffusion2D / 3D and SphericalBiharmonicDiffusion2D / 3D. The tendency is −κ · Dm(Dm(h)), where Dm is the masked no-flux harmonic operator of Pattern 3 (the inner Diffusion* / SphericalDiffusion* is built with the outer mask). Dry inputs are zeroed with jnp.where first, so land may hold NaN or a fill value. Because the second pass also zeroes the wet→dry fluxes, the dry zeros of the intermediate Dm(h) are never read: the coast is a no-flux wall for both h and ∇²h, exactly like the closed domain walls. The result is conservative (Σ_wet ∂h/∂t = 0) and symmetric on the wet cells, and no land value reaches a wet cell. (Before #292 the inner Laplacian was unmasked and post-multiplied by mask.h, which read land values and was not conservative.)

docs.title: Pattern A vs Pattern B for 3-D operators
docs.text:
The 3-D wrappers that vmap an inner 2-D operator over z-levels (Vorticity3D, Coriolis3D, Spherical*3D, MomentumAdvection3D) use Pattern A (post-compute): the inner 2-D op is always constructed mask=None and the 3-D wrapper owns the mask, applying * self.mask.<stagger> after the vmap and zero_z_ghosts. This is cleaner than trying to thread per-z mask slices into the vmap'd 2-D op.

Diffusion3D (and BiharmonicDiffusion3D, built on it) is the exception and uses Pattern B (vmap with per-z sliced masks) because its intermediate flux masking makes Pattern A incorrect. See the Diffusion module docstring for the implementation.

docs.title: Advection hierarchy pre-build
docs.text:
Advection1D / Advection2D / Advection3D are the special case where "mask as field" matters for performance, not just ergonomics. When constructed with a mask, __init__ pre-builds the (2, 4, 6, 8, 10) adaptive stencil hierarchy via mask.get_adaptive_masks(...) — once, up-front — and stores the result on the operator. Every subsequent call then uses the cached hierarchy, narrowed at dispatch time (by the narrow_mask_hierarchy helper) to the subset of tiers the chosen reconstruction method needs:

adv = fvx.Advection2D(grid=grid, mask=mask)  # builds (2,4,6,8,10) hierarchies

# First call uses the cached hierarchies; no get_adaptive_masks recomputation.
dh_dt = adv(h, u, v, method="weno5")

# A second method call on the same instance reuses the cache and
# narrows to (2, 4) on the fly for WENO3.
dh_dt = adv(h, u, v, method="weno3")

This is the main reason the Advection API moved from a per-call mask= kwarg to a class field: masks under JIT now compile once per Advection* instance instead of once per (instance, method) pair.

docs.title: Changing the mask on an operator
docs.text:
equinox Modules are immutable — op.mask = new_mask will raise. To "change" a mask on an operator, use eqx.tree_at to produce a new operator instance with the field updated:

import equinox as eqx

# Start with one mask ...
adv_summer = fvx.Advection2D(grid=grid, mask=summer_mask)

# ... and produce a new instance with a different mask.  The grid and
# reconstruction module are shared (no copy); only `mask` (and, for
# Advection, the pre-built hierarchies — eqx.tree_at reconstructs the
# __init__ path correctly for all affected fields) is swapped.
adv_winter = eqx.tree_at(lambda o: o.mask, adv_summer, winter_mask)

For composed operators (Divergence2D, Vorticity2D, MomentumAdvection2D, etc.) the outer self.mask is independent of the mask stored on the internal sub-operators, so you may also need to swap those — the simpler alternative is usually to just construct a fresh operator from scratch:

# Cleaner for composed ops
vort_winter = fvx.Vorticity2D(grid=grid, mask=winter_mask)

docs.title: Migration from the old per-call kwarg API
docs.text:
Some operators used to take mask= as a per-call keyword argument. In the current API, the mask is always a class field. Translation:

# Old (removed)
adv = fvx.Advection2D(grid=grid)
adv(h, u, v, method="weno5", mask=mask)

cor = fvx.Coriolis2D(grid=grid)
cor(u, v, f, mask=mask)

# New
adv = fvx.Advection2D(grid=grid, mask=mask)
adv(h, u, v, method="weno5")

cor = fvx.Coriolis2D(grid=grid, mask=mask)
cor(u, v, f)

Diffusion2D, Diffusion3D, diffusion_2d, Difference2D.grad_perp, kinetic_energy, enstrophy, and potential_enstrophy used to take raw-array mask_h / mask_u / mask_v keyword arguments. Those are all removed:

  • Diffusion2D / Diffusion3D take a Mask2D / Mask3D class field instead.
  • diffusion_2d (the Layer-2 free function) is mask-free. If you want masked diffusion, use the class operator.
  • Difference2D.grad_perp uses the self.mask class field (set on Difference2D at construction).
  • kinetic_energy / enstrophy / potential_enstrophy are Layer-2 mask-free. Apply masks at the call site:
ke = fvx.kinetic_energy(u, v) * mask.h
z  = fvx.enstrophy(omega)     * mask.xy_corner_strict
pe = fvx.potential_enstrophy(q, h) * mask.xy_corner_strict

docs.title: Multigrid Helmholtz Solver
docs.text: This page covers the theory behind the geometric multigrid solver in finitevolX, its variable-coefficient Helmholtz operator, and the three differentiation strategies for computing gradients through the solve.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
The spectral and capacitance-matrix solvers in finitevolX handle constant-coefficient Helmholtz equations efficiently. However, many ocean modelling tasks require solving the variable-coefficient generalisation:

\[ abla \cdot igl(c(x,y)\, abla u igr) - \lambda\,u = f \]

where \(c(x,y)\) is a spatially varying coefficient (e.g. layer thickness, diffusivity, or Rossby-radius field) and the domain may be irregular (masked).

Application Equation \(c(x,y)\) \(\lambda\) Variable-thickness QG \( abla \cdot (H\, abla \psi) - \psi/R_d^2 = q\) Layer thickness \(H(x,y)\) \(1/R_d^2\) Spatially varying diffusion \( abla \cdot (\kappa\, abla T) = f\) Diffusivity \(\kappa(x,y)\) 0 Topographic PV inversion \( abla \cdot (f_0^2/N^2 \cdot abla \psi) - eta y\,\psi = q\) Stratification-dependent Varies

Spectral methods cannot handle spatially varying \(c(x,y)\) because the eigenvalue decomposition assumes constant coefficients. CG can handle it, but converges slowly without a good preconditioner. Geometric multigrid is the standard approach: it provides both a fast standalone solver and an excellent preconditioner for CG.

docs.title: Geometric Multigrid: Overview
docs.text: Multigrid accelerates iterative solvers by exploiting a hierarchy of progressively coarser grids. The key insight: simple smoothers (e.g. Jacobi) efficiently damp high-frequency error on any grid, but leave low-frequency error untouched. By restricting the problem to a coarser grid, those low-frequency components become high-frequency — and can be damped cheaply.

docs.title: The V-Cycle
docs.text:
The fundamental building block is the V-cycle, a recursive algorithm that visits each level of the grid hierarchy:

Level 0 (finest)    ●───smooth───●───────────────────────●───smooth───●
                         ↓ restrict                   prolong ↑
Level 1             ·····●───smooth───●───────●───smooth───●·····
                              ↓ restrict   prolong ↑
Level 2 (coarsest)  ··········●───exact solve───●··········

Algorithm for v_cycle(u, rhs, level):

  1. If at the coarsest level: solve exactly (bottom solve).
  2. Pre-smooth: apply \(\nu_1\) weighted Jacobi iterations.
  3. Residual: compute \(r = f - A u\).
  4. Restrict: transfer \(r\) to the coarse grid, \(r_c = R\,r\).
  5. Recurse: solve \(A_c\,e_c = r_c\) on the coarse grid (V-cycle), with the Galerkin operator \(A_c = R\,A\,P\).
  6. Prolongate: interpolate \(e_c\) back to the fine grid.
  7. Correct: \(u \leftarrow u + e_{\text{fine}}\).
  8. Post-smooth: apply \(\nu_2\) weighted Jacobi iterations.

Multiple V-cycles are applied to drive the residual to convergence.

docs.title: Variable-Coefficient Helmholtz Stencil
docs.text:
On the finest level the operator is discretised using a 5-point finite-volume stencil. Face coefficients \(c_x\) and \(c_y\) live on the staggered faces between cell centres:

\[ (Au)_{j,i} = \frac{c_{x,j,i}\,(u_{j,i+1} - u_{j,i}) - c_{x,j,i-1}\,(u_{j,i} - u_{j,i-1})}{\Delta x^2} + \frac{c_{y,j,i}\,(u_{j+1,i} - u_{j,i}) - c_{y,j-1,i}\,(u_{j,i} - u_{j-1,i})}{\Delta y^2} - \lambda\,u_{j,i} \]

Face coefficients are computed by averaging the cell-centre coefficient \(c(x,y)\) to the faces:

\[ c_{x,j,i} = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(c_{j,i} + c_{j,i+1}\bigr) \cdot m_{x,j,i} \]

where \(m_{x,j,i} = 1\) only when both cells \((j,i)\) and \((j,i+1)\) are wet (inside the mask). Faces between a wet and a dry cell are set by the boundary condition below.

docs.title: Boundary Conditions
docs.text:
build_multigrid_solver(..., bc=...) sets the condition on every face between a wet cell and a dry one (land, or outside the array), on every level:

bc Wet–dry face Use for "dirichlet" (default) keeps its coefficient; the dry neighbour's value is \(0\) the streamfunction \(\psi\) at X points (QG PV inversion), \(\psi = 0\) on the coast "neumann" zero coefficient: no flux pressure / free surface at T points (pass mask.h)

With bc="dirichlet" and coeff=None the finest-level operator is exactly masked_laplacian with dry neighbours zero: for \(\psi\) on Mask2D.xy_corner_strict the wall sits on the dry X nodes next to the wet ones (index \(0\) and \(N-2\) on a rectangle built with from_interior). The wet–dry faces only add to the diagonal,

\[ (Au)_{j,i} \mathrel{-}= \Bigl(\sum_{\text{wet–dry faces}} \frac{c_{j,i}}{h^2}\Bigr)\, u_{j,i}, \]

with \(h = \Delta x\) or \(\Delta y\) and \(c_{j,i}\) the wet cell's coefficient. The operator is negative definite for every \(\lambda \ge 0\).

With bc="neumann" the operator annihilates a constant on each connected wet component, so at \(\lambda = 0\) it is singular. The solver then works in the zero-mean gauge: it projects the right-hand side onto its solvable (zero-mean) part and returns the zero-mean solution on each component.

Out-of-bounds neighbours are zero-padded, so nothing wraps periodically across opposite edges.

docs.title: Weighted Jacobi Smoother
docs.text:
The smoother updates the solution pointwise:

\[ u^{(k+1)} = u^{(k)} + \omega\,D^{-1}\bigl(f - A\,u^{(k)}\bigr) \]

where \(D = \text{diag}(A)\) is the diagonal of the operator and \(\omega \in (0, 1)\) is the relaxation weight. The diagonal is precomputed during the offline build phase. The default \(\omega = 0.8\) damps every mode in the upper half of the 5-point spectrum by at least \(3/5\) per sweep; \(\omega\) near 1 barely damps the checkerboard mode (\(|1 - 2\omega|\)).

Why Jacobi, not Gauss-Seidel?

Red-black Gauss-Seidel is the traditional multigrid smoother, but it requires sequential updates that are difficult to express efficiently in JAX. Weighted Jacobi is fully parallel, composes naturally with jax.lax.fori_loop, and is symmetric, which keeps the V-cycle symmetric.

docs.title: Coarsening
docs.text:
A dimension of \(n\) points coarsens to \(\lceil n/2 \rceil = (n+1) /\!/ 2\), with coarse point \(J\) on fine point \(2J\). Odd sizes coarsen like even ones, so a standard \((N+2)\) grid (interior plus ghost ring) is as deep as \(N\): \(34 \to 17 \to 9 \to 5\), \(130 \to 65 \to \dots \to 5\) (6 levels), \(258 \to \dots \to 5\) (7 levels). n_levels=None coarsens while both dimensions stay \(\ge 4\).

Mask-coarsening rule. A coarse point is wet if its coincident fine point \((2J, 2I)\) is wet. A coarse point whose coincident fine point is dry but whose interpolation support (fine points \(2J-1, 2J, 2J+1\) in each direction) touches a wet fine point is added too, unless its prolongation column is a linear combination of the other added columns (checked with a column-pivoted QR per cluster at build time). So coasts get an extra layer of coarse unknowns and narrow channels keep one, while a one-cell lake or channel at an odd index — up to four coarse points with identical columns — keeps exactly one: \(P\) has full column rank, and \(A_c\) is non-singular (Dirichlet) or singular only by the constants (Neumann, \(\lambda = 0\)). The coarse operator sees the actual fine geometry through the Galerkin product below, not through the coarse mask.

docs.title: Prolongation (Coarse to Fine)
docs.text:
Bilinear interpolation between the nested points:

\[ v^f_{2J,2I} = v^c_{J,I}, \qquad v^f_{2J+1,2I} = \tfrac12\bigl(v^c_{J,I} + v^c_{J+1,I}\bigr), \qquad v^f_{2J+1,2I+1} = \tfrac14 \textstyle\sum_{\text{4 neighbours}} v^c \]

with dry coarse values taken as zero, then scaled row-wise: \(P = \mathrm{diag}(s)\,P_0\,\mathrm{diag}(m^c)\), with \(s = m^f\) for bc="dirichlet" (the correction tapers to the zero wall value) and \(s = m^f / (P_0\,m^c)\) for bc="neumann" (renormalised over wet coarse points, so constants are interpolated exactly).

docs.title: Restriction (Fine to Coarse)
docs.text: Restriction is the scaled transpose of prolongation, \(R = \tfrac14 P^{\mathsf T}\) — away from walls the 9-point full-weighting average with weights \((4, 2, 2, 1)/16\). Being the transpose makes \(\langle R r, e\rangle = \tfrac14\langle r, P e\rangle\) exactly, which the symmetry of the V-cycle relies on.

docs.title: Coarse Operators
docs.text: Every coarse operator is the Galerkin product \(A_c = R\,A\,P\), a 9-point stencil computed once at build time (SciPy sparse products). It inherits the fine wall condition, coefficient and geometry, and it keeps the operator symmetric and negative (semi)definite on every level.

docs.title: Bottom Solver
docs.text: The coarsest level (at most a few dozen unknowns on a square grid) is solved exactly: its inverse on the wet points is precomputed at build time from a symmetric eigendecomposition, dropping eigenvalues below \(10^{-10}\max|\mu|\). That is the exact inverse of a non-singular operator and the pseudo-inverse of the singular Neumann \(\lambda = 0\) operator (returning the zero-mean correction) without the \(\sim 10^{13}\) entries its round-off-sized null eigenvalues would otherwise give.

docs.title: Symmetry
docs.text: With \(R = \tfrac14 P^{\mathsf T}\), Galerkin coarse operators, an exact bottom solve and as many pre- as post-smoothing sweeps (n_pre == n_post, the default), one V-cycle from a zero guess, \(r \mapsto \texttt{v\_cycle}(0, r)\), is a symmetric linear operator: \(\langle M r_1, r_2\rangle = \langle r_1, M r_2\rangle\) to round-off. That is what CG needs from a preconditioner; make_multigrid_preconditioner refuses a solver with n_pre != n_post.

docs.title: Grid Hierarchy Construction
docs.text:
The build_multigrid_solver factory performs offline precomputation (using NumPy / SciPy) to build the level hierarchy:

  1. Finest operator: the 5-point stencil from \(c(x,y)\), the mask and bc.
  2. Transfers: coarse mask and \(P\) per level (rules above).
  3. Galerkin coarse operators \(A_c = R A P\) and their diagonals \(D^{-1}\) for the smoother.
  4. Bottom inverse on the coarsest wet points.

The resulting MultigridSolver is an immutable equinox.Module — all arrays are frozen JAX arrays, and all integer parameters (n_levels, n_pre, etc.) are static fields for efficient JIT compilation. Any grid shape works with any n_levels \(\ge 1\) (n_levels=1 is a direct dense solve, allowed up to 4096 wet points).

docs.title: Differentiating Through the Solve
docs.text:
A key advantage of implementing multigrid in JAX is that we can compute gradients of a loss function through the linear solve:

\[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \ell\bigl(A(\theta)^{-1} f(\theta)\bigr) \]

where \(\theta\) parameterises the coefficient field \(c(x,y)\), the RHS \(f\), or both. finitevolX provides three differentiation strategies with different cost/accuracy trade-offs.

docs.title: Strategy 1: Implicit Differentiation (Default)
docs.text:
The default __call__ method uses jax.lax.custom_linear_solve to compute gradients via the implicit function theorem (IFT).

Given the linear system \(A u = f\), the gradient of a scalar loss \(\ell(u)\) with respect to the RHS is:

\[ \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial f} = A^{-T} \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial u} \]

Since \(A\) is symmetric (\(A = A^T\)), the adjoint solve is just another multigrid call with the same operator.

Properties:

  • Forward: \(K\) V-cycles (identical to unrolled)
  • Backward: 1 multigrid solve (the adjoint equation)
  • Memory: \(O(1)\) — no iteration history stored
  • Gradients: exact (up to solver tolerance)

When to use

This is the default and recommended mode. Use it whenever you need gradients through the solve (e.g. learning \(c(x,y)\) or \(\lambda\) from data).

docs.title: Strategy 2: One-Step Differentiation
docs.text:
The solve_onestep method implements the approach of Bolte, Pauwels & Vaiter (NeurIPS 2023). It runs \(K\) V-cycles for convergence, but only differentiates through the last cycle:

\[ u_K = V\bigl(\underbrace{V(\cdots V(0, f) \cdots, f)}_{\text{stop\_gradient after } K{-}1 \text{ cycles}},\; f\bigr) \]

The gradient approximation error is \(O(\rho)\) where \(\rho\) is the V-cycle convergence rate (\(\approx 0.07\) on the default settings; on a \(34^2\) basin the one-step gradient is within 4 % of the implicit one).

Properties:

  • Forward: \(K\) V-cycles (identical)
  • Backward: 1 V-cycle (autodiff through only the last)
  • Memory: \(O(1\text{ V-cycle})\)
  • Gradients: approximate, error \(O(\rho)\)

When to use

When you need cheap gradients and can tolerate small approximation error — e.g. in training loops where the solver is called many times and the gradient noise from one-step differentiation is small relative to stochastic gradient noise.

docs.title: Strategy 3: Unrolled Differentiation
docs.text:
The solve_unrolled method differentiates through every V-cycle iteration via jax.lax.fori_loop:

Properties:

  • Forward: \(K\) V-cycles
  • Backward: \(K\) V-cycles (replay all iterations)
  • Memory: \(O(K)\) — stores intermediate states for backprop
  • Gradients: exact through the iteration process

When to use

When you specifically need gradients through the iteration dynamics itself (e.g. analysing convergence behaviour, or when the number of iterations is very small).

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Mode Backward cost Memory Gradient quality Implicit (__call__) 1 multigrid solve \(O(1)\) Exact (IFT) One-step (solve_onestep) 1 V-cycle autodiff \(O(1)\) Approximate, \(O(\rho)\) error Unrolled (solve_unrolled) \(K\) V-cycles \(O(K)\) Exact (through iterations)

docs.title: Multigrid as a Preconditioner
docs.text:
A single V-cycle is an excellent preconditioner for CG. This is useful when:

  • You want the convergence guarantees of CG (Krylov method) but need faster convergence than a spectral preconditioner provides.
  • The variable-coefficient problem is poorly conditioned.
  • You want to combine multigrid's coarse-grid correction with CG's global optimality.

make_multigrid_preconditioner wraps one V-cycle as a closure compatible with solve_cg; the V-cycle is symmetric (see above), as CG requires. On a circular basin with \(\lambda = 4\) and rtol=1e-8, CG then takes 6 iterations at both \(128^2\) and \(256^2\), against 33 and 47 with the FFT spectral preconditioner.

docs.title: Convergence Theory
docs.text:
Multigrid with a good smoother and an accurate coarse-grid correction reduces the residual by a fixed factor \(\rho\) per V-cycle, independent of grid size. Measured per-cycle residual reduction (default V(3,3), \(\omega = 0.8\), circular basin, \(\lambda = 4\), Dirichlet, cycles 5–8):

Grid Levels \(\rho\) per cycle \(34^2\) 4 0.064–0.066 \(130^2\) 6 0.066–0.069 \(258^2\) 7 0.068–0.073

(The first cycle reduces it by about 0.02.) Geometry matters: on the rectangle of the Solver Comparison \(\rho\) is 0.063–0.064, but in its circular basin with an island it is 0.14 at \(130^2\) and 0.17 at \(258^2\), so 5 V-cycles leave a relative residual of \(7 \times 10^{-5}\) / \(4 \times 10^{-4}\) there; use more cycles, or CG + multigrid (7 iterations at both sizes). On the plain circular basin this means:

  • 5 V-cycles reduce the residual by about \(3 \times 10^{-7}\)
  • The cost per V-cycle is \(O(N)\) where \(N = N_y \times N_x\) (each level costs a quarter of the previous, geometric series)
  • Total cost: \(O(N)\) — optimal for elliptic solves

Measured on CPU (float64, jitted, circular basin, \(\lambda = 4\)): 5 V-cycles take 2.7 ms at \(128^2\) and 17 ms at \(256^2\); CG with the multigrid preconditioner (rtol=1e-8) 6.6 ms / 6 iterations and 40 ms / 6 iterations, against 27 ms / 33 and 220 ms / 47 for CG with the FFT preconditioner.

Narrow features (\(34^2\), cycles 5–8; an island, and two basins joined by a one-cell channel in an odd or an even column):

Mask Dirichlet \(\lambda=0\) / \(4\) Neumann \(\lambda=0\) / \(4\) CG + MG iterations island 0.080 / 0.059 0.148 / 0.095 5–6 odd-column channel 0.088 / 0.053 0.475 / 0.232 5–7 even-column channel 0.090 / 0.053 0.226 / 0.089 5–6

Dirichlet stays near the basin rate. Neumann is slower where a thin channel carries the flux between basins (the near-null "sloshing" mode is poorly represented by bilinear coarse functions), most at \(\lambda = 0\); the V-cycle remains a good CG preconditioner there (5–7 iterations at rtol=1e-8 on all of these masks), which is the recommended use on such coasts.

For variable coefficients the Galerkin coarse operators follow the coefficient, so the rate stays close to these values for moderate coefficient contrast; strongly anisotropic or high-contrast coefficients degrade point-Jacobi smoothing.

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text:
Is c(x,y) constant (or nearly so)?
├── Yes → Use spectral solver (fastest, O(N log N))
│         Or capacitance method for masked domains
└── No (variable coefficient) ↓

Is the domain rectangular (no mask)?
├── Yes → Multigrid standalone (method="multigrid")
│         build_multigrid_solver(np.ones(...), dx, dy, coeff=c)
└── No (masked/irregular domain) ↓

Is the domain simple with small N_b?
├── Yes → Multigrid standalone (handles masks natively)
└── No (complex domain, poor convergence) ↓

Default → Multigrid-preconditioned CG
          make_multigrid_preconditioner() + solve_cg()

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Briggs, Henson & McCormick (2000) — A Multigrid Tutorial, 2nd ed. (standard reference for geometric multigrid)
  • Trottenberg, Oosterlee & Schuller (2001) — Multigrid (comprehensive treatment including variable coefficients)
  • Bolte, Pauwels & Vaiter (NeurIPS 2023) — One-step differentiation of iterative algorithms
  • Blondel et al. (ICML 2022) — Efficient and modular implicit differentiation
  • Louity — qgsw-pytorch (reference PyTorch multigrid Helmholtz implementation)

docs.title: Multigrid Solver: Usage Guide
docs.text: This page covers practical usage of finitevolX's multigrid Helmholtz solver, from quick-start examples to variable-coefficient problems and differentiable solves.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
import finitevolx as fvx

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

# 1. Define a grid (any shape: odd and N + 2 sizes coarsen fully)
Ny, Nx = 64, 64
dx, dy = 1.0 / Nx, 1.0 / Ny
mask = np.ones((Ny, Nx))  # rectangular domain

# 2. Build the solver (offline, once)
solver = fvx.build_multigrid_solver(mask, dx, dy, lambda_=10.0)

# 3. Solve (online, JIT-compilable)
rhs = jnp.sin(jnp.pi * jnp.arange(Ny)[:, None] / Ny) * \
      jnp.sin(jnp.pi * jnp.arange(Nx)[None, :] / Nx)
u = solver(rhs)

docs.title: Building the Solver
docs.text: build_multigrid_solver precomputes the entire level hierarchy offline (mask coarsening, transfer weights, Galerkin coarse operators, the exact bottom solve). This is done once; the returned solver is then cheap to call repeatedly.

docs.title: Rectangular Domain
docs.text:
mask = np.ones((64, 64))
solver = fvx.build_multigrid_solver(mask, dx, dy, lambda_=10.0)

docs.title: Masked (Irregular) Domain
docs.text:
# Circular basin
Y, X = np.mgrid[:64, :64]
mask = ((X - 32)**2 + (Y - 32)**2 < 28**2).astype(float)

solver = fvx.build_multigrid_solver(mask, dx, dy, lambda_=10.0)
u = solver(rhs * jnp.array(mask))  # zero RHS outside domain

docs.title: With Mask2D
docs.text:
cgrid_mask = fvx.Mask2D.from_mask(ocean_mask)
# psi at X points (xy_corner_strict), psi = 0 on the coast: the default
solver = fvx.build_multigrid_solver(cgrid_mask, dx, dy, lambda_=10.0)

docs.title: Boundary Condition
docs.text:
bc="dirichlet" (the default) takes the value beyond every wet–dry face as zero: the streamfunction problem, the same operator as fvx.masked_laplacian. bc="neumann" puts no flux through wet–dry faces: the pressure / free-surface problem on the T-point mask.

# Pressure at T points, zero normal flux at the coast.  At lambda_ = 0 the
# solution is returned in the zero-mean gauge on each wet component.
p_solver = fvx.build_multigrid_solver(
    np.asarray(cgrid_mask.h, dtype=float), dx, dy, lambda_=0.0, bc="neumann"
)

docs.title: Variable Coefficient
docs.text:
# Spatially varying diffusivity
coeff = 1.0 + 0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * X / 64)
