solver = fvx.build_multigrid_solver(
    mask, dx, dy,
    lambda_=10.0,
    coeff=coeff,
)
u = solver(rhs)

docs.title: Controlling the Hierarchy
docs.text:
solver = fvx.build_multigrid_solver(
    mask, dx, dy,
    lambda_=10.0,
    n_levels=3,     # number of grid levels (default: auto)
    n_pre=3,        # pre-smoothing iterations
    n_post=3,       # post-smoothing iterations (keep equal to n_pre)
    omega=0.8,      # Jacobi relaxation weight
    n_cycles=5,     # V-cycles per solve
    bc="dirichlet", # or "neumann" (zero flux at the coast)
)

Auto level detection

When n_levels=None (default), the factory coarsens both dimensions with n -> (n + 1) // 2 while both stay >= 4. For a 64x64 grid this gives 5 levels (64 -> 32 -> 16 -> 8 -> 4), for a 34x34 grid (32 interior cells plus the ghost ring) 4 levels (34 -> 17 -> 9 -> 5). The coarsest level is solved exactly.

docs.title: Solve Modes
docs.text: The solver provides three methods with different autodiff characteristics.

docs.title: Implicit Differentiation (Default)
docs.text:
u = solver(rhs)  # uses jax.lax.custom_linear_solve

The backward pass solves the adjoint equation with multigrid — same cost as the forward pass, O(1) memory. Recommended for most use cases.

docs.title: One-Step Differentiation
docs.text:
u = solver.solve_onestep(rhs)

Differentiates through only the last V-cycle. Cheapest backward pass, with approximate gradients (error proportional to the convergence rate).

docs.title: Unrolled Differentiation
docs.text:
u = solver.solve_unrolled(rhs)

Differentiates through all V-cycle iterations. O(n_cycles) memory cost.

docs.title: Multigrid as a CG Preconditioner
docs.text:
A single multigrid V-cycle makes an excellent preconditioner for solve_cg, especially for variable-coefficient problems. See the Preconditioner Comparison in the elliptic solvers docs for a full ranking of all available preconditioners.

# Build solver and preconditioner
mg_solver = fvx.build_multigrid_solver(
    mask, dx, dy, lambda_=10.0, coeff=coeff
)
mg_precond = fvx.make_multigrid_preconditioner(mg_solver)

# Define the operator
mask_jnp = jnp.array(mask)
def A(x):
    """Variable-coefficient Helmholtz operator."""
    # For constant coeff, use masked_laplacian directly.
    # For variable coeff, use the multigrid's internal operator.
    from finitevolx._src.solvers.multigrid import _apply_operator
    return _apply_operator(x, mg_solver.levels[0])

# Solve with multigrid-preconditioned CG
u, info = fvx.solve_cg(
    A, rhs * mask_jnp,
    preconditioner=mg_precond,
    rtol=1e-8,
    atol=1e-8,
)
u = u * mask_jnp
print(f"Converged in {info.iterations} iterations")

docs.title: Gradient Through the Solve
docs.text:
def loss(rhs):
    u = solver(rhs)  # implicit diff (default)
    return jnp.sum(u ** 2)

grad_rhs = jax.grad(loss)(rhs)

docs.title: Learning a Spatially Varying Coefficient
docs.text:
import optax

# Parameterise the coefficient field
log_coeff = jnp.zeros((Ny, Nx))  # learnable, initialised to c=1

def forward(log_coeff, rhs):
    coeff = jnp.exp(log_coeff)
    solver = fvx.build_multigrid_solver(
        mask, dx, dy, lambda_=10.0, coeff=np.asarray(coeff)
    )
    return solver(rhs)

def loss_fn(log_coeff):
    u_pred = forward(log_coeff, rhs)
    return jnp.mean((u_pred - u_target) ** 2)

# Note: build_multigrid_solver is offline (numpy), so for gradient-based
# learning you would typically fix the solver and differentiate only
# through the RHS, or rebuild the solver at each outer iteration.

docs.title: Comparing Gradient Strategies
docs.text:
def loss_implicit(rhs):
    return jnp.sum(solver(rhs) ** 2)

def loss_onestep(rhs):
    return jnp.sum(solver.solve_onestep(rhs) ** 2)

def loss_unrolled(rhs):
    return jnp.sum(solver.solve_unrolled(rhs) ** 2)

g_implicit = jax.grad(loss_implicit)(rhs)
g_onestep = jax.grad(loss_onestep)(rhs)
g_unrolled = jax.grad(loss_unrolled)(rhs)

# g_implicit and g_unrolled should agree closely
# g_onestep may differ by O(rho), about 0.04 on the default settings

docs.title: JIT Compilation
docs.text:
import equinox as eqx

@eqx.filter_jit
def solve(solver, rhs):
    return solver(rhs)

u = solve(solver, rhs)  # compiled on first call, fast thereafter

docs.title: Batched Solves with vmap
docs.text:
# Solve for multiple RHS fields at once
rhs_batch = jnp.stack([rhs1, rhs2, rhs3])  # (3, Ny, Nx)

@eqx.filter_jit
def batch_solve(solver, rhs_batch):
    return jax.vmap(solver)(rhs_batch)

u_batch = batch_solve(solver, rhs_batch)  # (3, Ny, Nx)

docs.title: Tuning Guide
docs.text:
Parameter Default Effect n_cycles 5 Each cycle reduces the residual by about 0.07 (basins), so 5 cycles give about 3e-7. Neumann on one-cell channels or islands is slower (0.1-0.5): use the V-cycle as a CG preconditioner there. n_pre / n_post 3 More smoothing = better rate per cycle (0.12 at 2, 0.05 at 4), at higher cost. Keep them equal for a symmetric V-cycle (required by make_multigrid_preconditioner). omega 0.8 Jacobi weight; 0.8 damps the high-frequency half of the spectrum best. Values near 1 leave the checkerboard mode undamped. n_levels auto Any shape, any n_levels; fewer levels make the dense bottom solve larger (at most 4096 wet points). bc "dirichlet" "neumann" for zero flux at the coast (T-point pressure / free surface).

Quick convergence check

u = solver(rhs)
from finitevolx._src.solvers.multigrid import _apply_operator
residual = jnp.linalg.norm(rhs - _apply_operator(u, solver.levels[0]))
print(f"Residual norm: {residual:.2e}")

docs.title: Multilayer vs. 3D Discretization
docs.text: This page explains the crucial distinction between multilayer operators (via jax.vmap over independent 2D layers) and true 3D operators in finitevolX, and shows how to use each correctly.

docs.title: Two Different Meanings of a Leading Axis
docs.text:
When you have an array of shape [N, Ny, Nx] in ocean or atmosphere modelling, the leading axis N can mean one of two fundamentally different things:

Use case Leading axis meaning Example models Multilayer / baroclinic / modal Layer or mode index QG n-layer, baroclinic SW True 3D discretization Vertical spatial dimension z Primitive equations

finitevolX provides explicit support for both, but they must not be confused because their ghost-cell conventions are opposite.

docs.title: Concept
docs.text:
In a multilayer model (e.g., n-layer quasi-geostrophic or baroclinic shallow water), the fluid column is divided into nl discrete layers. Each layer is a complete, physically real 2D horizontal field with its own dynamics. There are no "ghost" layers — every slice k = 0 … nl-1 holds a real physical field.

The JAX-idiomatic way to apply any 2D horizontal operator to all layers at once is jax.vmap, which vectorises the call over the leading axis without any overhead. finitevolX exposes this pattern through the multilayer helper:

import jax.numpy as jnp
import finitevolx as fvx

grid = fvx.CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(64, 64, 1e4, 1e4)
diff2d = fvx.Difference2D(grid=grid)

nl = 3                                     # number of layers
h = jnp.ones((nl, grid.Ny, grid.Nx))      # [nl, Ny, Nx]

# Apply diff_x_T_to_U to every layer in one vectorised call
dh_dx = fvx.multilayer(diff2d.diff_x_T_to_U)(h)   # shape [nl, Ny, Nx]

For operators that take multiple arguments (e.g., divergence), pass the bound method directly — :func:jax.vmap batches each positional argument over the leading axis independently:

u = jnp.ones((nl, grid.Ny, grid.Nx))
v = jnp.ones((nl, grid.Ny, grid.Nx))

div = fvx.multilayer(diff2d.divergence)(u, v)

docs.title: What multilayer does
docs.text:
• Wraps fn with jax.vmap, batching over the first axis.
  • The 2D stencil (ghost-cell ring, interior writes) is completely unchanged.
  • All nl slices are processed; there is no "outer ghost layer" concept.

docs.title: Concept
docs.text:
In a true 3D primitive-equation model, the leading axis is a spatial vertical coordinate. The discretization uses the same ghost-cell convention as the horizontal dimensions: the top (k = 0) and bottom (k = Nz-1) layers are ghost shells that must be filled by vertical boundary conditions before chaining operators. Only the interior k = 1 … Nz-2 layers are written by the stencil.

grid3d = fvx.CartesianGrid3D.from_interior(64, 64, 10, 1e4, 1e4, 50.0)
diff3d = fvx.Difference3D(grid=grid3d)

# h has shape [Nz, Ny, Nx]; Nz = 12 total (10 interior + 2 ghost)
h = jnp.ones((grid3d.Nz, grid3d.Ny, grid3d.Nx))

dh_dx = diff3d.diff_x_T_to_U(h)
# dh_dx[0]  = 0   ← ghost layer (k=0), not written
# dh_dx[1:-1] ≠ 0 ← interior layers, written
# dh_dx[-1] = 0   ← ghost layer (k=Nz-1), not written

docs.title: Key Differences at a Glance
docs.text: Property multilayer(fn) Difference3D Leading axis meaning Layer / mode index Vertical z dimension Ghost layers at k=0, k=N-1 ❌ None — all slices are real ✅ Required — top/bottom are ghost shells Which slices are written All k = 0 … nl-1 Only interior k = 1 … Nz-2 Underlying mechanism jax.vmap(fn) over axis 0 Explicit [1:-1, …] slice writes Correct for Baroclinic / QG layered models Primitive-equation 3D models

docs.title: Equivalence in the Interior
docs.text:
Although the two approaches differ at the boundary layers, they produce identical results in the horizontal interior for the shared interior z-levels:

import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
import finitevolx as fvx

grid2d = fvx.CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(8, 8, 1.0, 1.0)
grid3d = fvx.CartesianGrid3D.from_interior(8, 8, 4, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0)

diff2d = fvx.Difference2D(grid=grid2d)
diff3d = fvx.Difference3D(grid=grid3d)

Nz = grid3d.Nz   # 6 total (4 interior + 2 ghost)
h = jnp.arange(Nz * grid3d.Ny * grid3d.Nx, dtype=float).reshape(
    Nz, grid3d.Ny, grid3d.Nx
)

ml_result = fvx.multilayer(diff2d.diff_x_T_to_U)(h)
d3_result = diff3d.diff_x_T_to_U(h)

# Interior z-levels AND horizontal interior agree exactly
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    ml_result[1:-1, 1:-1, 1:-1],
    d3_result[1:-1, 1:-1, 1:-1],
)

# But the boundary layers differ:
# Difference3D: k=0, k=5 are zero (ghost shells)
print(d3_result[0].max())    # 0.0
print(d3_result[-1].max())   # 0.0

# multilayer: k=0, k=5 are real (non-zero) layers
print(ml_result[0].max())    # non-zero
print(ml_result[-1].max())   # non-zero

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Use multilayer(fn) when your leading axis indexes independent physical layers or modes. Every layer is real; jax.vmap is the correct, efficient way to batch over them.
  • Use Difference3D when your leading axis is a spatial vertical coordinate that requires top/bottom ghost shells for boundary conditions.
  • The two are not interchangeable. Applying Difference3D to a true multilayer field silently zeros out the top and bottom layers, which are physically real in that context.

docs.title: Writing fast stencils
docs.text:
finitevolX operators are plain jnp slicing (see Raw Stencils). How a stencil is written still decides what XLA compiles, especially for reverse-mode AD (jax.grad, jax.vjp), which data assimilation and training call far more often than the forward pass. These rules come from profiling every operator; the measurements, the negative results and the roadmap are in the stencil performance deep dive.

Where the numbers come from

All timings here are XLA:CPU (2-vCPU VM, JAX 0.10, float32). The structural effects (number of pads in the VJP, number of fusions, temporary buffers) are backend-independent; the speedups are not. Re-measure on GPU / TPU with scripts/benchmark_operators.py before relying on a ratio there.

docs.title: The cost model in one paragraph
docs.text: A stencil is memory-bound: the ideal compiled program reads each input once and writes each output once, inside one fused loop. Every static slice h[a:b, c:d] is free in the forward pass, but its transpose in the VJP is a pad of the cotangent, one per slice expression. XLA then has to sum those pads, and when there are many (or when a full-size intermediate sits between two stencils) it splits the program into several fusions with temporary buffers. Fewer distinct reads and no full-size intermediates keep it as one pass.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. Slice each offset once. Bind shifted views to names and reuse them, rather than re-slicing inside each sub-expression. For the 3×3 neighbourhood use _neighbours(h) (operators/stencils.py):
nb = _neighbours(h)  # nb.c, nb.e, nb.w, nb.n, nb.s, nb.ne, ...  [..., Ny-2, Nx-2]
# same arithmetic as (diff_x_fwd(h) - diff_x_bwd(h)) / dx**2
d2x = ((nb.e - nb.c) - (nb.c - nb.w)) / dx**2

Keep the arithmetic of the composed form so the forward pass is bitwise-identical, and say so in a comment that names the composed form. Laplacian VJP: 1.5–2.3× faster; spherical Laplacian 2.0–2.3×; Arakawa Jacobian VJP: 4.0–4.4× faster.

This rule is for linear and bilinear stencils. For heavy nonlinear stencils (WENO) it did not help and sometimes hurt: their VJP cost is dominated by something else (see the deep dive, §3.1).

  1. Don't build a full-size intermediate just to slice it again. zeros_like(h).at[1:-1, 1:-2].set(flux) followed by flux[1:-1, 1:-1] - flux[1:-1, :-2] materialises the flux array. Compute only the faces the next stencil reads and add zero wall faces as a pad of the result (see diffusion._diffusion_2d_impl). 2-D diffusion: forward and VJP ~2× faster, one fusion, no temporaries; 3-D diffusion: forward 2–3×, VJP 1.5–1.9×.

  2. Fuse sums of operators. op_a(u) + op_b(v) with each returning a padded full-size array is two passes plus an add; one interior(a + b) is one pass (Difference3D.divergence: 1.5–2.5× faster forward).

  3. Materialise an intermediate that the next stencil reads at several offsets. XLA may otherwise fuse a cheap producer into every shifted read and recompute it per offset. _materialize(x) (an optimization_barrier, identity for values and derivatives) keeps it as one buffer: the biharmonic's first Laplacian is the example (VJP fusions 11 → 5; forward 1.2–1.5× and VJP 1.4–1.9× faster together with rule 2).

  4. Zero ghost slabs with a pad, not scatters. zero_z_ghosts pads the interior slabs, which also lets XLA skip computing the discarded ones.

  5. Unroll small constant contractions. jnp.einsum over a jnp.stack of shifted views (the WENO-7/9 smoothness indicators qᵀ B q) lowers to a stack, a dot and transposes of the stacked field. Writing the quadratic form as nested Python sums over the constant coefficients keeps it one elementwise fusion: WENO-7 advection forward ~11× faster (WENO-9 ~14×), JVP 4–6× faster.

  6. Measure the VJP with an external cotangent. Benchmark jax.vjp(op, *x)[1](ct) with a fixed random ct. A loss such as 0.5 * sum(op(x)**2) makes the cotangent a function of the inputs, XLA fuses it back in, and rankings can invert.

docs.title: Known open problem: the advection VJP
docs.text: The reverse pass of the WENO / TVD advection operators costs 10–35× their forward pass on XLA:CPU (WENO-5 2-D: ~1 ms forward, ~30 ms VJP), which makes advection the dominant cost of any adjoint or training loop. The rewrites above do not fix it; the deep dive (§3.1, §5) has the profile, the experiments that did not work and the plan.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
• scripts/benchmark_operators.py times the forward pass, the VJP and the JVP of every operator and reports XLA fusion counts, temporary bytes and an efficiency figure against an elementwise roofline; --profile REGEX prints the most expensive XLA kernels of a VJP:
uv run python scripts/benchmark_operators.py --n 514 --repeat 3 --out before.json
# … change code …
uv run python scripts/benchmark_operators.py --n 514 --repeat 3 --out after.json
uv run python scripts/benchmark_operators.py --compare before.json after.json
uv run python scripts/benchmark_operators.py --profile "Advection2D.weno5"

On a shared machine, sequential runs are noisy (±30 % below 0.3 ms, and occasional 2× outliers on larger cases): use --repeat, run the before / after pair more than once, and trust a speedup only when the fusion count or the slices column moved with it.

  • tests/test_stencil_lowering.py pins the lowering contract without any timing: the VJP jaxpr of each rewritten operator contains exactly one pad per distinct offset, each rewrite equals its composed form, and the WENO-7 jaxpr contains no dot_general. Add a case there when you rewrite an operator for speed.

docs.title: Solver Comparison
docs.text:
This page compares finitevolX's elliptic solvers on the problem they all solve — the streamfunction Helmholtz equation on the C-grid,

\[ (\nabla^2 - \lambda)\,\psi = f \ \text{ on the wet X points}, \qquad \psi = 0 \ \text{ on the wall / coast X nodes}, \]

(see the wall table) — with measured numbers: build time, solve time, gradient time, iteration counts, memory and error against a sparse direct solve.

Reproducing these numbers

Every number and figure on this page comes from scripts/generate_solver_figures.py:

uv run python scripts/generate_solver_figures.py

Hardware: a 2-vCPU cloud VM, XLA:CPU, float64, JAX 0.10.1, shared with other jobs while it ran. Iteration counts and errors are deterministic; timings are the minimum over 7 jitted calls (3 for gradients; builds: minimum of 2, multigrid builds minimum of 7 in a later run after a build-speed fix) and still vary by tens of percent between runs. Compare orders of magnitude and ratios, not the third digit. On a GPU the balance shifts towards the FFT-based and matrix-free methods.

For a visual walk-through of the solvers on four geometries (including a variable-coefficient one), see the Elliptic Solvers notebook.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Domains the unit square (CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(N, N, 1, 1)); a rectangle, and a circular basin of radius 0.45 with a disc island of radius 0.1, both as Mask2D from a T-point ocean mask; ψ uses mask.xy_corner_strict Sizes \(N = 128\) and \(256\) interior cells per side (arrays \((N+2)^2\); 16 129 / 65 025 wet ψ nodes on the rectangle, 9 635 / 39 063 in the island basin; 508 / 1 020 and 399 / 795 coast nodes) λ 4 (screened, \(R_d = 0.5\)) and 0 (Poisson) RHS \(f = \sin 3\pi x \cos 2\pi y + e^{-[(x-0.3)^2 + (y-0.7)^2]/0.01}\) on the wet nodes Reference SciPy sparse LU (SuperLU) of the 5-point matrix on the wet nodes — the matrix of masked_laplacian; its residual is checked to round-off Error \(\max\lvert\psi - \psi_{\text{LU}}\rvert / \max\lvert\psi_{\text{LU}}\rvert\) CG tolerance rtol = 1e-8, atol = 1e-8 max|f|, i.e. \(\max\lvert f - A\psi\rvert \le 2\times10^{-8} \max\lvert f\rvert\)

The methods:

Row Call spectral DST streamfunction_from_vorticity(f, dx, dy, bc="dst", lambda_=λ) (rectangle only) capacitance build_capacitance_solver(mask, dx, dy, lambda_=λ) (DST base), then solver(f) CG + DST / FFT solve_cg(masked_laplacian, f, preconditioner=make_spectral_preconditioner(dx, dy, λ, bc=...)) CG + multigrid the same with make_multigrid_preconditioner(build_multigrid_solver(mask, dx, dy, lambda_=λ)) CG (none) no preconditioner multigrid (5 V / 8 V) the multigrid solver on its own, 5 V-cycles (the default) or 8 sparse LU (SciPy) the reference; NumPy on the CPU — no jit, vmap or grad

The columns: build is the one-off construction (NumPy / SciPy, not jitted); solve is one jitted solve; grad is one jitted jax.grad of \(\tfrac12\sum\psi^2\) with respect to \(f\) (forward plus adjoint solve); precomputed is the memory of the arrays the built solver holds (for sparse LU, the factors).

docs.title: Where the error sits
docs.text: Island basin, 128², λ = 4: the solution, then the error of capacitance (round-off), CG + FFT and CG + multigrid (the CG tolerance) and 5 multigrid V-cycles (largest next to the island).

docs.title: What the numbers say
docs.text:
• Every method solves the same problem. The direct methods agree with sparse LU to \(10^{-14}\), CG to its tolerance (\(10^{-11}\)–\(10^{-9}\)), on both domains: one wall, one operator.
  • Rectangle: spectral wins. The DST solve takes 0.5 / 2.9 ms at 128² / 256², 3–4.5× faster than SciPy's sparse LU and at least 5× faster than any other JAX solver, with nothing to build.
  • Fixed mask: capacitance is exact and the fastest masked solve at 256². 4.6–15 ms per solve: as fast as CG + multigrid at 128² and 2–3.6× faster at 256², after a 1.9–5.3 s build that stores 1.5–9 MiB (\(N_c^2\) for 400–1 020 coast nodes). It pays off when the same mask and λ are reused many times.
  • CG + multigrid is the fastest CG, at any size. 5 iterations on the rectangle and 7 in the island basin at both 128² and 256² (the count does not grow with \(N\)), 5–38 ms, with 1.6–6.1 MiB: 2.6–6.6× faster than the best spectral-preconditioned CG. The hierarchy builds in 20–58 ms on both domains, cheap enough to rebuild when the mask or λ changes.
  • Spectral preconditioners need no setup, but their iterations grow with \(N\): 31–63 with the FFT, 15–48 with the DST (on the rectangle the DST differs from the C-grid operator only at the array edge, so it stays at 15). At 128² a DST step costs ~3× an FFT step on XLA:CPU, so CG + FFT is often faster despite more iterations; at 256² the two steps cost about the same. Unpreconditioned CG takes 340–760 iterations (0.1–1.1 s).
  • Standalone multigrid is the cheapest iterative solve (2.4–2.8 ms / 16.5–18 ms), but its accuracy depends on the geometry: 5 V-cycles (the default) give \(2\)–\(3\times10^{-7}\) on the rectangle but \(4\times10^{-5}\)–\(1.5\times10^{-4}\) in the island basin; 8 cycles give \(\le 5\times10^{-11}\) and \(10^{-7}\)–\(10^{-6}\). Wrap it in CG when you need a tolerance.
  • λ = 0 costs nothing extra. The ψ wall is Dirichlet, so the Poisson problem is non-singular for every method; only the FFT preconditioner takes more iterations (41 / 63 vs 31 / 47 on the rectangle).
  • Gradients cost about one more solve. For every JAX method, grad takes 1.5–2.7× the forward solve: the adjoint of a symmetric solve is the same solve.
  • Jit the solver as an argument, not a closure. Closing over a built solver embeds its arrays in the program as constants, which XLA then constant-folds: compiling the closed-over capacitance solve of the 256² island basin took 8 minutes. Pass it in (eqx.filter_jit(lambda s, f: s(f))(solver, f)), as the script does.

docs.title: 201 asked whether the elliptic problems should be solved with a full
docs.text:
(dense) matrix, a tridiagonal one or a sparse one. For the 2-D C-grid problem at these sizes:

  • Dense is out: the 5-point matrix has \(n\) = 16 129 / 65 025 unknowns on the rectangle, so the matrix alone is 2 GiB / 32 GiB in float64 and its LU costs \(O(n^3)\). The useful dense matrix is the capacitance matrix: dense only on the \(N_c\) coast nodes (1.5–9 MiB here), with the bulk handled by the fast rectangular solve.
  • Tridiagonal does not apply directly: the 2-D 5-point operator is block tridiagonal, not tridiagonal. solve_tridiagonal (gaussx) is for 1-D and vertical problems (implicit vertical diffusion, layer coupling); the fast rectangular 2-D solve is the spectral one.
  • Sparse direct (SciPy SuperLU, the reference rows): fast on a CPU — 0.9–13 ms per solve after a 27–334 ms factorisation — but its fill-in takes 7–72 MiB (4–12× the multigrid hierarchy) and it runs outside JAX: no jit, vmap, grad or GPU. The JAX-native sparse route is matrix-free: CG on masked_laplacian (nothing stored) with the multigrid preconditioner (1.6–6.1 MiB), differentiable at about twice the solve cost.

docs.title: When to Use What
docs.text:
Rectangle, constant coefficient?
├── Yes → Spectral (method="spectral"): exact, fastest
└── No (masked) ↓

Fixed mask and λ, many solves, setup affordable?
├── Yes → Capacitance (method="capacitance"): exact, a few ms per solve
└── No (the mask or λ changes, or a very long coastline) ↓

Need the CG tolerance (or a variable coefficient)?
├── Yes → CG + multigrid preconditioner: 5–7 iterations, any size
└── No → Multigrid alone: a few V-cycles, the cheapest iterative solve
          (more cycles near islands / narrow channels)

No setup at all → CG with the default spectral preconditioner
                  (iterations grow with N)

docs.title: Spatial Operators
docs.text: This page covers the theory behind the higher-level spatial operators in finitevolX: divergence, vorticity (relative and potential), diffusion, Coriolis, momentum advection (vortex-force form), kinetic energy, and diagnostic quantities.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The spatial operators build on the primitive difference and interpolation operators to compute physically meaningful quantities on the Arakawa C-grid. The table below lists the main operators and what they compute:

Operator Module Output location Physical quantity Divergence2D divergence T-points \( abla \cdot (u, v)\) Vorticity2D.relative_vorticity vorticity X-points \(\zeta = \partial v/\partial x - \partial u/\partial y\) Vorticity2D.potential_vorticity vorticity X-points \(q = (\zeta + f)/h\) Vorticity2D.pv_flux_energy_conserving vorticity U/V-points \((q\,Uh, q\,Vh)\) Diffusion2D / diffusion_2d diffusion T-points \( abla \cdot (\kappa\, abla h)\) BiharmonicDiffusion2D diffusion T-points \(-\kappa\, abla^4 h\) Coriolis2D coriolis U/V-points \((+\overline{f_X ar{v}}, -\overline{f_X ar{u}})\), energy-conserving MomentumAdvection2D momentum U/V-points Vortex-force form Vorticity2D.enstrophy / .potential_enstrophy vorticity X-points \( frac12\zeta^2\), \( frac12 q^2 h\) Energetics2D diagnostics T-points KE, Bernoulli potential, APE Strain2D diagnostics T/X-points shear & tensor strain, \(\sigma^2\), Okubo–Weiss QGPotentialVorticity2D diagnostics T-points \(q = abla^2\psi/f_0 + eta(y - y_0)/f_0\) (− stretching) ArakawaJacobian2D / arakawa_jacobian jacobian T-points / interior \(J(f, g)\)

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
The flux-form divergence of the horizontal velocity field at T-points:

\[ \delta_{j,i} = \frac{u_{j,i+\frac{1}{2}} - u_{j,i-\frac{1}{2}}}{\Delta x} + \frac{v_{j+\frac{1}{2},i} - v_{j-\frac{1}{2},i}}{\Delta y} \]

In the shallow-water model the continuity equation is \(\partial h/\partial t + \nabla \cdot (h\,\mathbf{u}) = 0\), so computing the divergence of the mass flux \((hu, hv)\) gives the thickness tendency \(-\delta(hu, hv)\).

For a non-divergent velocity field (\(\delta = 0\)), the mass flux form and the simpler advective form agree. On a C-grid, the discrete divergence is exactly zero for any velocity field derived from a streamfunction via grad_perp — this is the key property that makes QG models mass-conservative.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from finitevolx import CartesianGrid2D, Divergence2D, divergence_2d

grid = CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(64, 64, 1e6, 1e6)

# Class-based
div_op = Divergence2D(grid=grid)
delta = div_op(u, v)              # T-points

# Functional (no grid object needed)
delta = divergence_2d(u, v, dx=grid.dx, dy=grid.dy)

docs.title: Relative Vorticity
docs.text:
The relative vorticity at X-points (NE corners):

\[ \zeta_{j+\frac{1}{2}, i+\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{v_{j+\frac{1}{2},i+1} - v_{j+\frac{1}{2},i}}{\Delta x} - \frac{u_{j+1,i+\frac{1}{2}} - u_{j,i+\frac{1}{2}}}{\Delta y} \]

This is the discrete curl of the 2-D velocity field. It is placed at X-points because this is the natural location for diff_x_V_to_X and diff_y_U_to_X.

docs.title: Potential Vorticity (Shallow Water)
docs.text:
The shallow-water potential vorticity at X-points:

\[ q_{j+\frac{1}{2}, i+\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{\zeta_{j+\frac{1}{2}, i+\frac{1}{2}} + f_{j+\frac{1}{2}, i+\frac{1}{2}}}{h_{j+\frac{1}{2}, i+\frac{1}{2}}} \]

where \(f\) and \(h\) are interpolated from T-points to X-points via T_to_X.

Thin-layer singularity

\(q\) is set to NaN where \(h = 0\) to avoid division by zero. Guard against this with a minimum thickness clamp before calling the PV operator.

docs.title: PV Fluxes
docs.text:
Vorticity2D offers two ways of combining \(q\) (at X-points) with a pair of face fields \((F_u, F_v)\) at U/V-points:

Method Form U-point value pv_flux_energy_conserving multiply at the corners, then average \(\overline{q\,\overline{F_u}^{y}}^{y}\) pv_flux_enstrophy_conserving average \(q\) to the face, then multiply \(\overline{q}^{y}\,F_u\) pv_flux_blend linear blend \(\alpha E + (1-\alpha) Z\) —

The names refer to the vortex-force use (Sadourny 1975): when the cross-face transport is used — \(+q\,V\) in the \(u\)-equation, \(-q\,U\) in the \(v\)-equation, as MomentumAdvection2D forms it — the corner-product form conserves total energy and the average-then-multiply form conserves potential enstrophy for non-divergent flow. Passed the same-component fields, e.g. (q, u*h, v*h), the methods return the PV transport flux \((q\,Uh, q\,Vh)\) and neither label applies.

The blend is not the Arakawa–Lamb (1981) scheme

pv_flux_blend is a linear blend of the two Sadourny forms and, for \(0 < \alpha < 1\), conserves neither invariant exactly. The Arakawa–Lamb (1981) scheme is a distinct eight-point stencil and is not implemented. The old name pv_flux_arakawa_lamb (and scheme="al" below) is a deprecated alias that warns (#283).

The corner products are formed on the full arrays, so the first interior row and column read the south / west ghost corners of the caller's ghost-filled \(q\), \(u\), \(v\): fill them (periodic, free-slip, …) before calling.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from finitevolx import CartesianGrid2D, Vorticity2D

grid = CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(64, 64, 1e6, 1e6)
vort = Vorticity2D(grid=grid)

# Relative vorticity at X-points
zeta = vort.relative_vorticity(u, v)

# Shallow-water PV at X-points
q = vort.potential_vorticity(u, v, h, f)

# PV transport flux (q*Uh, q*Vh) at U/V-points
qu, qv = vort.pv_flux_energy_conserving(q, u*h, v*h)

docs.title: Harmonic Diffusion
docs.text:
The harmonic (Laplacian) diffusion computes the tracer tendency \(\partial h/\partial t = abla \cdot (\kappa\, abla h)\) in flux form using forward-then-backward differences:

  1. East-face flux (forward T → U): $$ F_{j,i+ rac{1}{2}}^x = \kappa_{j,i+ rac{1}{2}}\, rac{h_{j,i+1} - h_{j,i}}{\Delta x} $$

  2. North-face flux (forward T → V): $$ F_{j+ rac{1}{2},i}^y = \kappa_{j+ rac{1}{2},i}\, rac{h_{j+1,i} - h_{j,i}}{\Delta y} $$

  3. Tendency (backward U/V → T): $$ rac{\partial h}{\partial t} igg|{j,i} = rac{F}{2}}^x - F_{j,i- rac{1}{2}}^x}{\Delta x

  4. rac{F_{j+ rac{1}{2},i}^y - F_{j- rac{1}{2},i}^y}{\Delta y} $$

For uniform \(\kappa\) this reduces to \(\kappa\, abla^2 h\). For spatially varying \(\kappa\) (e.g. near coastlines or mixed-layer parameterisations) the flux form ensures discrete conservation of the diffused quantity. A T-point \(\kappa\) field is averaged to each face, \(\kappa_{j,i+ rac{1}{2}} = frac{1}{2}(\kappa_{j,i} + \kappa_{j,i+1})\) (and likewise in \(y\)), which keeps the operator symmetric and second-order accurate; the spherical operators do the same. With wall="open" the wall faces average the edge cell with the ghost cell of \(\kappa\), so fill the \(\kappa\) halo consistently with the tracer BC (wrapped for periodic, a copy of the edge cell for zero gradient).

Boundary conditions by default: Face fluxes at domain walls are zero (no-flux, closed-wall), giving a homogeneous Neumann BC \(\partial h/\partial n = 0\).

docs.title: Biharmonic Diffusion
docs.text:
Biharmonic diffusion applies the harmonic operator twice:

\[ rac{\partial h}{\partial t} = -\kappa\, abla^4 h = -\kappa\, abla^2( abla^2 h) \]

It damps small scales much more strongly than large scales: for a wavenumber \(k\), harmonic damping scales as \(\kappa k^2\) while biharmonic scales as \(\kappa k^4\). This is used to remove grid-scale noise without excessively damping the resolved mesoscale.

Which diffusion to use

  • Harmonic (Diffusion2D): simple, physically motivated, appropriate for tracer diffusion when scale-selectivity is not critical.
  • Biharmonic (BiharmonicDiffusion2D): preferred for velocity diffusion in eddy-resolving models because it acts mainly on unresolved scales. Requires a larger \(\kappa\) to achieve the same total dissipation.

docs.title: Mask Support
docs.text: All diffusion classes take an optional mask= (Mask2D / Mask3D) field. Fluxes through faces with a dry side are zeroed and land-cell tendencies are zeroed, giving natural no-flux BCs at irregular coastlines without any additional code. The masked biharmonic operators apply this masked no-flux Laplacian \(D_m\) twice, \(-\kappa\,D_m(D_m h)\), after zeroing the dry inputs: the coast is no-flux for both \(h\) and \(\nabla^2 h\), land values (even NaN) never enter the wet tendency, and the operator conserves \(\sum_\text{wet} h\).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from finitevolx import Diffusion2D, BiharmonicDiffusion2D, diffusion_2d
from finitevolx import CartesianGrid2D

grid = CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(64, 64, 1e6, 1e6)

# Class-based harmonic diffusion (unmasked)
diff_op = Diffusion2D(grid=grid)
dh_dt = diff_op(h, kappa=100.0)

# With masking — mask is a class field, not a per-call kwarg.
# Diffusion applies the intermediate flux-masking pattern internally
# (flux_x *= mask.u, flux_y *= mask.v, tendency *= mask.h).
diff_op_masked = Diffusion2D(grid=grid, mask=mask)
dh_dt = diff_op_masked(h, kappa=100.0)

# Biharmonic (scale-selective)
biharm_op = BiharmonicDiffusion2D(grid=grid)
dh_dt = biharm_op(h, kappa=1e9)

# Functional API (no grid object, mask-free)
dh_dt = diffusion_2d(h, kappa=100.0, dx=grid.dx, dy=grid.dy)

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
The Coriolis term is the vortex force with the planetary vorticity \(f\). Coriolis2D uses the energy-conserving corner-product form of Sadourny (1975), the same construction as the 'energy' vortex force of MomentumAdvection2D: \(f\) (given at T-points) is averaged to the X-points, multiplied there by the cross velocity averaged to the corner, and the product is averaged back to the faces:

\[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\bigg|_{\text{Cor}} = +\overline{f_X\,\overline{v}^{x}}^{y}, \qquad \frac{\partial v}{\partial t}\bigg|_{\text{Cor}} = -\overline{f_X\,\overline{u}^{y}}^{x}, \qquad f_X = \overline{f}^{xy}. \]

Both tendencies come from the same corner products, so the kinetic-energy tendency \(\sum u\,\dot u + \sum v\,\dot v\) vanishes to round-off for any \(f\), including a \(\beta\)-plane, on a periodic domain or a closed basin (with the wall BCs of BoundaryConditionSet.closed(point="U") / "V"). For uniform \(f\) it reduces to the familiar \(+f\,\overline{v}^{xy}\), \(-f\,\overline{u}^{xy}\) (Interpolation2D.V_to_U / U_to_V). The form used before #289, \(f_{\text{on-U}}\,\overline{v}_{\text{on-U}}\), conserves energy only for uniform \(f\).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from finitevolx import CartesianGrid2D, Coriolis2D

grid = CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(64, 64, 1e6, 1e6)
cor = Coriolis2D(grid=grid)

# f at T-points
f = jnp.full((grid.Ny, grid.Nx), 1e-4)

du_cor, dv_cor = cor(u, v, f)

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
The vector-invariant (vortex-force) form of the horizontal momentum advection separates the advection into a vorticity flux and a kinetic-energy gradient:

\[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\bigg|_{\text{adv}} = +(\zeta\,v)_{\text{on-U}} - \frac{\partial K}{\partial x} \] \[ \frac{\partial v}{\partial t}\bigg|_{\text{adv}} = -(\zeta\,u)_{\text{on-V}} - \frac{\partial K}{\partial y} \]

where \(\zeta = \partial v/\partial x - \partial u/\partial y\) is the relative vorticity at X-points, \(K = \tfrac{1}{2}(\bar{u}^2 + \bar{v}^2)\) is the kinetic energy at T-points, and \((\zeta\,v)_{\text{on-U}}\) is the vorticity-flux product interpolated to U-points.

This form has important discrete conservation properties depending on how the vorticity-flux product is evaluated. Three schemes are available:

Scheme Discrete form of \((\zeta\,v)_{\text{on-U}}\) Key property Reference 'energy' (default) \(\overline{\zeta\,\overline{v}^{xy}}^{y}\): product at the corners, then average Conserves total KE for non-divergent flow Sadourny (1975) E-scheme 'enstrophy' \(\overline{\zeta}^{y}\,\overline{v}^{xy}\): average to the face, then multiply Conserves potential enstrophy Sadourny (1975) Z-scheme 'blend' \(\tfrac13 E + \tfrac23 Z\) Conserves neither exactly linear blend, not Arakawa & Lamb (1981); 'al' is a deprecated alias

When to use each scheme

  • 'energy': energy-conserving vortex force, the usual choice for long integrations.
  • 'enstrophy': preferred when enstrophy conservation matters (e.g. turbulence spindown experiments).
  • 'blend': a ⅓–⅔ blend of the two; it is not the Arakawa–Lamb (1981) scheme, which conserves both (not implemented, #283).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from finitevolx import CartesianGrid2D, MomentumAdvection2D

grid = CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(64, 64, 1e6, 1e6)

# Energy-conserving (default)
madv = MomentumAdvection2D(grid=grid)
du_adv, dv_adv = madv(u, v)

# Enstrophy-conserving
madv_z = MomentumAdvection2D(grid=grid)
du_adv, dv_adv = madv_z(u, v, scheme="enstrophy")

# 1/3 energy + 2/3 enstrophy blend
du_adv, dv_adv = madv(u, v, scheme="blend")

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
The Arakawa (1966) Jacobian \(J(f, g) = \partial f/\partial x\,\partial g/\partial y - \partial f/\partial y\,\partial g/\partial x\) is the classical advection operator for QG models. Unlike simple centred differences, the three-term Arakawa average

\[ J(f, g) = \tfrac{1}{3}(J^{++} + J^{+\times} + J^{\times+}) \]

conserves energy, enstrophy, and satisfies \(J(f, f) = 0\) and \(\int J(f, g)\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\) exactly at the discrete level.

The three terms are: - \(J^{++}\): standard centred (advective) form - \(J^{+\times}\): flux form in one direction - \(J^{\times+}\): flux form in the other direction

Conservation under a mask

The discrete identities above hold for the unmasked operator with suitable boundary conditions (e.g. \(\psi\) constant on the boundary). ArakawaJacobian2D(grid, mask=mask) zeroes land inputs and dry output cells, so sums over a masked domain such as \(\sum J\) or \(\sum q\,J\) are not guaranteed to vanish exactly.

Output shape

The class ArakawaJacobian2D returns the full [..., Ny, Nx] array with a zero ghost ring (and dry cells zeroed when given a mask), ready for a time-stepping loop. The functional arakawa_jacobian returns only the interior [..., Ny−2, Nx−2]; the caller must embed it into the full array.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from finitevolx import ArakawaJacobian2D, CartesianGrid2D, arakawa_jacobian

grid = CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(64, 64, 1e6, 1e6)

# QG vorticity advection: J(psi, q)
# psi, q have shape [Ny, Nx] with one ghost cell on each side
jac = ArakawaJacobian2D(grid=grid, mask=mask)   # mask optional
Jpsi_q = jac(psi, q)
# Jpsi_q has shape [Ny, Nx]; ghost ring and dry cells are 0

# Functional form: interior only, no mask
Jpsi_q_int = arakawa_jacobian(psi, q, dx=grid.dx, dy=grid.dy)
# Jpsi_q_int has shape [Ny-2, Nx-2]

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text:
What spatial operator do you need?
│
├── Divergence ∇·(u, v)
│   └── Divergence2D  or  divergence_2d
│
├── Relative vorticity ζ = ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y
│   ├── Class-based → Vorticity2D.relative_vorticity
│   └── Functional  → Difference2D.curl
│
├── Shallow-water PV q = (ζ+f)/h
│   └── Vorticity2D.potential_vorticity
│
├── Tracer diffusion ∂q/∂t = ∇·(κ∇q)
│   ├── Harmonic   → Diffusion2D  or  diffusion_2d
│   └── Biharmonic → BiharmonicDiffusion2D  (scale-selective)
│
├── Coriolis tendency (f×v, −f×u)
│   └── Coriolis2D
│
├── Momentum advection ∂u/∂t|adv
│   ├── Conservative vortex-force form → MomentumAdvection2D
│   └── QG vorticity advection         → ArakawaJacobian2D  or  arakawa_jacobian
│
└── Diagnostics (KE, APE, enstrophy, Okubo-Weiss, …)
    ├── Energy                → Energetics2D
    ├── Strain / Okubo-Weiss  → Strain2D
    ├── Enstrophy             → Vorticity2D.enstrophy / .potential_enstrophy
    ├── QG PV                 → QGPotentialVorticity2D
    └── See [Diagnostics API reference](api/diagnostics.md)

docs.title: Raw Stencil Primitives
docs.text:
This page explains the theory behind the raw stencil functions in finitevolx, walking from the continuous equations through the Gauss divergence theorem to the discrete stencils that the library implements.

For details on ghost-cell layout, same-size array conventions, and boundary interactions, see the C-Grid Discretization page.

docs.title: 1. The Continuous Equations
docs.text:
Geophysical fluid dynamics models solve conservation laws — partial differential equations that express the conservation of mass, momentum, and tracers:

\[ \frac{\partial q}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}(q) = 0 \]

where \(q\) is a conserved density (layer thickness \(h\), momentum \(hu\), tracer concentration \(c\), etc.) and \(\mathbf{F}(q)\) is the corresponding flux vector. In two dimensions this expands to:

\[ \frac{\partial q}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial F^x}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial F^y}{\partial y} = 0 \]

For example, in the shallow-water mass equation \(q = h\) and \(\mathbf{F} = (hu,\, hv)\), giving the familiar continuity equation:

\[ \frac{\partial h}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial (hu)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial (hv)}{\partial y} = 0 \]

These are continuous equations defined at every point in space. To solve them numerically, we need to represent them on a finite grid.

docs.title: Integrating over a control volume
docs.text:
Rather than approximating derivatives at a point (as finite-difference methods do), the finite-volume method works with the integral form of the conservation law. We divide the domain into non-overlapping cells \(\Omega_{j,i}\) and integrate the conservation law over each cell:

\[ \int_{\Omega_{j,i}} \frac{\partial q}{\partial t}\, dA + \int_{\Omega_{j,i}} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}\, dA = 0 \]

docs.title: The Gauss divergence theorem
docs.text:
The key step is applying the Gauss divergence theorem (also known as the divergence theorem or Green's theorem in 2D) to convert the volume integral of the divergence into a surface integral over the cell boundary:

\[ \int_{\Omega_{j,i}} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}\, dA = \oint_{\partial \Omega_{j,i}} \mathbf{F} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\, ds \]

where \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) is the outward unit normal to the cell boundary and \(ds\) is the line element along the boundary. This gives us:

\[ \frac{d}{dt} \int_{\Omega_{j,i}} q\, dA = -\oint_{\partial \Omega_{j,i}} \mathbf{F} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\, ds \]

The physical meaning is clear: the rate of change of \(q\) inside a cell equals the net flux through its faces. This is exact — no approximation has been made yet.

docs.title: Discretizing: cell averages and face fluxes
docs.text:
Now we introduce approximations. Define the cell average:

\[ \bar{q}_{j,i} = \frac{1}{|\Omega_{j,i}|} \int_{\Omega_{j,i}} q\, dA \]

For a rectangular cell with sides \(\Delta x\) and \(\Delta y\), the boundary integral decomposes into four face contributions — east, west, north, south. Approximating the flux as constant along each face:

\[ \oint_{\partial \Omega} \mathbf{F} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\, ds \approx \underbrace{F^x_{j,\, i+\frac{1}{2}}}_{\text{east}} \Delta y - \underbrace{F^x_{j,\, i-\frac{1}{2}}}_{\text{west}} \Delta y + \underbrace{F^y_{j+\frac{1}{2},\, i}}_{\text{north}} \Delta x - \underbrace{F^y_{j-\frac{1}{2},\, i}}_{\text{south}} \Delta x \]

Dividing by the cell area \(\Delta x \Delta y\):

\[ \frac{d\bar{q}_{j,i}}{dt} = -\frac{F^x_{j,\, i+\frac{1}{2}} - F^x_{j,\, i-\frac{1}{2}}}{\Delta x} -\frac{F^y_{j+\frac{1}{2},\, i} - F^y_{j-\frac{1}{2},\, i}}{\Delta y} \]

This is the semi-discrete finite-volume equation: continuous in time, discrete in space. Two things are now apparent:

  1. Cell averages (\(\bar{q}_{j,i}\)) naturally live at cell centres.
  2. Face fluxes (\(F^x_{j,i+½}\), \(F^y_{j+½,i}\)) naturally live at cell faces.

This is exactly the Arakawa C-grid staggering — it is not an arbitrary choice but a direct consequence of the Gauss divergence theorem.

docs.title: Why stagger the grid?
docs.text:
The finite-volume derivation tells us that scalar quantities and fluxes live at geometrically different locations: centres vs. faces. Storing them at the same location (a co-located or "A-grid") introduces computational modes and requires explicit filtering. The Arakawa C-grid respects the natural staggering by assigning:

  • Scalars (thickness, pressure, tracers) to cell centres (T-points)
  • x-fluxes and x-velocity to east faces (U-points)
  • y-fluxes and y-velocity to north faces (V-points)
  • Vorticity and related quantities to cell corners (X-points)
   V[j,i] ──── X[j,i] ──── V[j,i+1]
     │                        │
     │        T[j,i]          │
     │                        │
   V[j-1,i] ── X[j-1,i] ── V[j-1,i+1]

   U[j,i-1]    U[j,i]      U[j,i+1]
Point Position Physical role T \((j,\, i)\) — cell centre Scalars: thickness \(h\), pressure \(p\), tracers U \((j,\, i+\tfrac{1}{2})\) — east face x-velocity \(u\), east-face flux \(F^x\) V \((j+\tfrac{1}{2},\, i)\) — north face y-velocity \(v\), north-face flux \(F^y\) X \((j+\tfrac{1}{2},\, i+\tfrac{1}{2})\) — NE corner Vorticity \(\zeta\), potential vorticity \(q\)

docs.title: The discrete divergence theorem on a C-grid
docs.text:
With this layout, the semi-discrete equation from Section 2 maps directly to array operations. The discrete divergence of the velocity field at T-point \((j, i)\) reads the four surrounding face values:

\[ (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u})_{j,i} = \frac{u_{j,\, i+\frac{1}{2}} - u_{j,\, i-\frac{1}{2}}}{\Delta x} + \frac{v_{j+\frac{1}{2},\, i} - v_{j-\frac{1}{2},\, i}}{\Delta y} \]

Each term is a backward difference of a face quantity returning to the cell centre — this is diff_x_bwd(u) / dx + diff_y_bwd(v) / dy.

Similarly, the curl (relative vorticity) at X-point \((j+½, i+½)\) reads the four surrounding face values:

\[ \zeta_{j+\frac{1}{2},\, i+\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{v_{j+\frac{1}{2},\, i+1} - v_{j+\frac{1}{2},\, i}}{\Delta x} - \frac{u_{j+1,\, i+\frac{1}{2}} - u_{j,\, i+\frac{1}{2}}}{\Delta y} \]

Each term is a forward difference of a face quantity advancing to the corner — this is diff_x_fwd(v) / dx - diff_y_fwd(u) / dy.

Discrete conservation

Because the east-face flux of cell \((j,i)\) is identically the west-face flux of cell \((j, i+1)\), the finite-volume scheme conserves the total integral of \(q\) over the domain to machine precision (up to boundary fluxes). This telescoping property is built into the C-grid layout and is preserved by the raw stencils.

docs.title: Ghost cells and the interior() helper
docs.text:
In finitevolx, every array has the same total shape [Ny, Nx] with a one-cell ghost ring on each side. The physical interior occupies [1:-1, 1:-1]. Raw stencils return arrays of shape (Ny-2, Nx-2) — the interior only. The interior(values, like) helper pads the result back to full grid shape with zeros in the ghost ring.

For full details on ghost-cell layout and boundary interactions, see the C-Grid Discretization page.

docs.title: 4. The 3-Layer Architecture
docs.text:
finitevolx organises its spatial operators into three layers:

Layer What Example 1 — Raw stencils Pure index arithmetic, no scaling diff_x_fwd(h) returns h[j, i+1] − h[j, i] 2 — Scaled primitives Layer 1 + metric scaling Difference2D.diff_x_T_to_U(h) returns diff_x_fwd(h) / dx 3 — Compound operators Compose Layer 2 Difference2D.divergence(u, v) = diff_x_U_to_T(u) + diff_y_V_to_T(v)

Layer 1 — the raw stencils documented here — is the foundation. These functions perform no metric scaling (no division by \(\Delta x\), \(R\cos\varphi\,\Delta\lambda\), etc.) and no ghost-ring padding. They return interior-sized arrays that the caller can scale by any coordinate metric, making them reusable across Cartesian, spherical, cylindrical, and curvilinear coordinate systems.

docs.title: Forward differences
docs.text:
A forward difference shifts the output one half-step in the positive direction. These map centre-points to face/corner-points.

Forward x-difference (T → U or V → X):

\[ \Delta_x\, h_{j,\, i+\frac{1}{2}} = h_{j,\, i+1} - h_{j,\, i} \] 
def diff_x_fwd(h):
    return h[1:-1, 2:] - h[1:-1, 1:-1]

Forward y-difference (T → V or U → X):

\[ \Delta_y\, h_{j+\frac{1}{2},\, i} = h_{j+1,\, i} - h_{j,\, i} \] 
def diff_y_fwd(h):
    return h[2:, 1:-1] - h[1:-1, 1:-1]

docs.title: Backward differences
docs.text:
A backward difference shifts the output one half-step in the negative direction. These map face/corner-points back to centre-points.

Backward x-difference (U → T or X → V):

\[ \Delta_x\, h_{j,\, i} = h_{j,\, i+\frac{1}{2}} - h_{j,\, i-\frac{1}{2}} \] 
def diff_x_bwd(h):
    return h[1:-1, 1:-1] - h[1:-1, :-2]

Backward y-difference (V → T or X → U):

\[ \Delta_y\, h_{j,\, i} = h_{j+\frac{1}{2},\, i} - h_{j-\frac{1}{2},\, i} \] 
def diff_y_bwd(h):
    return h[1:-1, 1:-1] - h[:-2, 1:-1]

docs.title: Composing second derivatives
docs.text:
The Laplacian is a forward-then-backward composition:

\[ \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2} \approx \frac{\Delta_x^{\text{fwd}} h - \Delta_x^{\text{bwd}} h}{\Delta x^2} \] 
d2h_dx2 = (diff_x_fwd(h) - diff_x_bwd(h)) / dx**2
d2h_dy2 = (diff_y_fwd(h) - diff_y_bwd(h)) / dy**2
laplacian = d2h_dx2 + d2h_dy2

This is exactly how Difference2D.laplacian is implemented internally.

docs.title: 6. Averaging Stencils
docs.text: Interpolation between grid locations uses arithmetic averages of nearest neighbours. Like the difference stencils, these return interior-sized arrays with no ghost-ring padding.

docs.title: 2-point averages
docs.text:
Forward x-average (T → U or V → X):

\[ \bar{h}_{j,\, i+\frac{1}{2}} = \tfrac{1}{2}(h_{j,\, i} + h_{j,\, i+1}) \] 
def avg_x_fwd(h):
    return 0.5 * (h[1:-1, 1:-1] + h[1:-1, 2:])

Backward x-average (U → T or X → V):

\[ \bar{h}_{j,\, i} = \tfrac{1}{2}(h_{j,\, i-\frac{1}{2}} + h_{j,\, i+\frac{1}{2}}) \] 
def avg_x_bwd(h):
    return 0.5 * (h[1:-1, 1:-1] + h[1:-1, :-2])

The y-direction analogues avg_y_fwd and avg_y_bwd follow the same pattern along the j-axis.

docs.title: 4-point bilinear averages
docs.text:
For diagonal transfers (T ↔ X, U ↔ V), a 4-point bilinear average is used:

T → X (NE corner average):

\[ \bar{h}_{j+\frac{1}{2},\, i+\frac{1}{2}} = \tfrac{1}{4} (h_{j,i} + h_{j,i+1} + h_{j+1,i} + h_{j+1,i+1}) \] 
def avg_xy_fwd(h):
    return 0.25 * (h[1:-1, 1:-1] + h[1:-1, 2:]
                   + h[2:, 1:-1] + h[2:, 2:])

X → T (SW corner average):

\[ \bar{q}_{j,i} = \tfrac{1}{4} (q_{j+\frac{1}{2},i+\frac{1}{2}} + q_{j-\frac{1}{2},i+\frac{1}{2}} + q_{j+\frac{1}{2},i-\frac{1}{2}} + q_{j-\frac{1}{2},i-\frac{1}{2}}) \]

U → V (avg_xbwd_yfwd) and V → U (avg_xfwd_ybwd) use the same 4-point pattern but with mixed forward/backward shifts in each direction.

docs.title: 8. Usage: Building Custom Operators
docs.text: The raw stencils are designed as building blocks for custom operators, especially when working with non-Cartesian coordinate systems where the standard Difference2D / Interpolation2D classes (which divide by scalar dx, dy) are not appropriate.

docs.title: Example: Custom spherical gradient
docs.text:
On a latitude-longitude grid, the x-metric depends on latitude:

\[ \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\bigg|_{j,i+\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{h_{j,i+1} - h_{j,i}}{R\cos\varphi_j\,\Delta\lambda} \] 
from finitevolx import diff_x_fwd, interior

# Pure index arithmetic — same for any coordinate system
raw = diff_x_fwd(h)

# Apply spherical metric (array, not scalar!)
scaled = raw / (R * cos_lat[1:-1, 1:-1] * dlon)

# Pad back to full grid shape with zero ghost ring
result = interior(scaled, h)

docs.title: Example: Strain from raw stencils
docs.text:
from finitevolx import diff_x_fwd, diff_y_fwd, diff_x_bwd, diff_y_bwd, interior

# Shear strain at X-points: dv/dx + du/dy
shear = interior(
    diff_x_fwd(v) / dx + diff_y_fwd(u) / dy,
    u,
)

# Tensor strain at T-points: du/dx - dv/dy
tensor = interior(
    diff_x_bwd(u) / dx - diff_y_bwd(v) / dy,
    u,
)

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
• Pure functions: Every stencil is a stateless function of a single array argument. No grid objects, no side effects.
  • JAX-compatible: All stencils work with jax.jit, jax.vmap, and jax.grad out of the box.
  • No metric scaling: The caller chooses whether to divide by dx, R·cos(φ)·dλ, or any other metric. This keeps the stencils coordinate-system-agnostic.
  • Interior-only output: Results have shape (Ny-2, Nx-2) — the interior without the ghost ring. Use interior(result, like) to pad back to full grid shape.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Arakawa, A. & Lamb, V. R. (1977). Computational design of the basic dynamical processes of the UCLA general circulation model. Methods in Computational Physics, 17, 173-265.
  • Sadourny, R. (1975). The dynamics of finite-difference models of the shallow-water equations. J. Atmos. Sci., 32, 680-689.
  • LeVeque, R. J. (2002). Finite Volume Methods for Hyperbolic Problems. Cambridge University Press.

docs.title: Time Integration for Ocean Models
docs.text: This page covers the theory behind the time integration schemes in finitevolX, explains why certain methods are preferred for ocean and atmosphere modelling, and provides practical guidance for choosing a scheme.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Ocean models advance state variables (velocity, free surface, tracers) by solving systems of the form

\[ \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial t} = \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{y}, t) \]

where \(\mathbf{F}\) contains spatial operators (advection, pressure gradient, diffusion, Coriolis, etc.) already discretised on the Arakawa C-grid.

The choice of time-stepping method controls stability, accuracy, and efficiency. Ocean PDEs have specific characteristics that make some schemes much more appropriate than others.

docs.title: Key Constraints in Ocean PDEs
docs.text: Constraint Physical origin Consequence for time stepping CFL condition Fast gravity/barotropic waves Limits \(\Delta t\) unless split or implicit Multiple timescales Barotropic (\(c \sim 200\) m/s) vs baroclinic (\(c \sim 2\) m/s) Split-explicit or IMEX preferred Monotonicity / positivity Tracer concentrations must stay non-negative SSP methods preserve these properties Long integrations Climate runs: \(10^6\)–\(10^8\) steps Cost per step matters; 1 RHS eval/step is valuable Stiff vertical diffusion Thin surface layers with strong mixing Implicit treatment avoids tiny \(\Delta t\)

docs.title: Explicit Runge-Kutta
docs.text:
The workhorses of ocean modelling. Each step evaluates the RHS \(s\) times (one per stage) and combines them to achieve order \(p\).

Method Order Stages SSP Best for Forward Euler 1 1 C=1 Debugging, sub-stepping inner loops Heun / RK2 2 2 C=1 Simple models, moderate accuracy SSP-RK3 3 3 C=1 Default choice — best balance of accuracy, stability, and SSP Classic RK4 4 4 No High-accuracy reference solutions SSP-RK(10,4) 4 10 C=6 When you need 4th-order and SSP (large CFL)

SSP (Strong Stability Preserving) methods guarantee that any convex functional (TV norm, positivity, entropy) that is non-increasing under Forward Euler is also non-increasing under the SSP-RK method, up to a CFL number scaled by the SSP coefficient \(C\).

Recommendation

SSP-RK3 (rk3_ssp_step / RK3SSP) is the default choice for most ocean PDE work. It is the optimal 3rd-order SSP method (C=1) and is used by ROMS, MOM6, and many other models.

docs.title: Multistep Methods
docs.text:
Multistep methods reuse RHS evaluations from previous time steps, so they require only one new RHS evaluation per step — half the cost of Heun. The trade-off is that they need history and a bootstrap phase.

Method Order RHS evals/step Notes Adams-Bashforth 2 (AB2) 2 1 Used in MITgcm, NEMO Adams-Bashforth 3 (AB3) 3 1 Needs 2-step history and a ≥ 2nd-order start (RK3 in AB3Solver); a first-order start gives order 2 Leapfrog + Robert-Asselin 2 for \(\alpha = 0\), 1 for \(\alpha > 0\) 1 Classic NWP scheme; computational mode damped by filter

Leapfrog trade-offs

Leapfrog is a centred (non-dissipative) scheme, making it attractive for wave propagation. However, it supports a spurious computational mode that must be damped by the Robert-Asselin filter (parameter \(\alpha\), typically 0.01–0.1). The filter introduces \(O(\alpha)\) dissipation and lowers the scheme to first order for any \(\alpha > 0\) (measured rates 1.21, 1.14, 1.08 at \(\alpha = 0.05\) on \(y' = -1.5y\); 2.2 at \(\alpha = 0\)). The Robert–Asselin–Williams (RAW) filter would restore second order; it is not implemented.

docs.title: IMEX (Implicit-Explicit)
docs.text:
IMEX methods split the RHS into a non-stiff part treated explicitly and a stiff part treated implicitly:

\[ \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial t} = \underbrace{\mathbf{F}_E(\mathbf{y})}_{\text{advection, Coriolis}} + \underbrace{\mathbf{F}_I(\mathbf{y})}_{\text{vertical diffusion}} \]

The implicit part requires solving a linear system at each step (e.g., a tridiagonal solve for vertical diffusion columns), but this allows much larger \(\Delta t\) than fully explicit treatment of stiff terms.

finitevolX provides IMEX-SSP2(2,2,2): a 2nd-order method where the explicit part is SSP and the implicit part is A-stable (SDIRK with \(\gamma = 1 - 1/\sqrt{2}\)). It is the Pareschi–Russo SSP2(2,2,2) scheme: stage 1 solves \(Y_1 = y_n + \gamma\,\Delta t\,F_I(Y_1)\); stage 2 solves \(Y_2 = y_n + \Delta t\,F_E(Y_1) + (1-2\gamma)\Delta t\,F_I(Y_1) + \gamma\,\Delta t\,F_I(Y_2)\); the update averages both stages, \(y_{n+1} = y_n + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{2}\left[F_E(Y_i) + F_I(Y_i)\right]\).

docs.title: Split-Explicit
docs.text:
The dominant strategy in realistic ocean models (ROMS, MOM6, NEMO). The key insight: barotropic gravity waves are 100x faster than baroclinic internal waves, but the barotropic equations are 2D (cheap).

Algorithm:

  1. Subcycle the 2D barotropic equations with \(N\) small classical RK4 steps (\(\Delta t_{\text{fast}} = \Delta t_{\text{slow}} / N\)), with an optional slow (baroclinic) forcing held fixed over the cycle. RK4 is neutrally stable for the oscillatory gravity-wave mode to \((\omega\Delta t_{\text{fast}})^6/144\) per substep; a Forward-Euler subcycle would amplify it by \(\sqrt{1 + (\omega\Delta t_{\text{fast}})^2}\) per substep, unconditionally.
  2. Time-average the barotropic solution over the cycle with the trapezoidal rule (both end points, exact for a linear trend) to filter fast oscillations.
  3. Advance the 3D baroclinic equations with one Forward-Euler slow step (first order in \(\Delta t_{\text{slow}}\)) using the averaged barotropic state, then call the user's couple_2d_to_3d(state_3d, state_2d_avg).

The returned barotropic state is the instantaneous end-of-cycle state (so it stays on time), not the average. Making the 3D state consistent with the averaged barotropic one — e.g. replacing the depth mean of the 3D velocity by the averaged barotropic transport — is the caller's job, done in couple_2d_to_3d.

This decouples the barotropic CFL from the slow timestep, allowing \(\Delta t_{\text{slow}}\) to be set by the (much slower) baroclinic dynamics.

docs.title: Semi-Lagrangian
docs.text:
Instead of advancing fields on a fixed grid (Eulerian), semi-Lagrangian methods trace characteristic curves backward from each grid point, then interpolate the old field at the departure point.

Key property: unconditionally stable — the CFL number can exceed 1, which is impossible with explicit Eulerian advection. This makes semi-Lagrangian attractive for models where the flow speed is high relative to the grid spacing (e.g., atmospheric models, ECMWF IFS).

The trade-off is that interpolation introduces numerical diffusion, and monotonicity/conservation requires additional corrections.

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text:
Is vertical diffusion stiff?
├── Yes → Use IMEX (imex_ssp2_step) for the stiff/non-stiff split
└── No ↓

Do you have barotropic/baroclinic splitting?
├── Yes → Use split-explicit (split_explicit_step)
└── No ↓

Do you need CFL > 1 for advection?
├── Yes → Use semi-Lagrangian (semi_lagrangian_step)
└── No ↓

Is cost per step critical (very long runs)?
├── Yes → Use AB2 (ab2_step) — 1 RHS eval/step
└── No ↓

Default → SSP-RK3 (rk3_ssp_step / RK3SSP)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Shu & Osher (1988) — SSP-RK3 foundations
  • Gottlieb, Shu & Tadmor (2001) — Strong stability-preserving methods
  • Ketcheson (2008) — SSP-RK(10,4) with low-storage implementations
  • Durran (2010) — Numerical Methods for Fluid Dynamics
  • Pareschi & Russo (2005) — IMEX Runge-Kutta methods
  • Shchepetkin & McWilliams (2005) — Split-explicit time stepping in ROMS
  • Robert (1966) — The Robert-Asselin time filter
  • Staniforth & Cote (1991) — Semi-Lagrangian integration schemes

docs.title: Time Integration: Usage Guide
docs.text: This page covers practical usage of finitevolX's time integration module, from quick-start examples to building custom diffrax solvers.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
The fastest way to time-step a PDE: use a pure functional step function inside a loop.

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import finitevolx as fvx

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

# 1. Define your spatial RHS (any JAX pytree in, same pytree out)
grid = fvx.CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(64, 64, 1e4, 1e4)

def rhs(state):
    """Right-hand side: returns tendency with same pytree structure."""
    h, u, v = state
    # ... your spatial operators here ...
    return dh_dt, du_dt, dv_dt

# 2. Set up initial conditions
h0 = jnp.ones((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))
u0 = jnp.zeros((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))
v0 = jnp.zeros((grid.Ny, grid.Nx))
state = (h0, u0, v0)

# 3. Time-step with SSP-RK3
dt = 10.0  # seconds
for n in range(1000):
    state = fvx.rk3_ssp_step(state, rhs, dt)

All pure functional integrators accept any JAX pytree as state — tuples, dicts, nested structures, or single arrays all work transparently.

docs.title: Pure Functional Integrators
docs.text: These are standalone functions with no external dependencies beyond JAX. They show exactly how each scheme works and are ideal for learning, prototyping, and simple models.

docs.title: Explicit Runge-Kutta
docs.text:
All share the same signature: step_fn(state, rhs_fn, dt) -> new_state.

SSP-RK3 (recommended)Forward EulerHeun (RK2)Classic RK4 
from finitevolx import rk3_ssp_step

state = rk3_ssp_step(state, rhs, dt)

from finitevolx import euler_step

state = euler_step(state, rhs, dt)

from finitevolx import heun_step

state = heun_step(state, rhs, dt)

from finitevolx import rk4_step

state = rk4_step(state, rhs, dt)

docs.title: Adams-Bashforth (Multistep)
docs.text:
Multistep methods require history from previous steps. The caller must thread the history through the loop.

from finitevolx import ab2_step, euler_step

# Bootstrap: one Euler step to get the first RHS history
rhs_nm1 = rhs(state)
state = euler_step(state, rhs, dt)

# Main loop: AB2 makes only 1 RHS evaluation per step
for n in range(n_steps):
    state, rhs_n, rhs_nm1 = ab2_step(state, rhs, dt, rhs_nm1)
    rhs_nm1 = rhs_n  # shift history

ab3_step is similar but requires two history levels (rhs_nm1, rhs_nm2). Bootstrap them with at least second-order steps (e.g. two rk3_ssp_steps): the crude start rhs_nm2 = rhs_nm1 = f(y0) lowers AB3 to second order. AB3Solver does the RK3 bootstrap for you inside diffrax.diffeqsolve (fixed, uniform steps):

import diffrax as dfx
from finitevolx import AB3Solver

sol = dfx.diffeqsolve(dfx.ODETerm(rhs), AB3Solver(), t0=0.0, t1=1.0, dt0=0.01, y0=y0)

docs.title: Leapfrog with Robert-Asselin Filter
docs.text:
A three-level scheme that stores the previous state. The filter damps the computational mode.

from finitevolx import leapfrog_raf_step, euler_step

# Bootstrap
state_nm1 = state
state = euler_step(state, rhs, dt)

for n in range(n_steps):
    state_new, state_filtered = leapfrog_raf_step(
        state, state_nm1, rhs, dt, alpha=0.05
    )
    state_nm1 = state_filtered  # filtered middle level
    state = state_new

docs.title: IMEX-SSP2
docs.text:
For problems with stiff + non-stiff splitting (e.g., advection + vertical diffusion).

from finitevolx import imex_ssp2_step

def rhs_explicit(state):
    """Non-stiff: advection, Coriolis, pressure gradient."""
    return tendency_explicit

def rhs_implicit(state):
    """Stiff: vertical diffusion."""
    return tendency_implicit

def implicit_solve(rhs, gamma_dt):
    """Solve: Y - gamma_dt * F_I(Y) = rhs for Y.

    For vertical diffusion, this is a tridiagonal (TDMA) solve
    along each water column.
    """
    return solved_state

for n in range(n_steps):
    state = imex_ssp2_step(
        state, rhs_explicit, rhs_implicit, implicit_solve, dt
    )

docs.title: Split-Explicit
docs.text:
For barotropic/baroclinic mode splitting.

from finitevolx import split_explicit_step

def rhs_3d(state_3d, state_2d_avg):
    """Slow (baroclinic) tendency."""
    return tendency_3d

def rhs_2d(t_sub, state_2d, state_3d):
    """Fast (barotropic) tendency."""
    return tendency_2d

def couple(state_3d, state_2d_avg):
    """Ensure 3D/2D consistency after the slow step (the caller's job)."""
    return corrected_3d

def slow_forcing(state_3d):
    """Baroclinic forcing of the barotropic mode, held fixed over the cycle."""
    return forcing_2d   # same structure as state_2d

state_3d, state_2d = split_explicit_step(
    state_3d, state_2d,
    rhs_3d, rhs_2d, couple,
    dt_slow=600.0,    # baroclinic timestep
    n_substeps=30,    # 30 barotropic RK4 sub-steps
    slow_forcing=slow_forcing,   # optional
)

The fast mode is subcycled with RK4 (stable for oscillatory gravity waves), rhs_3d and couple receive the trapezoidal time mean of the fast state over the cycle, and the returned state_2d is the end-of-cycle state.

docs.title: Semi-Lagrangian Advection
docs.text:
Advects a 2D field by backtracking along characteristic curves.

from finitevolx import semi_lagrangian_step

# field: [Ny, Nx], u/v: velocity in m/s, dx/dy: grid spacing in m
new_field = semi_lagrangian_step(
    field, u, v, dx, dy, dt,
    interp_order=1,  # 1 = linear (monotone), 0 = nearest
    bc="periodic",   # or "edge" for clamped boundaries
)

docs.title: Diffrax Integration (Advanced)
docs.text: Diffrax is a JAX-native ODE/SDE library that provides adaptive stepping, checkpointing, dense output (SaveAt), and more. finitevolX provides Butcher-tableau solvers that plug directly into diffrax.diffeqsolve.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
import diffrax as dfx
from finitevolx import RK3SSP

def rhs(t, y, args):
    """diffrax convention: (t, y, args) -> dy/dt."""
    return -y  # your PDE RHS here

solver = RK3SSP()
sol = dfx.diffeqsolve(
    dfx.ODETerm(rhs),
    solver,
    t0=0.0,
    t1=100.0,
    dt0=0.1,
    y0=initial_state,
    saveat=dfx.SaveAt(ts=jnp.linspace(0, 100, 101)),
)

# sol.ys has shape [101, ...] — the state at each saved time

docs.title: Available Diffrax Solvers
docs.text:
Class Order Type Adaptive steps Usage ForwardEulerDfx 1 ERK no (raises) Debugging RK2Heun 2 ERK yes (embedded Euler) General SSP_RK2 2 ERK yes (embedded Euler) Same as Heun, SSP form RK3SSP 3 ERK yes (embedded Heun) Recommended RK4Classic 4 ERK no (raises) High accuracy SSP_RK104 4 ERK (10 stages) no (raises) Large CFL + 4th order IMEX_SSP2 2 IMEX (MultiTerm) yes (embedded 1st order) Stiff/non-stiff split AB3Solver 3 multistep (RK3 start) no (raises) One RHS per step, uniform dt SemiLagrangianSolver 1 semi-Lagrangian (SemiLagrangianTerm) no (raises) Advection at CFL > 1

"Adaptive steps" means stepsize_controller=dfx.PIDController(...) works; the solvers marked "no" have no embedded error estimate and raise under an adaptive controller rather than step blindly. For adaptive 4th / 5th order use diffrax's own Tsit5 or Dopri5.

# adaptive RK3-SSP
sol = dfx.diffeqsolve(
    dfx.ODETerm(rhs), RK3SSP(), t0=0.0, t1=10.0, dt0=0.1, y0=y0,
    stepsize_controller=dfx.PIDController(rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-8),
)

# IMEX: explicit + implicit terms; with fixed steps the implicit root finder
# needs its own tolerances
terms = dfx.MultiTerm(dfx.ODETerm(rhs_explicit), dfx.ODETerm(rhs_implicit))
solver = IMEX_SSP2(root_finder=dfx.VeryChord(rtol=1e-8, atol=1e-8))
sol = dfx.diffeqsolve(terms, solver, t0=0.0, t1=1.0, dt0=0.01, y0=y0)

# semi-Lagrangian: the term returns the velocity (u, v) in grid units / time
term = SemiLagrangianTerm(lambda t, q, args: (u_grid, v_grid))
sol = dfx.diffeqsolve(
    term, SemiLagrangianSolver(), t0=0.0, t1=10.0, dt0=0.5, y0=q0,
    saveat=dfx.SaveAt(ts=jnp.linspace(0.0, 10.0, 11)),
)

docs.title: The solve_ocean_pde Convenience Wrapper
docs.text:
A thin wrapper around diffeqsolve that optionally applies boundary conditions to the tendency at each stage evaluation.

from finitevolx import solve_ocean_pde, RK3SSP

def rhs(t, y, args):
    return compute_tendency(y)

def apply_bc(dydt):
    """Zero out tendency in ghost cells."""
    return dydt.at[0, :].set(0).at[-1, :].set(0)

sol = solve_ocean_pde(
    rhs,
    RK3SSP(),
    y0=initial_state,
    t0=0.0,
    t1=1000.0,
    dt0=1.0,
    bc_fn=apply_bc,
    saveat=dfx.SaveAt(t1=True),
)

Any other keyword goes straight to diffeqsolve (stepsize_controller=, adjoint=, max_steps=, throw=, ...). A fixed-step run gets max_steps = ceil((t1 - t0) / dt0) + 16 by default, so long runs are not cut off by diffrax's default of 4096 steps.

docs.title: Saving Trajectories
docs.text:
Diffrax's SaveAt gives fine-grained control over what to save:

# Save at specific times
saveat = dfx.SaveAt(ts=jnp.array([0.0, 10.0, 50.0, 100.0]))

# Save only the final state (default)
saveat = dfx.SaveAt(t1=True)

# Save every step (careful with memory)
saveat = dfx.SaveAt(steps=True)

sol = dfx.diffeqsolve(..., saveat=saveat)

docs.title: Manual Solver Interfaces (Advanced)
docs.text: For schemes that don't fit the standard Runge-Kutta framework (multistep, split-explicit), finitevolX provides equinox.Module-based solvers with explicit init/step interfaces.

docs.title: AB2Solver
docs.text:
from finitevolx import AB2Solver

def rhs(t, y):
    """Note: (t, y) signature, not (t, y, args)."""
    return -y

solver = AB2Solver()
solver, y = solver.init(rhs, t0=0.0, y0=jnp.array(1.0), dt=0.01)

for n in range(1, n_steps):
    y, solver = solver.step(rhs, t0 + n * dt, y, dt)

The solver is an immutable equinox Module — solver.step() returns a new solver object with updated history. This makes it fully compatible with jax.jit and functional JAX patterns.

docs.title: LeapfrogRAFSolver
docs.text:
from finitevolx import LeapfrogRAFSolver

solver = LeapfrogRAFSolver(alpha=0.05)
solver, y = solver.init(rhs, t0=0.0, y0=jnp.array(1.0), dt=0.01)

for n in range(1, n_steps):
    y, solver = solver.step(rhs, t0 + n * dt, y, dt)

docs.title: SplitExplicitRKSolver
docs.text:
from finitevolx import SplitExplicitRKSolver

solver = SplitExplicitRKSolver(n_substeps=30)

y_3d_new, y_2d_new = solver.step(
    rhs_slow,   # (t, y_3d, y_2d_avg) -> tendency_3d
    rhs_fast,   # (t_sub, y_2d, y_3d) -> tendency_2d
    t=0.0,
    y_3d=state_3d,
    y_2d=state_2d,
    dt_slow=600.0,
    slow_forcing=slow_forcing,        # optional, (y_3d) -> forcing_2d
    couple_2d_to_3d=couple,           # optional, (new_y_3d, y_2d_avg) -> y_3d
)

docs.title: Building a Custom Diffrax Solver
docs.text: You can define your own Butcher-tableau solver and immediately use it with diffeqsolve.

docs.title: Example: A Custom 2-Stage Method
docs.text:
import diffrax as dfx
import jax.numpy as jnp
from typing import Any, ClassVar

class MyRK2(dfx.AbstractERK):
    """Midpoint method (RK2).

    Butcher tableau:
        0   |
        1/2 | 1/2
        ----+--------
            | 0    1
    """

    tableau: ClassVar[dfx.ButcherTableau] = dfx.ButcherTableau(
        # c: abscissae for stages 1..s-1 (excludes first stage c=0)
        c=jnp.array([0.5]),
        # b_sol: weights for combining stages
        b_sol=jnp.array([0.0, 1.0]),
        # b_error: error estimate (zeros = no embedded method)
        b_error=jnp.zeros(2),
        # a_lower: strictly lower-triangular part, row by row
        a_lower=(jnp.array([0.5]),),
    )
    interpolation_cls: ClassVar[Any] = (
        dfx.ThirdOrderHermitePolynomialInterpolation.from_k
    )

# Use it exactly like the built-in solvers
sol = dfx.diffeqsolve(
    dfx.ODETerm(lambda t, y, args: -y),
    MyRK2(),
    t0=0.0, t1=1.0, dt0=0.01, y0=1.0,
)

docs.title: Key Rules for Butcher Tableaux in Diffrax
docs.text:
1. c has length num_stages - 1 — the first stage always has \(c_0 = 0\) (or set c1= for non-zero).
  2. a_lower is a tuple of arrays — a_lower[i] has length i + 1 and represents row i + 1 of the lower-triangular A matrix.
  3. b_error must be an array (not None) — use jnp.zeros(num_stages) if you don't have an embedded error estimate.
  4. b_sol must sum to 1 for consistency.
  5. c[i] must equal sum(a_lower[i]) — the row-sum condition.

docs.title: Example: Custom AbstractSolver (Non-RK)
docs.text:
For methods that don't fit the Runge-Kutta framework:

import diffrax as dfx
import jax
from diffrax import RESULTS
from typing import Any, ClassVar

class MyCustomSolver(dfx.AbstractSolver):
    """A solver with a completely custom step method."""

    term_structure: ClassVar[Any] = dfx.AbstractTerm
    interpolation_cls: ClassVar[Any] = dfx.LocalLinearInterpolation

    def order(self, terms):
        return 1

    def init(self, terms, t0, t1, y0, args):
        return None  # no solver state needed

    def step(self, terms, t0, t1, y0, args, solver_state, made_jump):
        del solver_state, made_jump
        dt = t1 - t0
        f0 = terms.vf(t0, y0, args)
        y1 = jax.tree.map(lambda y, f: y + dt * f, y0, f0)

        dense_info = dict(y0=y0, y1=y1)
        return y1, None, dense_info, None, RESULTS.successful

    def func(self, terms, t0, y0, args):
        return terms.vf(t0, y0, args)

docs.title: JIT Compilation
docs.text:
All integrators are fully jax.jit-compatible. For best performance, JIT the entire time-stepping loop:

@jax.jit
def integrate(state, n_steps):
    def body(carry, _):
        return fvx.rk3_ssp_step(carry, rhs, dt), None

    final_state, _ = jax.lax.scan(body, state, None, length=n_steps)
    return final_state

result = integrate(initial_state, 10000)

Using jax.lax.scan instead of a Python loop avoids retracing and enables XLA to optimise the entire integration as a single compiled kernel.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
This section documents the public API of finitevolX, organised by category.

Browse the sidebar to find documentation for grids, masks, operators, solvers, and time integration methods.

docs.title: Advection Operators
docs.text: Flux-form advection operators for scalar transport on staggered C-grids.

docs.title: finitevolx.Advection1D
docs.text:
Bases: Module

1-D advection operator.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default grid CartesianGrid1D

The underlying 1-D grid.

required mask Mask1D or None

Optional land/ocean mask; every method is then land-safe. Dry inputs are zeroed with jnp.where (so NaN on land cannot leak), the upwind-biased methods go through upwind_flux with the pre-built adaptive stencil hierarchy (falling back to narrower stencils near coastlines, so no chosen stencil reads a dry cell), the face fluxes on dry faces (mask.u false) are zeroed before the divergence (no flux through the coast), and dry T-cells are exactly zero. None (default) matches the unmasked behaviour bit for bit.

None Source code in finitevolx/_src/advection/advection.py 
class Advection1D(eqx.Module):
    """1-D advection operator.

    Parameters
    ----------
    grid : CartesianGrid1D
        The underlying 1-D grid.
    mask : Mask1D or None, optional
        Optional land/ocean mask; every method is then land-safe.  Dry
        inputs are zeroed with ``jnp.where`` (so ``NaN`` on land cannot
        leak), the upwind-biased methods go through ``upwind_flux`` with
        the pre-built adaptive stencil hierarchy (falling back to
        narrower stencils near coastlines, so no chosen stencil reads a
        dry cell), the face fluxes on dry faces (``mask.u`` false) are
        zeroed before the divergence (no flux through the coast), and
        dry T-cells are exactly zero.  ``None`` (default) matches the
        unmasked behaviour bit for bit.
    """

    grid: CartesianGrid1D
    mask: Mask1D | None
    recon: Reconstruction1D
    _mask_hierarchy_x: dict[int, Bool[Array, "Nx"]] | None

    def __init__(
        self,
        grid: CartesianGrid1D,
        mask: Mask1D | None = None,
    ) -> None:
        self.grid = grid
        self.mask = mask
        self.recon = Reconstruction1D(grid=grid)
        if mask is not None:
            self._mask_hierarchy_x = mask.get_adaptive_masks(
                stencil_sizes=_HIERARCHY_SIZES
            )
        else:
            self._mask_hierarchy_x = None

    def __call__(
        self,
        h: Float[Array, "Nx"],
        u: Float[Array, "Nx"],
        method: str = "upwind1",
        wall: str = "closed",
    ) -> Float[Array, "Nx"]:
        """Advective tendency -d(h*u)/dx at T-points.

        dh[i] = -(fe[i+1/2] - fe[i-1/2]) / dx

        Parameters
        ----------
        h : Float[Array, "Nx"]
            Scalar at T-points.
        u : Float[Array, "Nx"]
            Velocity at U-points.
        method : str
            Reconstruction method: ``'naive'``, ``'upwind1'``, ``'upwind2'``,
            ``'upwind3'``, ``'weno3'``, ``'weno5'``, ``'wenoz5'``,
            ``'weno7'``, ``'weno9'``, or a flux-limiter TVD scheme:
            ``'minmod'``, ``'van_leer'``, ``'superbee'``, ``'mc'``.
        wall : {"closed", "open"}, default "closed"
            Lateral-boundary treatment.  ``"closed"`` (default, unchanged)
            writes the tendency only on the strict interior ``[2:-2]`` and
            treats the domain walls as no-flux — the wall-adjacent interior
            cells hold stale values.  ``"open"`` writes the full interior
            ``[1:-1]`` and computes the two domain-wall face fluxes with a
            first-order upwind reconstruction that reads the ghost ring, so
            Dirichlet / outflow / periodic boundaries (applied by the caller
            to the ghost cells beforehand) drive the advective transport.
            The interior faces keep the requested high-order ``method``; the
            flux field stays single-valued, so mass is conserved exactly.
            ``"open"`` is not supported together with a ``mask``.

        Returns
        -------
        Float[Array, "Nx"]
            Advective tendency at T-points.
        """
        _validate_wall(wall, self.mask)
        if self.mask is not None:
            # Zero the dry inputs before any stencil reads them, so land
            # values (even NaN) reach neither the output nor its gradient.
            h = jnp.where(self.mask.h, h, 0.0)  # [Nx]
            u = jnp.where(self.mask.u, u, 0.0)  # [Nx]
        # ── masked path: route through upwind_flux with adaptive stencils ─
        if self._mask_hierarchy_x is not None and method in _MASK_DISPATCHABLE:
            rfx, sizes = _rec_funcs_for_method_1d(self.recon, method)
            mh = narrow_mask_hierarchy(self._mask_hierarchy_x, sizes)
            fe = upwind_flux(h, u, dim=0, rec_funcs=rfx, mask_hierarchy=mh)
        # ── unmasked path: existing per-method dispatch ─────────────────
        elif method == "naive":
            fe = self.recon.naive_x(h, u)
        elif method == "upwind1":
            fe = self.recon.upwind1_x(h, u)
        elif method == "upwind2":
            fe = self.recon.upwind2_x(h, u)
        elif method == "upwind3":
            fe = self.recon.upwind3_x(h, u)
        elif method == "weno3":
            fe = self.recon.weno3_x(h, u)
        elif method == "weno5":
            fe = self.recon.weno5_x(h, u)
        elif method == "wenoz5":
            fe = self.recon.wenoz5_x(h, u)
