ApplyMask holds a Mask2D and ExplicitStep holds a whole graph, so their records are for inspection only: ApplyMask is forbid_in_yaml and persists through serialize_weights / with_weights, and nested graphs are rebuilt by pipekit's YAML loader rather than from_state.

docs.title: Composing finitevolX with pipekit¶
docs.text:
finitevolX ships two tiers of the same operators:

Tier A  finitevolx                 Difference2D(grid).diff_x_T_to_U(h)
        arrays in, arrays out      eqx.Module / pure function, no config
                │
                ▼
Tier B  finitevolx.pipekit         Difference(grid=G, axis="x", src="T", dst="U")
        pipekit Operators          JSON config · eqx leaves · Sequential / Graph
                │
                ▼
pipekit Graph / Sequential / Rollout — diagnostics pipelines, DA glue, emulators

Tier B is the same arithmetic (each operator is one Tier-A call) with a configuration you can save, a node you can wire into a pipekit.Graph, and pytree leaves (f₀, β, g′, Δt) that jax.grad reaches.

When to use which. A model's right-hand side belongs in your model code — in somax, a Term tree, which is already pytree-native and IMEX-partitionable. Tier B is for everything around the model: diagnostics over a trajectory, stagger moves for plotting, ghost-ring and mask handling, reductions, and observation operators for assimilation. Below we still build a model RHS as a graph, because it makes a compact, checkable example.

Install the extra: pip install "finitevolx[pipekit]". Theory of the operators: C-grid discretization.

docs.title: 1. Linear rotating shallow water as a graph¶
docs.text:
On a doubly periodic C-grid with mean depth $H$, gravity $g$ and an $f$-plane $f = f_0$, for thickness anomaly $h$ (T-points) and velocity $(u, v)$ (U- and V-points):

$$ \partial_t h = -H\,(\delta_x u + \delta_y v), \qquad \partial_t u = +f\,\bar v - g\,\delta_x h, \qquad \partial_t v = -f\,\bar u - g\,\delta_y h . $$

The energy $E = \tfrac12 \sum (H(u^2 + v^2) + g h^2)\,\Delta A$ is conserved by the spatial scheme. A grid is a static tuple (nx_interior, ny_interior, Lx, Ly).

docs.title: Same program as hand-written finitevolX¶
docs.text: The same step written directly against Tier A gives a bit-identical state and compiles to the same program up to a few fusions (104 vs 101 here, on CPU), with no gathers or scatters on either side: under jit the pipekit layer is free.

docs.title: 2. A diagnostics pipeline over the trajectory¶
docs.text: Every Tier-B operator takes [*batch, Ny, Nx], so one graph evaluates relative vorticity ζ (X-points), the Okubo–Weiss parameter $W$ (T-points) and the total energy $E$ for every saved time at once; the reductions keep the time axis, [T, Ny, Nx] → [T].

docs.title: 3. Gradients through the graph¶
docs.text: f₀ is a leaf of the Coriolis node, so jax.grad of a loss on the trajectory reaches it through Rollout, ExplicitStep and the graph. Twin experiment: observe $h$ from the run with $f_0 = 20$, start from a wrong guess, and look at the misfit $\mathcal{L}(f_0) = \sum_t \lVert h_t(f_0) - h_t^{\text{obs}} \rVert^2$.

docs.title: 4. Configuration round trip¶
docs.text: Every operator's state is plain JSON; Operator.from_state rebuilds it. The grid is a tuple, learnable values are numbers.

diff_op = fvx.Difference2D(grid)
div_op = fvx.Divergence2D(grid)

# p = 0 on every wall face: Dirichlet1D(value=0) sets ghost = -interior.
wall = fvx.BoundaryConditionSet.closed()


def gradient(f):
    """(∂f/∂x at U, ∂f/∂y at V) on every face, the wall faces included.

    f's ghost ring must be filled.  The forward differences write U[1:-1, 1:-1]
    and V[1:-1, 1:-1]; the west / south wall faces U[:, 0] and V[0, :] are
    boundary-owned, so we add them:
    u[j, 1/2] = (f[j, 1] - f[j, 0]) / dx,  v[1/2, i] = (f[1, i] - f[0, i]) / dy.
    """
    u = diff_op.diff_x_T_to_U(f)  # [Ny, Nx]
    v = diff_op.diff_y_T_to_V(f)  # [Ny, Nx]
    u = u.at[1:-1, 0].set((f[1:-1, 1] - f[1:-1, 0]) / dx)
    v = v.at[0, 1:-1].set((f[1, 1:-1] - f[0, 1:-1]) / dy)
    return u, v


# --- Construct a known divergent velocity field ---
# A divergent potential φ at T-points (x = (i - 1/2) dx) that vanishes on the
# wall faces x = 0, Lx and y = 0, Ly; then u = ∂φ/∂x at U-points and
# v = ∂φ/∂y at V-points.  This guarantees ∇·u = ∇²φ in the discrete sense.
x_t = (jnp.arange(Nx) - 0.5) * dx  # [Nx]
y_t = (jnp.arange(Ny) - 0.5) * dy  # [Ny]
X_t, Y_t = x_t[None, :], y_t[:, None]
phi = jnp.sin(jnp.pi * X_t / Lx) * jnp.sin(jnp.pi * Y_t / Ly)
phi = phi + 0.3 * jnp.sin(2 * jnp.pi * X_t / Lx) * jnp.sin(jnp.pi * Y_t / Ly)
phi = wall(phi, dx, dy)  # the sines already mirror; this makes the wall explicit

# Divergent velocity: u = ∂φ/∂x at U-points, v = ∂φ/∂y at V-points
u, v = gradient(phi)

# Divergence at T-points
div_uv = div_op(u, v)
print(f"max |∇·u| = {float(jnp.abs(div_uv[1:-1, 1:-1]).max()):.4e}")

# --- Solve ∇²p = ∇·u and project ---
# Pass the full array: the wrapper solves the T interior [1:-1, 1:-1] with
# p = 0 on the faces (DST-II) and returns a zero ghost ring.
p_full = fvx.pressure_from_divergence(div_uv, dx, dy, bc="dst")
p_full = wall(p_full, dx, dy)  # fill the ghost ring: p = 0 on the faces

rhs = div_uv[1:-1, 1:-1]

# Pressure gradient at U/V points (wall faces included)

# Corrected velocity

v_corr = v - dp_dy

# Verify divergence-free

max_div_before = float(jnp.abs(div_uv[1:-1, 1:-1]).max())
max_div_after = float(jnp.abs(div_corr[1:-1, 1:-1]).max())

docs.title: Pressure Poisson Equation on the Arakawa C-Grid¶
docs.text: This notebook demonstrates solving the pressure Poisson equation $\nabla^2 p = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}$ on the Arakawa C-grid and using the result to project a velocity field to be divergence-free.

docs.title: C-Grid Variable Placement¶
docs.text:
X ── V ── X ── V ── X
    |         |         |
    U    T    U    T    U     T = tracer / pressure (cell centre)
    |         |         |     U = u-velocity (east face)
    X ── V ── X ── V ── X     V = v-velocity (north face)
    |         |         |     X = vorticity (corner)
    U    T    U    T    U
    |         |         |
    X ── V ── X ── V ── X

The C-grid divergence at T-points uses backward differences of face velocities, while the pressure gradient uses forward differences. Their composition $\nabla \cdot \nabla p$ gives exactly the 5-point Laplacian, which the spectral DST-II solver inverts when $p = 0$ sits on the wall faces.

docs.title: 1. Grid Construction¶
docs.text: We build a CartesianGrid2D with a 2-cell ghost ring. The interior has nx × ny T-points; the full array shape is (ny+2) × (nx+2).

docs.title: Grid point locations¶
docs.text: A small 8×4 grid shows how T, U, and V points are staggered.

docs.title: 2. Divergence-Free Projection¶
docs.text:
The pressure-projection method (Chorin splitting) removes divergence from a velocity field in three steps:

  1. Compute $ abla \cdot \mathbf{u}$ at T-points
  2. Solve $ abla^2 p = abla \cdot \mathbf{u}$ with $p = 0$ on walls
  3. Correct: $\mathbf{u}^* = \mathbf{u} - abla p$

Because the C-grid divergence and gradient operators compose to the exact 5-point Laplacian, the corrected velocity is discretely divergence-free.

Where the wall is: pressure lives at T points (cell centres), and the walls are the cell faces half a cell outside the first / last interior T point. A Dirichlet1D boundary condition puts $p = 0$ on the face by mirroring the interior into the ghost cell (ghost = -interior), and that is exactly the DST-II (staggered Dirichlet) spectral solver, which fvx.pressure_from_divergence(..., bc="dst") applies to the T interior of the full array. The wall-face normal velocities u[:, 0] (west) and v[0, :] (south) are boundary-owned: no forward operator writes them, so we fill them from the same gradient.

docs.title: 3. DST-I vs DST-II: Which Solver?¶
docs.text:
Both solvers take the T interior as their unknowns; they differ in where the zero sits:

  • DST-II puts $p = 0$ on the cell faces, half a cell outside the first / last T point (ghost = -interior): the C-grid wall, and what Dirichlet1D imposes.
  • DST-I puts $p = 0$ on the virtual nodes one step outside, i.e. at the ghost-cell centres (ghost = 0): a wall half a cell too far out.

Each is the exact inverse of its own discrete operator, so the Laplacian residual alone cannot tell them apart; the distance to φ (which vanishes on the faces) can.

docs.title: 4. Module Class Interface¶
docs.text: spectraldiffx provides equinox Module classes for solver composition. StaggeredDirichletHelmholtzSolver2D wraps DST-II and is convenient for cell-centred workflows and JIT compilation.

docs.title: 5. Convenience Wrapper¶
docs.text: finitevolX provides one-line convenience functions that dispatch to the correct spectral solver based on the bc parameter.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text: Concept Detail Pressure location T-points (cell centres) on the C-grid Correct solver DST-II: $p = 0$ on the wall faces (Dirichlet1D, ghost = −interior) DST-I $p = 0$ at the ghost-cell centres (ghost = 0): the wall half a cell too far out Projection $\mathbf{u}^* = \mathbf{u} - \nabla p$ removes divergence to machine precision C-grid advantage $\partial p/\partial x$ at U-points, $\partial p/\partial y$ at V-points — no interpolation Module class StaggeredDirichletHelmholtzSolver2D wraps DST-II for equinox workflows Convenience fvx.pressure_from_divergence(div_u, dx, dy) on the full array — defaults to DCT (Neumann, on the faces)

adv_op = fvx.Advection2D(grid=grid)
vort_op = fvx.Vorticity2D(grid=grid)


def tendency(q_field):
    """Compute dq_a/dt and return (tendency, psi, u, v).

    Steps:
      1. Invert q_a -> psi  (Helmholtz)
      2. psi -> (u, v)      (geostrophic balance)
      3. PV advection:      -u . grad(q_a)
      4. Beta term:         -beta * v  (at T-points)
      5. Wind forcing:      F(y)       (constant in time)
      6. Bottom drag:       -r * zeta  (drag on VORTICITY, not PV)
      7. Diffusion:         nu * laplacian(q_a)
    """
    # 1. Invert PV -> streamfunction
    psi_field = invert_streamfunction(q_field)

    # 2. Geostrophic velocity
    u_field, v_field = geostrophic_velocity(psi_field)

    # 3. PV advection: -u . grad(q_a)  (writes to interior [2:-2, 2:-2])
    q_rhs = adv_op(q_field, u_field, v_field, method="upwind1")

    # 4. Beta term: -beta * v at interior T-points
    #    We interpolate v from V-points to T-points first.
    v_center = interp_op.V_to_T(v_field)
    q_rhs = q_rhs.at[1:-1, 1:-1].add(-beta * v_center[1:-1, 1:-1])

    # 5. Wind forcing (already on full grid with zero ghosts)
    q_rhs = q_rhs + wind_curl

    # 6. Bottom drag: -r * zeta (NOT -r * q_a!)
    #    Drag acts on relative vorticity zeta = laplacian(psi).
    #    If we dragged q_a instead, we would get an extra +r*psi/Ld^2 term
    #    that acts as anti-damping on the interface displacement.
    zeta = diff_op.laplacian(psi_field)
    q_rhs = q_rhs - drag * zeta

    # 7. Diffusion: nu * laplacian(q_a)
    q_rhs = q_rhs + viscosity * diff_op.laplacian(q_field)

    return q_rhs, psi_field, u_field, v_field


def apply_bc(q_field):
    """Re-enforce wall BCs: zero ghost ring (psi = 0 on walls)."""
    return fvx.pad_interior(q_field, mode="constant")


def pv_tendency(q_field):
    """Tendency function compatible with heun_step: q -> dq/dt."""
    q_rhs, _, _, _ = tendency(apply_bc(q_field))
    return q_rhs

Why drag on $\zeta$, not $q_a$?

The PV anomaly is $q_a = \zeta - \psi/L_d^2$. If we write the drag as $-r\,q_a$, we get $-r\,\zeta + r\,\psi/L_d^2$. The second term is a positive feedback: it amplifies the interface displacement instead of damping it. Physical bottom drag acts on the flow velocity (and hence on $\zeta = \nabla^2 \psi$), not on the full PV.

docs.title: 1.5-Layer Quasi-Geostrophic Double-Gyre Model¶
docs.text:
This notebook builds a 1.5-layer quasi-geostrophic (QG) model step by step using finitevolx operators on the Arakawa C-grid. The physical setup is an active upper layer of depth $H$ over an infinitely deep, resting abyssal layer. The density difference between the two layers defines a reduced gravity $g'$, which sets the internal Rossby deformation radius $L_d$.

The model is forced by a classical double-gyre wind-curl pattern and dissipated by bottom drag and lateral viscosity. This is the simplest system that produces the western-intensified gyres, inertial recirculation, and mesoscale eddies that characterise mid-latitude ocean basins.

docs.title: Governing equations (Formulation B -- PV anomaly)¶
docs.text:
The prognostic variable is the PV anomaly

$$q_a = \zeta - rac{\psi}{L_d^2}$$

where $\zeta = abla^2 \psi$ is the relative vorticity and $\psi$ is the streamfunction. The resting state $\psi = 0$ gives $q_a = 0$. The evolution equation is

$$\partial_t q_a = -\mathbf{u} \cdot abla q_a \;-\; eta\,v \;+\; F \;-\; r\,\zeta \;+\; u\, abla^2 q_a$$

The streamfunction is recovered from the PV anomaly by inverting the Helmholtz equation

$$\left( abla^2 - rac{1}{L_d^2} ight)\psi = q_a$$

and the geostrophic velocity follows from

$$u = - rac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad v = + rac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}$$

docs.title: Term-by-term breakdown¶
docs.text:
Term Expression Physical meaning Advection $-\mathbf{u} \cdot 
abla q_a$ Nonlinear transport of PV by the geostrophic flow Beta effect $- eta\,v$ Planetary-vorticity advection (Rossby-wave restoring) Wind forcing $F(y)$ Double-gyre wind-curl input of PV Bottom drag $-r\,\zeta$ Linear friction on relative vorticity (Ekman spin-down) Diffusion $
u\,
abla^2 q_a$ Laplacian viscosity for grid-scale dissipation

docs.title: 1. The Rossby Deformation Radius¶
docs.text:
The first baroclinic Rossby radius of deformation sets the length scale at which rotation and stratification compete:

$$L_d = \frac{\sqrt{g' H}}{f_0}$$

where $g' = g\,\Delta\rho/\rho_0$ is the reduced gravity across the interface, $H$ is the active-layer thickness, and $f_0$ is the reference Coriolis parameter. Motions at scales $\gg L_d$ are dominated by rotation and behave barotropically; motions at scales $\sim L_d$ feel the stratification and develop baroclinic instability.

For mid-latitude ocean basins, $L_d \approx 30$--$50$ km. We use $L_d = 40$ km here.

Parameter Symbol Value Units Meaning Domain length x $L_x$ $5.12 \times 10^6$ m Zonal basin extent (~5000 km) Domain length y $L_y$ $5.12 \times 10^6$ m Meridional basin extent Coriolis parameter $f_0$ $9.375 \times 10^{-5}$ s$^{-1}$ Reference rotation rate (~30 N) Beta $\beta$ $1.754 \times 10^{-11}$ m$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$ Meridional Coriolis gradient Rossby radius $L_d$ $4 \times 10^4$ m Deformation radius (40 km) Bottom drag $r$ $5 \times 10^{-8}$ s$^{-1}$ Ekman spin-down rate Viscosity $\nu$ $5 \times 10^4$ m$^2$ s$^{-1}$ Laplacian diffusivity Wind amplitude $F_0$ $2 \times 10^{-12}$ s$^{-2}$ Peak PV forcing Time step $\Delta t$ 4000 s ~1.1 hours

docs.title: 2. C-Grid Placement for QG¶
docs.text:
On the Arakawa C-grid, the QG variables live at specific stagger locations. The PV anomaly $q_a$ and streamfunction $\psi$ are T-point (cell-centre) quantities, while the velocity components sit on the appropriate faces:

    X ── V ── X ── V ── X
    |         |         |
    U   T,q   U   T,q   U     T = psi, q_a (cell centre)
    |   psi   |   psi   |     U = u-velocity (east/west face)
    X ── V ── X ── V ── X     V = v-velocity (north/south face)
    |         |         |     X = relative vorticity zeta (corner)
    U   T,q   U   T,q   U
    |   psi   |   psi   |
    X ── V ── X ── V ── X

The relative vorticity $\zeta = \partial v/\partial x - \partial u/\partial y$ naturally lives at X-points (corners), and must be interpolated to T-points for the drag term. The full grid array has shape (ny+2, nx+2) with a one-cell ghost ring encoding the solid-wall boundary condition $\psi = 0$ on all four walls.

docs.title: 4. Wind-Curl Forcing¶
docs.text:
The double-gyre wind pattern drives an anticyclonic (clockwise) subtropical gyre in the southern half and a cyclonic (counterclockwise) subpolar gyre in the northern half:

$$F(y) = -F_0 \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi\,y}{L_y}\right)$$

This is negative in the southern half ($0 < y < L_y/2$, driving anticyclonic circulation) and positive in the northern half ($L_y/2 < y < L_y$, driving cyclonic circulation). The two gyres share a boundary at the mid-basin latitude, where the Gulf-Stream-like western boundary current separates from the coast.

fvx.WindCurl2D computes this forcing from the wind stress itself: the C-grid curl of the stress, divided by $\rho_0 H$, at X-points. A zonal stress $\tau_x = -\tau_0 \cos(2\pi y / L_y)$ has $\mathrm{curl}\,\tau / (\rho_0 H) = -\tau_0 (2\pi/L_y) \sin(2\pi y/L_y) / (\rho_0 H)$, so $\tau_0 = F_0 \rho_0 H L_y / (2\pi)$ gives the peak forcing $F_0$. The stress is evaluated at every T-point, ghost ring included, and the X-point forcing is averaged to the T-points where $q_a$ lives.

docs.title: 5. Streamfunction Inversion¶
docs.text:
The key diagnostic step in QG is inverting the PV anomaly for the streamfunction. Given $q_a$ at T-points, we solve the Helmholtz equation

$$\left(\nabla^2 - \frac{1}{L_d^2}\right)\psi = q_a$$

with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions $\psi = 0$ on all four basin walls (no-normal-flow).

finitevolx provides solve_helmholtz_dst for this problem. In this model $\psi$ is a T-point field whose ghost ring is zero (the inversion below pads the interior solution with zeros), and DST-I applied to the T interior [1:-1, 1:-1] is the exact inverse of the 5-point Laplacian with that zero ghost ring: it places $\psi = 0$ at the ghost-cell centres, half a cell outside the wall faces. That is a first-order wall position; a face Dirichlet wall for a T-point field is DST-II (solve_helmholtz_dst2, ghost = -interior). The convenience wrappers streamfunction_from_vorticity / pv_inversion solve for an X-point $\psi$ (wall nodes 0 and N-2), so they are not a drop-in replacement for this T-point formulation.

The lambda_ parameter is $1/L_d^2$, which enters the Helmholtz equation as the screening term that couples the streamfunction to the interface displacement.

docs.title: 6. Geostrophic Velocity Recovery¶
docs.text:
From the streamfunction $\psi$ at T-points, we recover the geostrophic velocity:

$$u = -\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad v = +\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}$$

On the C-grid, $\psi$ is first averaged to X-points (corners), and then the orthogonal derivatives place $u$ on U-points and $v$ on V-points:

Step 1: psi (T-point) --[avg to corners]--> psi_X (X-point)
Step 2: u = -d(psi_X)/dy  at U-points    shape: (Ny, Nx)
         v = +d(psi_X)/dx  at V-points    shape: (Ny, Nx)

docs.title: 7. PV Tendency Function¶
docs.text: We now assemble the full PV tendency, line by line. Each physical process maps onto a specific finitevolx operation.

docs.title: 8. Time Stepping¶
docs.text: We use the Heun method (explicit RK2 predictor-corrector) from finitevolx.heun_step. This is second-order accurate and stable for advection-dominated problems with a suitable CFL constraint.

docs.title: Short demo run¶
docs.text: We run a brief integration (~500 steps) from a small sinusoidal PV perturbation to demonstrate the model mechanics. This is too short for full spin-up, but enough to see the wind forcing begin to organise the circulation into the double-gyre pattern.

docs.title: 9. Results¶
docs.text:
We plot the final state as a 4-panel figure: PV anomaly, SSH (height), speed, and relative vorticity.

Boundary slicing: Native T-point fields ($q_a$, $\eta$) use [1:-1, 1:-1]. Interpolated/derived fields (speed, vorticity) use [2:-2, 2:-2] to avoid ghost-cell contamination at the boundary.

docs.title: 10. Full Simulation¶
docs.text:
A production run uses higher resolution and a long spin-up to reach statistical equilibrium. Typical parameters:

  • Grid: 64 x 64 interior points
  • Spin-up: 5000 steps (~230 days of silent integration)
  • Recording: 10000 steps (~460 days), sampling every 1000 steps

After spin-up, the western boundary currents intensify, the gyre separation develops inertial overshoot, and mesoscale eddies populate the inter-gyre region.

docs.title: 11. Summary¶
docs.text: Component finitevolx API Purpose Grid CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(nx, ny, Lx, Ly) C-grid with ghost ring Helmholtz inversion solve_helmholtz_dst(rhs, dx, dy, lambda_) $(\\nabla^2 - \\lambda)\\psi = q_a$ Differences Difference2D(grid) Finite differences, Laplacian Interpolation Interpolation2D(grid) T-to-X, V-to-T, U-to-T, X-to-T Advection Advection2D(grid)(q, u, v, method="upwind1") PV transport Vorticity Vorticity2D(grid).relative_vorticity(u, v) $\\zeta$ at X-points Boundary conditions pad_interior(q, mode="constant") Zero ghost ring (solid walls) Time stepping heun_step(q, tendency_fn, dt) Heun / RK2 predictor-corrector

docs.title: Key modelling choices¶
docs.text:
1. Formulation B (PV anomaly): the prognostic variable $q_a = \zeta - \psi/L_d^2$ keeps the resting state at zero, simplifying initial and boundary conditions.
  2. Explicit beta term ($-\beta v$): planetary-vorticity advection is handled as a source term rather than absorbed into $q_a$.
  3. Drag on vorticity ($-r\zeta$, not $-r q_a$): avoids spurious anti-damping of the interface displacement.
  4. DST-I solver: matches finitevolx's ghost-cell convention where $\psi = 0$ at the array boundary (vertex Dirichlet).

def tendency(eta_field, u_field, v_field):
    """Compute the nonlinear shallow-water tendencies on the C-grid.

    Returns (d_eta/dt, du/dt, dv/dt), all at their native stagger points.
    """
    # --- Continuity: d(eta)/dt = -div((H+eta)*u) + nu*lap(eta) ---
    layer_depth = mean_depth + eta_field  # H + eta         [Ny, Nx]
    eta_rhs = adv(
        layer_depth,
        u_field,
        v_field,  # -div((H+eta)*u) [Ny, Nx]
        method="upwind1",
    )
    eta_rhs = eta_rhs + viscosity * diff.laplacian(eta_field)  # + nu*lap(eta)

    # --- Momentum advection: -(u . grad) u, -(u . grad) v ---
    u_on_t = interp.U_to_T(u_field)  # u at T-points   [Ny, Nx]
    v_on_t = interp.V_to_T(v_field)  # v at T-points   [Ny, Nx]

    du_dx, du_dy = centered_gradients(u_on_t)  # grad(u) at T    [Ny, Nx]
    dv_dx, dv_dy = centered_gradients(v_on_t)  # grad(v) at T    [Ny, Nx]
    u_adv = interp.T_to_U(u_on_t * du_dx + v_on_t * du_dy)  # -> U  [Ny, Nx]
    v_adv = interp.T_to_V(u_on_t * dv_dx + v_on_t * dv_dy)  # -> V  [Ny, Nx]

    # --- Coriolis: f*v at U-points, -f*u at V-points ---
    v_on_u = interp.V_to_U(v_field)  # v at U-points   [Ny, Nx]
    u_on_v = interp.U_to_V(u_field)  # u at V-points   [Ny, Nx]
    coriolis_on_u = interp.T_to_U(coriolis)  # f at U-points   [Ny, Nx]
    coriolis_on_v = interp.T_to_V(coriolis)  # f at V-points   [Ny, Nx]

    # --- u-momentum: -g*d(eta)/dx - adv + f*v + F_x - r*u + nu*lap(u) ---
    u_rhs = -gravity * diff.diff_x_T_to_U(eta_field)  # pressure grad
    u_rhs = u_rhs - u_adv  # - (u . grad) u
    u_rhs = u_rhs + coriolis_on_u * v_on_u  # + f*v
    u_rhs = u_rhs + wind_u  # + F_x
    u_rhs = u_rhs - drag * u_field  # - r*u
    u_rhs = u_rhs + viscosity * diff.laplacian(u_field)  # + nu*lap(u)

    # --- v-momentum: -g*d(eta)/dy - adv - f*u - r*v + nu*lap(v) ---
    v_rhs = -gravity * diff.diff_y_T_to_V(eta_field)  # pressure grad
    v_rhs = v_rhs - v_adv  # - (u . grad) v
    v_rhs = v_rhs - coriolis_on_v * u_on_v  # - f*u
    v_rhs = v_rhs - drag * v_field  # - r*v
    v_rhs = v_rhs + viscosity * diff.laplacian(v_field)  # + nu*lap(v)

    return eta_rhs, u_rhs, v_rhs

def apply_bc(state):

    return tuple(fvx.pad_interior(f, mode="constant") for f in state)

docs.title: Nonlinear Shallow Water Equations on the Arakawa C-Grid¶
docs.text:
This notebook extends the linear shallow-water model to the nonlinear case. The two key additions are:

  1. The continuity equation uses the full layer depth $H + \eta$ instead of the constant reference depth $H$.
  2. The momentum equations include nonlinear advection $-(\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{u}$.

docs.title: Governing equations¶
docs.text:
$$ rac{\partial \eta}{\partial t} = - abla \cdot igl[(H + \eta)\,\mathbf{u} igr] + u\, abla^2 \eta $$

$$ rac{\partial u}{\partial t} = -g\, rac{\partial \eta}{\partial x} - (\mathbf{u} \cdot abla) u + f\,v - r\,u + u\, abla^2 u + F_x $$

$$ rac{\partial v}{\partial t} = -g\, rac{\partial \eta}{\partial y} - (\mathbf{u} \cdot abla) v - f\,u - r\,v + u\, abla^2 v $$

Compared to the linear version:

  • Continuity: $-H\, abla \cdot \mathbf{u}$ becomes $- abla \cdot [(H + \eta)\,\mathbf{u}]$, coupling the free surface into the mass flux.
  • Momentum: the advection terms $-(\mathbf{u} \cdot abla) u$ and $-(\mathbf{u} \cdot abla) v$ are absent in the linear model.

We integrate these on a closed-basin Arakawa C-grid driven by a double-gyre wind stress, using finitevolx.heun_step (Heun/RK2).

docs.title: 1. What's New vs the Linear Model¶
docs.text:
Term Linear Nonlinear Continuity $-H\, abla \cdot \mathbf{u}$ $- abla \cdot [(H+\eta)\,\mathbf{u}]$ Momentum advection absent $-(\mathbf{u} \cdot abla) u$, $-(\mathbf{u} \cdot abla) v$ Pressure gradient $-g\,\partial_x \eta$ $-g\,\partial_x \eta$ (same -- see note below) Coriolis, drag, diffusion unchanged unchanged New operator -- Advection2D (upwind flux reconstruction)

Note on the pressure gradient: the nonlinear model uses the same $-g\,\partial_x \eta$ as the linear model, not the full Bernoulli function $B = g\eta + frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{u}|^2$. Using the full Bernoulli together with the separate advection $-(\mathbf{u}\cdot abla) \mathbf{u}$ would double-count the kinetic-energy gradient $ abla( frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{u}|^2)$, which is already contained in the advection term.

docs.title: 2. Grid and Parameters¶
docs.text: We use the same domain and physics as the linear shallow-water notebook. The grid is a closed-basin Arakawa C-grid with a 2-cell ghost ring (zero = solid walls).

docs.title: 3. Initial Conditions and Forcing¶
docs.text:
The setup is identical to the linear shallow-water notebook:

  • Initial $\eta$: a gentle sinusoidal bump.
  • Coriolis: beta-plane $f = f_0 + \beta (y - L_y/2)$.
  • Wind: double-gyre pattern $F_x = -A\cos(2\pi y / L_y)$.

We pad interior fields with a zero ghost ring (solid-wall BCs), then edge-pad the Coriolis and wind fields so that interpolations near the walls see physical values rather than zeros.

docs.title: 4. The Advection Operator¶
docs.text:
The key new ingredient is Advection2D. It computes the advective flux divergence $-\nabla \cdot (h\,\mathbf{u})$ at T-points using upwind flux reconstruction.

adv_op = fvx.Advection2D(grid=grid)
tendency = adv_op(h, u, v, method="upwind1")
  • h is the scalar field being advected (at T-points).
  • u, v are the advecting velocities (at U- and V-points).
  • method="upwind1" selects first-order upwind reconstruction; higher orders ("weno3", "weno5", etc.) are also available.

The operator returns the tendency $-\nabla \cdot (h\,\mathbf{u})$, which is exactly what appears in the continuity equation.

docs.title: 5. The Nonlinear Continuity Equation¶
docs.text:
In the linear model, the continuity equation is:

$$ rac{\partial \eta}{\partial t} = -H\, abla \cdot \mathbf{u} + u\, abla^2 \eta $$

In the nonlinear model, $H$ is replaced by the full layer depth $H + \eta$:

$$ rac{\partial \eta}{\partial t} = - abla \cdot igl[(H + \eta)\,\mathbf{u} igr] + u\, abla^2 \eta $$

This means we advect the total depth $H + \eta$ rather than just using a constant $H$ times the velocity divergence. In code:

layer_depth = mean_depth + eta
eta_rhs = adv(layer_depth, u, v, method="upwind1")  # -div((H+eta)*u)
eta_rhs = eta_rhs + viscosity * diff.laplacian(eta)  # + nu * lap(eta)

Stability note: when $\eta$ becomes large and negative, $H + \eta$ can approach zero or go negative, causing the model to blow up. In practice we monitor the minimum depth to ensure it stays positive.

docs.title: 6. Momentum Advection¶
docs.text:
The nonlinear momentum equations add the terms:

$$ -(\mathbf{u} \cdot abla) u = -\left(u\, rac{\partial u}{\partial x} + v\, rac{\partial u}{\partial y} ight) $$

$$ -(\mathbf{u} \cdot abla) v = -\left(u\, rac{\partial v}{\partial x} + v\, rac{\partial v}{\partial y} ight) $$

Implementation: we interpolate $u$ and $v$ to T-points, compute centred gradients there, form the dot product, then interpolate back to the correct staggered position (U or V).

Why not use the Bernoulli pressure gradient? The full Bernoulli function is $B = g\eta + frac{1}{2}(u^2 + v^2)$. Its gradient includes $ abla( frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{u}|^2)$, which is already contained in the advection term $(\mathbf{u} \cdot abla)\mathbf{u}$ via the vector identity:

$$ (\mathbf{u} \cdot abla)\mathbf{u} = abla\!\left( frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{u}|^2 ight) + ( abla imes \mathbf{u}) imes \mathbf{u} $$

Using $- abla B$ together with $-(\mathbf{u}\cdot abla)\mathbf{u}$ would double-count the kinetic-energy gradient. So we keep the pressure gradient as simply $-g\, abla\eta$.

docs.title: 7. Tendency Function¶
docs.text: The full right-hand side assembles all terms. Each line is annotated with the corresponding equation term.

docs.title: 8. Time Stepping¶
docs.text: We use finitevolx.heun_step (Heun/RK2 predictor-corrector) and run a short integration of 500 steps. After each step, we re-apply wall boundary conditions (zero ghost cells) using fvx.pad_interior.

docs.title: 9. Results¶
docs.text:
We plot four diagnostics:

  1. Free-surface anomaly $\eta$ -- the sea-surface height perturbation.
  2. Speed $|\mathbf{u}|$ -- flow magnitude at T-points.
  3. Relative vorticity $\zeta = \partial v/\partial x - \partial u/\partial y$.
  4. Total depth $H + \eta$ -- must remain positive everywhere.

Boundary slicing: Native T-point fields ($\eta$, total depth) use [1:-1, 1:-1]. Interpolated/derived fields (speed, vorticity) use [2:-2, 2:-2] to avoid ghost-cell contamination at the boundary.

docs.title: 10. Full Simulation¶
docs.text:
The production script at scripts/shallow_water.py runs a longer integration (150 000 spin-up steps + 15 000 recording steps) on a 64 x 64 grid and saves an animated GIF of the free-surface evolution.

# Full nonlinear shallow-water configuration:
#   nx, ny = 64, 64
#   Lx, Ly = 5.12e6, 5.12e6
#   dt = 200 s, spinup = 150000 steps, record = 15000 steps
#   Same physics: g=9.81, H=500, f0=9.375e-5, beta=1.754e-11
#   New: Advection2D for continuity, centered advection for momentum

docs.title: Linear vs Nonlinear Comparison¶

import finitevolx as fvx

IMG_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "images" / "spde_prior"
IMG_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
from pathlib import Path import gaussx import jax import jax.numpy as jnp import matplotlib matplotlib.use("Agg") import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import finitevolx as fvx jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True) IMG_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "images" / "spde_prior" IMG_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) In [ ]: Copied! 
ny, nx = 96, 128  # [Ny, Nx]
Lx, Ly = 2.0, 1.5
dx, dy = Lx / nx, Ly / ny
ell = 0.15  # correlation length
alpha = 2
kappa = np.sqrt(8 * (alpha - 1)) / ell  # ν = α − d/2 = 1 in 2-D
tau = 1.0

# K = κ² − ∇²_h = −(∇²_h − κ²), a DiagonalizedOperator, never materialised
K = -fvx.helmholtz_operator((ny, nx), dx, dy, lambda_=kappa**2, bc="dct")
# Q = τ² K^α: same transform pair, eigenvalues τ² (κ² − Λ)^α
Q = gaussx.DiagonalizedOperator(
    tau**2 * K.eigenvalues**alpha, K.forward, K.inverse, K.in_shape, normal=True
)


def marginal_variance(Q: gaussx.DiagonalizedOperator) -> jnp.ndarray:
    """diag(Q⁻¹) for a separable orthonormal basis V = Vy ⊗ Vx.

    diag(Vᵀ Λ⁻¹ V)[j, i] = Σ_{k,l} Vy[k, j]² Vx[l, i]² / Λ[k, l], computed
    from the two 1-D bases (O(Ny² + Nx²) memory) rather than the
    (Ny·Nx)² matrix.
    """
    ny, nx = Q.in_shape
    # 1-D orthonormal DCT-II matrices: column j is the transform of e_j
    Vy = fvx.dctn(jnp.eye(ny), type=2, axes=[0], norm="ortho")  # [k, j]
    Vx = fvx.dctn(jnp.eye(nx), type=2, axes=[0], norm="ortho")  # [l, i]
    return (Vy**2).T @ (1.0 / Q.eigenvalues) @ (Vx**2)  # [Ny, Nx]


# rescale τ so the interior marginal standard deviation is 1
var = marginal_variance(Q)  # [Ny, Nx]
tau = float(jnp.sqrt(var[ny // 2, nx // 2]))
Q = gaussx.DiagonalizedOperator(
    tau**2 * K.eigenvalues**alpha, K.forward, K.inverse, K.in_shape, normal=True
)
std = jnp.sqrt(marginal_variance(Q))  # [Ny, Nx]

# exact samples x = Q^{-1/2} z, elementwise in the eigenvalues
B_half = gaussx.sqrt(gaussx.inv(Q))
keys = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(0), 2)
samples = [
    B_half.mv(jax.random.normal(k, (ny * nx,))).reshape(ny, nx) for k in keys
]
print(f"logdet Q = {float(gaussx.logdet(Q)):.1f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))
extent = [0, Lx, 0, Ly]
for ax, s, title in zip(axes[:2], samples, ["sample 1", "sample 2"]):
    im = ax.imshow(np.asarray(s), origin="lower", cmap="RdBu_r", extent=extent)
    ax.set_title(title)
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8)
im = axes[2].imshow(np.asarray(std), origin="lower", cmap="viridis", extent=extent)
axes[2].set_title("marginal std $\\sqrt{\\mathrm{diag}(Q^{-1})}$")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes[2], shrink=0.8)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(IMG_DIR / "rectangle_samples.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

The Neumann walls inflate the variance within about one correlation length of the boundary (up to $2\times$ on an edge, $4\times$ in a corner); extend the domain beyond the region of interest when that matters.

ny, nx = 96, 96
L = 1.5
dx = dy = L / nx
wet = np.zeros((ny, nx), dtype=bool)
wet[3:-3, 3:-3] = True  # basin with closed walls
wet[3:62, 44:52] = False  # a peninsula from the south wall
wet_flat = wet.ravel()

K_m = -fvx.masked_helmholtz_operator(wet, dx, dy, lambda_=kappa**2)
K_rect = -fvx.helmholtz_operator((ny, nx), dx, dy, lambda_=kappa**2, bc="dct")


def b_column_masked(j: int, i: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Row (j, i) of B = K_m^{-2}, on the full grid with land set to NaN."""
    v = jnp.zeros(ny * nx).at[j * nx + i].set(1.0)[wet_flat]  # [n_wet]
    col = gaussx.solve(K_m, gaussx.solve(K_m, v))  # [n_wet]
    full = np.full(ny * nx, np.nan)
    full[wet_flat] = np.asarray(col)
    full = full.reshape(ny, nx)
    return full / full[j, i]


def b_column_rect(j: int, i: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Row (j, i) of the rectangle prior, which ignores the land."""
    v = jnp.zeros(ny * nx).at[j * nx + i].set(1.0)
    col = gaussx.solve(K_rect, gaussx.solve(K_rect, v)).reshape(ny, nx)
    col = np.asarray(col / col[j, i])
    return np.where(wet, col, np.nan)


point = (30, 42)  # just west of the peninsula
corr_masked = b_column_masked(*point)
corr_rect = b_column_rect(*point)
east = (30, 53)  # just east of it, 11 cells (0.17) away
print(
    f"correlation across the peninsula: masked {corr_masked[east]:.2e}, "
    f"rectangle {corr_rect[east]:.3f}"
)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
for ax, corr, title in zip(
    axes,
    [corr_rect, corr_masked],
    ["rectangle prior (ignores land)", "masked prior (SPDE on the basin)"],
):
    land = np.where(wet, np.nan, 1.0)
    ax.imshow(land, origin="lower", cmap="Greys", vmin=0, vmax=1.5, extent=[0, L, 0, L])
    im = ax.imshow(corr, origin="lower", cmap="magma", vmin=0, vmax=1, extent=[0, L, 0, L])
    ax.plot((point[1] + 0.5) * dx, (point[0] + 0.5) * dy, "c*", ms=12)
    ax.set_title(title)
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8, label="correlation with ★")
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(IMG_DIR / "peninsula_correlation.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5)) for ax, corr, title in zip( axes, [corr_rect, corr_masked], ["rectangle prior (ignores land)", "masked prior (SPDE on the basin)"], ): land = np.where(wet, np.nan, 1.0) ax.imshow(land, origin="lower", cmap="Greys", vmin=0, vmax=1.5, extent=[0, L, 0, L]) im = ax.imshow(corr, origin="lower", cmap="magma", vmin=0, vmax=1, extent=[0, L, 0, L]) ax.plot((point[1] + 0.5) * dx, (point[0] + 0.5) * dy, "c*", ms=12) ax.set_title(title) fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8, label="correlation with ★") fig.tight_layout() fig.savefig(IMG_DIR / "peninsula_correlation.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight") plt.show()

The rectangle prior correlates the two sides of the peninsula through the land; the masked prior has to go around it, so the correlation across is much weaker. The same operator gives $\log\det Q$ (for hyperparameter likelihoods) through gaussx.logdet, and is differentiable in $\kappa$ and $\tau$ for learning them.

docs.title: SPDE Priors on the C-Grid with gaussx¶
docs.text:
A data-assimilation background covariance $B$ (or a Gaussian-process prior for an emulator) should live on the model's own grid and respect its coastline: two points on either side of a peninsula are far apart for the ocean even when they are close in a straight line. The SPDE approach (Lindgren, Rue & Lindström, 2011) gets this for free. Let

  • $\psi$ be a field on the ψ-points of the C-grid,
  • $ abla^2_h$ the model's 5-point Laplacian, with the land mask applied as $\psi = 0$ on land,
  • $\kappa > 0$ an inverse correlation length ($\ell \approx \sqrt{8 u}/\kappa$),
  • $\alpha \in \{1, 2, \dots\}$ the smoothness order and $ au$ an amplitude.

The Matérn-type precision is

$$ Q = au^2\,(\kappa^2 - abla^2_h)^{\alpha}, \qquad B = Q^{-1}. $$

finitevolX exposes $ abla^2_h - \lambda$ as a structured gaussx operator, so $Q$ inherits gaussx's exact solve, log-determinant and square root without ever forming a matrix. The marginal variance $\operatorname{diag}(Q^{-1})$ is the exception: gaussx.diag_inv builds the dense $(N_y N_x)^2$ basis for this operator (about 1.2 GB at $96 imes 128$), so section 1 computes it from the two 1-D bases instead.

  • helmholtz_operator(shape, dx, dy, lambda_, bc) — the rectangle operator as a gaussx.DiagonalizedOperator (FFT / DST-I / DCT-II);
  • masked_helmholtz_operator(mask, dx, dy, lambda_) — the masked operator of masked_laplacian as a gaussx.MaskedOperator whose solve is the capacitance method.

On a uniform grid the lumped mass matrix of the SPDE is $h^2 I$; it is absorbed into $ au$ here.

docs.title: 1. Rectangle: exact samples and marginal variance¶
docs.text: On a rectangle with Neumann walls (DCT-II), $K = \kappa^2 - \nabla^2_h$ is diagonal in the DCT basis with eigenvalues $\kappa^2 - \Lambda_{ji}$, so $Q = \tau^2 K^\alpha$ is too. A sample is $x = Q^{-1/2} z$ with $z \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$, and $\operatorname{diag}(Q^{-1})$ is exact.

docs.title: 2. A basin with a peninsula: correlations follow the ocean¶
docs.text:
With a land mask, $K_m = \kappa^2 - \nabla^2_h$ restricted to the wet points is no longer diagonal in any fast basin, but masked_helmholtz_operator solves it exactly with the capacitance method (two DST solves per right-hand side, after a one-off factorisation over the coastal ring). For $\alpha = 2$,

$$ B\,v = \tau^{-2} K_m^{-1} K_m^{-1} v, $$

so one column of $B$ (the correlation with a single point) costs two solves. Compare it with the same prior on the rectangle, which ignores the land.

docs.title: Where to go next¶
docs.text:
• Use $B$ as the background covariance in an EnKF / 3D-Var update with gaussx's Kalman primitives.
  • Swap $\nabla^2_h$ for an anisotropic or variable-coefficient operator (e.g. MultigridSolver with face coefficients) and solve with gaussx.CGSolver(preconditioner=fvx.make_gaussx_multigrid_preconditioner(mg)).

nx, ny = 128, 128
Lx, Ly = 2e6, 2e6  # 2000 km × 2000 km basin

grid = fvx.CartesianGrid2D.from_interior(nx, ny, Lx, Ly)
dx, dy = grid.dx, grid.dy

# Vortex parameters
Gamma = 1e5       # circulation (m²/s)
r0 = 300e3        # vortex radius (300 km)
x0, y0 = Lx / 2, Ly / 2  # centre of domain

# We construct ζ at the two C-grid locations, on the full [Ny, Nx] arrays
# of the grid (ghost ring included):
#
# - X-points (corners): X[j, i] sits at (x, y) = (i dx, j dy); the walls are
#   the X nodes 0 and N-2 (x = 0 and x = Lx), index N-1 is outside.  The
#   wrapper solves the wet nodes [1:-2, 1:-2] with ψ = 0 on the wall nodes.
# - T-points (cell centres): T[j, i] sits at ((i - 1/2) dx, (j - 1/2) dy);
#   the interior is [1:-1, 1:-1] and the walls are the faces half a cell
#   outside it (DST-II).

# X-point coordinates on the full array
x_X = jnp.arange(nx + 2)[None, :] * dx
y_X = jnp.arange(ny + 2)[:, None] * dy

# T-point coordinates of the interior cells
x_T = (jnp.arange(nx)[None, :] + 0.5) * dx
y_T = (jnp.arange(ny)[:, None] + 0.5) * dy

# Vorticity on each grid
r2_X = (x_X - x0) ** 2 + (y_X - y0) ** 2
zeta_X = (Gamma / (jnp.pi * r0**2)) * jnp.exp(-r2_X / r0**2)

r2_T = (x_T - x0) ** 2 + (y_T - y0) ** 2
zeta_T = (Gamma / (jnp.pi * r0**2)) * jnp.exp(-r2_T / r0**2)

print(f"max |ζ_X| = {float(jnp.abs(zeta_X).max()):.4e} s⁻¹ (vertex grid)")
print(f"max |ζ_T| = {float(jnp.abs(zeta_T).max()):.4e} s⁻¹ (cell-centre grid)")

Both placements converge at second order ($O(dx^2)$) because each solver's implicit zero sits on the wall: DST-I on the X wall nodes, DST-II on the cell faces. The spectral solvers invert the discrete $[1,-2,1]/dx^2$ Laplacian exactly, but the RHS was computed from the continuous $\nabla^2$, so that $O(dx^2)$ gap is the error. (Passing the T-point interior to DST-I instead would put the wall half a cell outside and drop to first order.)

docs.title: Streamfunction Inversion: T-point vs X-point Placement¶
docs.text:
The vorticity–streamfunction relation $\nabla^2 \psi = \zeta$ is the canonical elliptic inversion in geophysical fluid dynamics. On the Arakawa C-grid, the same physical equation requires different spectral solvers depending on where $\psi$ lives:

Placement Grid type Solver finitevolX API X-points (corners) Regular (vertex-centred) DST-I on X [1:-2, 1:-2] streamfunction_from_vorticity(bc="dst") T-points (cell centres) Staggered (cell-centred) DST-II solve_poisson_dst2 (direct)

docs.title: Where does $\psi$ live?¶
docs.text:
Option A: ψ at X-points (corners)     Option B: ψ at T-points (centres)
  ─────────────────────────────────      ──────────────────────────────────

  ψ ── · ── ψ ── · ── ψ                · ── · ── · ── · ── ·
  |         |         |                  |         |         |
  ·    ζ    ·    ζ    ·                  ·    ψ    ·    ψ    ·
  |         |         |                  |    ζ    |    ζ    |
  ψ ── · ── ψ ── · ── ψ                · ── · ── · ── · ── ·
  |         |         |                  |         |         |
  ·    ζ    ·    ζ    ·                  ·    ψ    ·    ψ    ·
  |         |         |                  |    ζ    |    ζ    |
  ψ ── · ── ψ ── · ── ψ                · ── · ── · ── · ── ·

  ψ at corners, ζ at centres             ψ and ζ co-located at centres
  Solver: DST-I (regular Dirichlet)      Solver: DST-II (staggered Dirichlet)

This notebook compares both placements on a Lamb–Oseen vortex test case.

docs.title: 1. Analytical Vortex (Lamb–Oseen)¶
docs.text:
We use a Gaussian vorticity field centred in a rectangular basin with $\psi = 0$ on the walls:

$$ \zeta(x, y) = \frac{\Gamma}{\pi r_0^2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{r^2}{r_0^2}\right) $$

where $r^2 = (x - x_0)^2 + (y - y_0)^2$.

docs.title: 2. X-point Inversion (DST-I)¶
docs.text: The finitevolX convenience wrapper streamfunction_from_vorticity puts $\psi$ at the X-points (corners). We pass the full [Ny, Nx] array: it solves the wet X nodes [1:-2, 1:-2] with DST-I, so that $\psi = 0$ falls exactly on the wall nodes 0 and N-2, and returns zeros there.

docs.title: 3. T-point Inversion (DST-II)¶
docs.text: For $\psi$ co-located with $\zeta$ at T-points (cell centres), we use the staggered Dirichlet solver directly.

docs.title: 4. Velocity Recovery¶
docs.text:
From each $\psi$ placement, we recover $(u, v)$ using C-grid differences.

From $\psi$ at X-points (corners):

  • $u = -\partial\psi/\partial y$ at U-points via diff_y_X_to_U (natural X→U map)
  • $v = +\partial\psi/\partial x$ at V-points via diff_x_X_to_V (natural X→V map)

From $\psi$ at T-points (cell centres):

  • Difference2D.grad_perp(psi) returns $(u, v)$ at (U, V) points directly, combining interpolation and differentiation in the correct staggered sense.

docs.title: 5. Error Analysis¶
docs.text: The two placements sample $\psi$ half a cell apart, so we average the X-point solution to the T-points before comparing; both solve the same basin, so the difference is the $O(dx^2)$ discretisation error.

docs.title: Convergence test¶
docs.text: We verify that both placements converge at $O(dx^2)$ against a manufactured solution $\psi_{\text{exact}} = \sin(\pi x / L_x) \sin(\pi y / L_y)$ which satisfies $\psi = 0$ on the walls $x = 0, L_x$ and $y = 0, L_y$, sampled at each placement's own points.

docs.title: 6. When to Use Which¶
docs.text: ψ at X-points (DST-I) ψ at T-points (DST-II) Natural for Vorticity–streamfunction formulation Pressure-like formulations Velocity recovery Direct difference X→U, X→V T→U, T→V (same as pressure gradient) BC enforcement ψ=0 on the X wall nodes (on the boundary) ψ=0 on the cell faces (half a spacing outside the T points) finitevolX API streamfunction_from_vorticity(bc="dst") Direct solve_poisson_dst2 Typical use case QG models, barotropic vorticity Projection methods, SSH diagnostics

def tendency(eta_field, u_field, v_field):
    """Compute the linear shallow-water tendencies on the C-grid.

    Parameters
    ----------
    eta_field, u_field, v_field : Float[Array, "Ny Nx"]
        Current state (all on the full (Ny, Nx) grid with ghost cells).

    Returns
    -------
    eta_rhs, u_rhs, v_rhs : Float[Array, "Ny Nx"]
        Time tendencies for each prognostic variable.
    """
    # === eta equation: d(eta)/dt = -H * div(u) + nu * laplacian(eta) ===

    # Divergence of velocity at T-points: shape (Ny, Nx)
    # Uses backward differences: div = du/dx + dv/dy
    eta_rhs = -mean_depth * diff_op.divergence(u_field, v_field)

    # Diffusion of eta at T-points: shape (Ny, Nx)
    # 5-point Laplacian stencil
    eta_rhs = eta_rhs + viscosity * diff_op.laplacian(eta_field)

    # === Coriolis cross-terms ===
    # f lives at T-points; we need it at U-points and V-points
    # v lives at V-points; we need it at U-points for f*v in the u-equation
    # u lives at U-points; we need it at V-points for f*u in the v-equation

    v_on_u = interp_op.V_to_U(v_field)  # V-pts -> U-pts, shape (Ny, Nx)
    u_on_v = interp_op.U_to_V(u_field)  # U-pts -> V-pts, shape (Ny, Nx)
    coriolis_on_u = interp_op.T_to_U(coriolis)  # T-pts -> U-pts, shape (Ny, Nx)
    coriolis_on_v = interp_op.T_to_V(coriolis)  # T-pts -> V-pts, shape (Ny, Nx)

    # === u equation: d(u)/dt = -g * d(eta)/dx + f*v - r*u + nu*lap(u) + F_x ===

    # Pressure gradient: -g * d(eta)/dx at U-points
    u_rhs = -gravity * diff_op.diff_x_T_to_U(eta_field)

    # Coriolis: +f*v at U-points (f averaged to U, v averaged to U)
    u_rhs = u_rhs + coriolis_on_u * v_on_u

    # Wind forcing + drag + diffusion, all at U-points
    u_rhs = u_rhs + wind_u - drag * u_field + viscosity * diff_op.laplacian(u_field)

    # === v equation: d(v)/dt = -g * d(eta)/dy - f*u - r*v + nu*lap(v) ===

    # Pressure gradient: -g * d(eta)/dy at V-points
    v_rhs = -gravity * diff_op.diff_y_T_to_V(eta_field)

    # Coriolis: -f*u at V-points (f averaged to V, u averaged to V)
    v_rhs = v_rhs - coriolis_on_v * u_on_v

    # Drag + diffusion, all at V-points (no meridional wind forcing)
    v_rhs = v_rhs - drag * v_field + viscosity * diff_op.laplacian(v_field)

    return eta_rhs, u_rhs, v_rhs


def apply_bc(state):
    """Re-apply wall (zero ghost-cell) boundary conditions.

    After each time step, ghost cells are zeroed out.  This enforces
    no-normal-flow at the basin walls for velocity, and homogeneous
    Dirichlet for eta.
    """
    return tuple(fvx.pad_interior(f, mode="constant") for f in state)


def rhs(state):
    """Tendency with BC enforcement, for use with heun_step."""
    return tendency(*apply_bc(state))

docs.title: Linear Shallow-Water Model: Double-Gyre Wind Forcing on a Beta-Plane¶
docs.text: This notebook builds a linear shallow-water model step by step on the Arakawa C-grid using finitevolx. The model simulates wind-driven ocean gyres in a closed rectangular basin -- the simplest configuration that produces the classic double-gyre circulation (an anticyclonic subtropical gyre in the south and a cyclonic subpolar gyre in the north).

docs.title: Governing equations¶
docs.text:
The linearised shallow-water equations on a beta-plane are:

$$\partial_t \eta = -H \, abla \cdot \mathbf{u} + u \, abla^2 \eta$$

$$\partial_t u = -g \,\partial_x \eta + f\,v - r\,u + u \, abla^2 u + F_x$$

$$\partial_t v = -g \,\partial_y \eta - f\,u - r\,v + u \, abla^2 v$$

where:

Symbol Meaning $\eta$ Free-surface anomaly (deviation from mean depth $H$) $u, v$ Zonal and meridional velocity components $H$ Mean fluid depth $g$ Gravitational acceleration $f = f_0 + eta y$ Coriolis parameter on a beta-plane $r$ Linear (Rayleigh) drag coefficient $ u$ Laplacian viscosity / diffusivity $F_x$ Zonal wind body-force acceleration

The wind forcing follows the standard double-gyre pattern:

$$F_x = -A \cos\!\left( rac{2\pi y}{L_y} ight)$$

This produces westward forcing (trade winds) near $y = 0$ and $y = L_y$, and eastward forcing (westerlies) near $y = L_y / 2$. The resulting wind-stress curl drives an anticyclonic (subtropical) gyre in the southern half and a cyclonic (subpolar) gyre in the northern half.

docs.title: 1. C-Grid Variable Placement¶
docs.text:
On the Arakawa C-grid, each prognostic variable lives at a different location within the grid cell:

    X ── V ── X ── V ── X
    |         |         |
    U    T    U    T    U     T = eta (cell centre)
    |         |         |     U = u-velocity (east face)
    X ── V ── X ── V ── X     V = v-velocity (north face)
    |         |         |     X = vorticity (corner)
    U    T    U    T    U
    |         |         |
    X ── V ── X ── V ── X

The staggering ensures that the discrete pressure gradient and Coriolis terms are naturally centred, minimising numerical dispersion.

Array layout: for nx interior T-points in $x$ and ny in $y$, the full array shape is (Ny, Nx) = (ny + 2, nx + 2) -- one ghost cell on each side. The physical interior occupies [1:-1, 1:-1].

docs.title: 3. Physical Parameters¶
docs.text:
We use values representative of a mid-latitude ocean basin on a beta-plane.

Parameter Value Units Meaning $L_x, L_y$ 5.12 x 10^6 m Basin dimensions (~5000 km square) $g$ 9.81 m s$^{-2}$ Gravitational acceleration $H$ 500 m Mean fluid depth (first baroclinic mode equivalent depth) $f_0$ 9.375 x 10$^{-5}$ s$^{-1}$ Reference Coriolis parameter (~40 N) $\beta$ 1.754 x 10$^{-11}$ m$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$ Meridional Coriolis gradient $r$ 5.0 x 10$^{-6}$ s$^{-1}$ Linear drag (damping timescale ~2.3 days) $\nu$ 5.0 x 10$^5$ m$^2$ s$^{-1}$ Laplacian viscosity (smooths grid-scale noise) $A$ 2.0 x 10$^{-7}$ m s$^{-2}$ Peak wind body-force acceleration $\Delta t$ 200 s Time step

docs.title: 4. Initial Conditions and Forcing¶
docs.text: We start from rest ($u = v = 0$) with a small surface perturbation. The Coriolis parameter varies linearly with $y$ (beta-plane), and the zonal wind forcing has the double-gyre cosine profile.

docs.title: 5. Operator Construction¶
docs.text:
finitevolx provides stateless operator modules that know about the grid spacing and stencil layout. We need three operators:

  • Difference2D -- finite differences: diff_x_T_to_U, diff_y_T_to_V, divergence, and laplacian.
  • Interpolation2D -- cross-averaging between staggered locations: T_to_U, T_to_V, V_to_U, U_to_V, U_to_T, V_to_T, X_to_T.
  • Vorticity2D -- relative_vorticity at corner (X) points.

docs.title: 6. Tendency Function¶
docs.text:
The right-hand side (RHS) computes time tendencies for $\eta$, $u$, and $v$. Each line below is annotated with:

  • which equation term it implements
  • the staggered grid location of the result

The key idea: operators move values between staggered locations. For example, diff_op.diff_x_T_to_U differentiates a T-point field and returns the result at U-points.

docs.title: 7. Time Stepping¶
docs.text:
We use Heun's method (also called the modified Euler method or explicit trapezoidal rule). It is a second-order Runge-Kutta scheme:

  1. Predictor (forward Euler): $\tilde{y} = y_n + \Delta t \, f(y_n)$
  2. Corrector (trapezoidal average): $y_{n+1} = y_n + \frac{\Delta t}{2} \bigl[f(y_n) + f(\tilde{y})\bigr]$

This is more stable than forward Euler and only requires two RHS evaluations per step.

For the demo we run a short integration (500 steps = 100,000 s ~ 1.2 days) with no spin-up -- just enough to see the wind forcing begin to drive circulation.

docs.title: 8. Results¶
docs.text:
We plot three diagnostic fields at the final time:

  1. Free-surface anomaly $\eta$ -- shows the pressure pattern
  2. Speed $|\mathbf{u}|$ -- magnitude of the velocity field
  3. Kinetic energy $\tfrac{1}{2}|\mathbf{u}|^2$ -- energy in the flow

Note on boundary slicing: Interpolated/derived fields (speed, KE) use [2:-2, 2:-2] instead of [1:-1, 1:-1] because the first interior row/column is contaminated by ghost-cell averaging (e.g. U_to_T at T-point [1,1] averages u[1,1] and u[1,0] where the ghost value is 0).

docs.title: 9. Full-Resolution Simulation¶
docs.text:
The production run uses a finer grid and long spin-up to reach quasi-steady state. These are the parameters used by the script scripts/swm_linear.py:

# Full-resolution configuration
nx, ny = 64, 64
Lx, Ly = 5.12e6, 5.12e6
gravity = 9.81
mean_depth = 500.0
f0 = 9.375e-5
beta = 1.754e-11
drag = 5.0e-6
viscosity = 5.0e5
wind_acceleration = 2.0e-7
dt = 200.0
spinup_steps = 150_000    # ~347 days silent spin-up
steps = 15_000            # ~35 days of recorded snapshots
snapshot_interval = 1_500  # save every ~3.5 days

Run it with:

uv run python scripts/swm_linear.py

The pre-rendered animation shows the spun-up double-gyre circulation:
